# How sure are you? Say that

"Are we fine for labels?" Mateo asked in the team chat at 16:42. "It should be fine," Diego answered at 16:44.

In June, Mateo, Tolva's co-founder and chief technology officer, read the reply in Montevideo and moved on. Diego was the engineer Tolva had placed in Rotterdam with Veldhaven, its largest client. He had a reason for his "should": that morning he had printed two hundred labels through the new interface at site one, and every one came out readable. He had not tested the printers at Veldhaven's other two distribution centers, sites two and three. He assumed they matched site one's.

They didn't. Sites two and three ran older firmware, and the label work slipped three weeks.

Diego wasn't careless, and he wasn't hiding anything. His reply held a fact he had checked and a guess he hadn't, together inside "should", and Mateo had no way to pull them apart.

## Guesses in plain sight

Behind every claim people act on is how much you know, how you know it and what you haven't checked. This book calls that the claim's size. Leave it out and the listener supplies one. You find out which size they chose when the date passes.

Say the size, and your word becomes something people can build a plan on, guesses included, because they know which parts are guesses.

## The sized claim

The sized claim has three parts.

- **The claim.** One sentence: what is true, or what will happen.
- **The basis.** How you know it, in one of four words, strongest first:
  - **Checked.** I ran it or read the record myself.
  - **Told.** A person, a document or a machine told me.
  - **Reasoned.** I worked it out from things checked or told.
  - **Assumed.** I am taking it as given.
- **The limit.** Where the claim stops, what has not been checked, and what would change it.

Here is Diego's reply at its real size:

"Site one, yes: I printed two hundred labels through the new interface this morning, and every one was readable. Sites two and three, I haven't checked. I'm assuming their printers match site one's. I can test site two on Thursday."

The firmware would still have been old. What would have changed is when Tolva found out, and whether anyone planned on a guess without knowing it was one. Every doubt that hid inside "should" is still there, now attached to two named sites and a Thursday.

This book's bet is that when any draft can sound sure, people will check with the person who can say how sure, and on what.

> **Line to keep:** Put the doubt in the claim, where people can use it.

## From hedge to limit

Naomi is a solo data consultant in Seattle. Veldhaven hired her in March to forecast when each truck would really arrive. Her forecast will feed Tolva's scheduler, which gives each truck a door and a time. By June she had six weeks of Veldhaven's gate logs to score it against. She is growing toward the calibrator: the habit of saying how sure we are, and testing a claim before the team acts on it.

### Practice: one claim at its real size

**Situation.** June. Claire, Veldhaven's vice president of operations, has asked Naomi in writing how the forecast is doing.

**First draft (what a careful consultant writes).** "Early results are encouraging overall, though they may vary somewhat between sites. It's probably too soon to draw firm conclusions, so I'd treat the current numbers as indicative for now."

**What's wrong.** Four hedges and no number. Every phrase protects the writer, and the fact Claire most needs, that site three is far behind, hides inside "may vary somewhat". Nothing here can turn out wrong, so nothing here can be planned on.

**Better.** "Over six weeks of your gate logs, the forecast was within thirty minutes for about eight arrivals in ten at sites one and two. At site three it was about five in ten. I checked each forecast against the log myself. I don't know yet why site three is worse, and none of the six weeks was a peak week, so I can't yet say how it will do in December. The first peak week's logs could move every number here."

**Why it works.** The first two sentences are the claim, the third gives its basis, and the last two are the limit. Naomi got there by asking what each hedge was unsure about. "May vary somewhat" became site three's number, and "probably too soon" became the missing peak week. "Encouraging" and "indicative" named nothing, so she cut them.

> **Research says:** Across eleven studies of advice about forecasts, advisers who said they were "not sure" were rated below confident ones. Advisers who gave a range, a probability or "more likely than" were not marked down, and given a choice, people more often picked the adviser whose advice carried its uncertainty. The advisers were strangers, so carrying this to your own colleagues is the book's reasoning: give the range, and drop the "not sure".

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Open the last status message you sent and label every claim in it with one of the four words, in the margin, for yourself. Then rewrite the claim that matters most as three sentences: the claim, its basis word, and its limit, including what would change it. Read it aloud once. **If you do only one, do this one.** **Done means** a colleague who hears it once can tell you which part you checked yourself and what would change your answer.

## What Claire had to decide

Naomi sent the rewritten report. Claire answered within the hour: "This is clear, and I still can't use it. On Tuesday I approve the go-live plan for all three sites. It has to name the sites where your forecast goes into the scheduler. Can you call me?"

Claire had asked in writing how the forecast was doing, and the report answered that. Her plan asked something else: which sites?

Naomi called and began with the sites. "Sites one and two. Site three, not yet. I'd put the forecast in the plan for the first two, and add site three when I can show you its numbers have caught up."

"Why is site three behind?"

"I don't know yet. What I do know is that it's behind in every one of the six weeks, so it isn't one bad week. I'll have a first answer by the end of the month."

"That I can put in the plan," Claire said.

A sized claim answers a question, and the question that counts is the one the listener has to decide. The listener sketch in *Who is listening* asks for that decision; if you can't name it, ask before you size anything. Then lead with the claim that answers the decision, with its limit in the same breath, and let the basis follow as far as the listener wants.

**Spar with an AI.** Rehearse asking for the decision first.

```text
Play an operations director who must make one decision with an estimate I am about to give you. Keep the decision to yourself unless I ask what it is. If I give the estimate before I ask, tell me once what you still can't decide. Then ask what my answer rests on and what would change it. At the end, tell me which sentence you would plan on, which you would check first, and which words sounded unsure and gave no reason.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Sound sure, or say how sure?

Sound confident, says one piece of advice. A listener who must act needs something to act on, and a speaker who wraps every sentence in "maybe" hands the listener the work of guessing. Its best case is a room that has to decide today, where a speaker who won't commit leaves everyone stuck.

Admit what you don't know, says the other. Nobody is right every time, and when the miss comes, the person who claimed too much pays more for it. In two experiments with mock witnesses, a mistake cost a witness more credibility when that witness had been confident about the very point they got wrong. Its best case is a forecast scored against the record every week, as Naomi's is, where every miss is seen.

The sized claim takes the true half of each. Be firm in your voice and exact in your claim. "About five in ten" can be said as steadily as "yes", and it should be. Give a number only when you have something under it.

## Dates, numbers and "I don't know"

Dates and numbers are claims too. For a date:

`[date], if [the one thing it depends on]. If not, [the other date]. I will know by [when].`

In June, Lucía, Tolva's co-founder and chief executive, filled it in for Veldhaven's chief executive: "Site one goes live on 14 September, if your security review passes in one round. If it needs a second round, the 28th. I'll know by 20 August."

Before you give a date for your own work, find the last job like it and how long it took. That is your basis, reasoned from something that happened.

> **Research says:** In a series of studies, people predicting when they would finish their own tasks were too optimistic, planning forward and setting aside how similar jobs had gone. Asked to connect the new task to those past jobs, they lost the bias, while people forecasting someone else's finish erred the other way. In these studies that link helped; they don't show every job runs late.

For a number, give a range and say what moves it. Once the old firmware was found, Diego's next message to Mateo had both: "Two to four weeks to fix. Four if Veldhaven can't update the printers at both sites in the same week."

"I don't know" is a limit said first. Follow it with what you do know and when you will know more.

## When the claim comes to you

Claims reach you every day without their size, from colleagues and from machines. Use the second-question test from *Start here*, all five, in order: *What is the point? What does it rest on? Where does it stop? What do you want from me? Who answers for it?* The first one without an answer is the next thing to find out.

Run it on Diego's reply. The point is clear: the labels are fine. What does it rest on? No answer, and that was Mateo's next thing to find out. One line would have found it: "Is that all three sites, or site one?"

Now run it on a machine. The week after the call, Naomi asked an assistant, one her contract with Veldhaven allows, to draft her weekly note from her results table. The draft was fluent, and its arithmetic was right: "Across Veldhaven's sites, about seven arrivals in ten land within thirty minutes of the forecast." The point: the forecast mostly works. What it rests on: her own table. Where it stops, and what would show it wrong: the draft doesn't say, so that is where she looked. Seven in ten was the average of all three sites, and site three's five in ten had disappeared inside it. The claim was the wrong size.

Whatever a machine tells you carries the basis word *told*, however fluent it sounds, until you check it. The fifth question has a standing answer: if nobody else answers for a claim, you do, the moment you pass it on. Naomi sent the note with three sites in it.

### Practice: test a claim that reached you

**Your turn (3 minutes).** Take the last summary an assistant drafted for you, or the last status claim a colleague sent. Put it through the second-question test, in order, and stop at the first question it can't answer. **Done means** you have written down the one thing you will check before you forward it.

## Words to use

- **The basis.** "I checked this myself." "I was told this by [who or what], and I haven't checked it." "I worked it out from [what]." "I'm assuming [what]. Nobody has checked it."
- **The limit.** "This covers [what]. It doesn't cover [what] yet." "What would change this is [one thing]."
- **A number.** "Between [low] and [high]. It's [high] if [one thing] happens."
- **"I don't know."** "I don't know yet. What I do know is [what]. I'll know by [when]."
- **When they need one answer.** "If you need one date for your plan, use [the later one]. I'll tell you by [when] if [the earlier one] holds."
- **A claim that reaches you.** "What is that based on?" "Is that checked, or were you told?" "Is that all three sites, or one?" "Who signs off on this before it goes out?"

### Phrases you will hear

- "Back of the envelope": a quick, rough calculation.
- "Off the top of my head": from memory, without checking.
- "Don't quote me on that": I'm not sure, so don't repeat it as fact.

## When it backfires

**On every sentence.** The sized claim is for claims someone will act on. Put a basis word on every line of a status message and the one assumption that matters gets lost among twenty that don't. Size what carries a decision, and say the rest plainly.

**Upward.** A senior person who asked for one date may hear your condition as an excuse. Give the date and its condition in one breath; if they still want one date, give the later one and say when you'll know about the earlier. Don't drop the limit to sound surer. Repeat the condition in writing afterward, so that if the date moves, the record shows what it depended on.

**Against a sure voice.** A sized claim can lose, at first, to someone who simply sounds certain. Researchers tested what happens when that person is shown wrong. A confident manner still helped, unless it was tied to a claim someone could check. Confidence stated in words, then shown wrong, was judged worse than caution.

**Culture and rank.** In some teams, "I haven't checked" said to a senior person sounds like skipping the work; in others, leaving it out sounds like hiding something. Ask how this team wants to hear a limit before the meeting where it matters.

**In a second language.** The four basis words are plain, and may carry your meaning more reliably than *should*, *might* and *could*, whose strength can shift from one speaker to the next. "I checked" is hard to misread.

# With a machine in the room

*On the page: decide before it drafts*

An assistant will hand you a finished message before you have decided what it is for. This part trained you to decide first.

In June, Bianca, Tolva's product manager, pasted a month of requests from Veldhaven's site managers into an assistant Tolva had approved for client work. She asked it for a message to Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, Tolva's largest client. Seconds later she had seventeen requests under five tidy headings. It was the message Bianca used to build by hand, every request forwarded and none chosen, only faster. Claire had one decision to make, and the list never said which. The assistant had no way to know what Tolva's engineers could finish before September. Bianca did. She deleted the list and wrote the point sentence first (what one named person should do, and the one reason):

"Claire should pick one of the two changes her site managers asked for most, because before September we can finish only one of them at site one."

Claire chose the same afternoon.

> **Line to keep:** The less you decide before the draft, the more the draft decides for you.

## Before the draft, and after it

**Before.** Write the point sentence with its limit. Add the listener sketch (what this person knows, has to decide and stands to lose) and the questions they will ask next, in order. Do it on paper or in your own file, and keep that page. Only you know what you mean, and only one question to your listener can check the sketch. When you ask for the draft, give it the page and tell it to ask you for any fact it lacks. If you don't, assume it will guess.

**After.** Put every label it chose through the observable version (what would a recording show?), and check that each assumption you gave it still sounds like one. Any claim you didn't give it is *told*, at best, until you check it. Then put the draft through the second-question test, with the page you kept beside it. The fifth question, *Who answers for it?*, is already settled: you answer for what goes out under your name.

> **Research says:** In one experiment, two-person crews were as likely as people working alone to miss a problem their automated system failed to flag. A review of such studies found this kind of miss in novices and experts, and training alone did not remove it. These studies tested automated aids, not assistants that write, so applying them to drafts is the book's inference, and so is the safeguard of writing your page first.

## Practice: two drafts, one point

**If you do only one, do this one.**

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Pick a message you must send this week that asks someone to decide or act.

1. On paper, write its point sentence with its limit, then the listener sketch, and turn the page over.
2. Give an assistant only your notes and ask it for the message.
3. Write the point its draft chose in one sentence: to whom, asking what, and why.
4. Turn your page back and mark each difference: listener, ask, reason, a dropped limit, an added fact.
5. Ask again with your page, or write the message yourself.

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

**Done means** a colleague can see both points side by side with every difference marked, and the message you send opens with your point sentence.

## When it backfires

Sometimes the draft's point is better than yours. Take it once you can say why and it passes the second-question test; then it is your decision.

When someone senior wants the message in ten minutes, skip the comparison and keep the point sentence. It is the decision you will be asked about.

In a second language, an assistant can help with the English once the point is decided. Then check that the polished English kept your ask and your limits.

## Record again

This part ends where the book began: sixty seconds, out loud, on what you are working on and why it matters. Write your point sentence first, then put the paper away and record. No assistant can say this minute for you.

Score it as you scored your first two takes:

1. **Sentences before the point.** How many came before the first one that says why the work matters? If none does, write "never".
2. **Hedges with no basis.** Each *probably*, *I think*, *should* or *hopefully* with no reason after it.
3. **One example.** One case that shows why it matters: a person, a number or a thing that happened. Background doesn't count.
4. **The ending.** An ask or a next step: yes or no.
5. **Said back.** One listener hears it once and writes your point in one sentence; an assistant given the transcript can stand in. Compare their sentence with your point sentence.

The filler count is optional; pauses, restarts and searching for a word never count, and if you stutter, work in a second language or pause to think, skip it. You can also write for three minutes without stopping, on the same prompt, and run the same checks. Put the results beside your two takes from *Start here*: your before and after, not anyone's norm.

*Safe practice: record only yourself, or others only with their consent and within your employer's rules.*

# Part 2. Clear voice

---

# Say less

Sarnik's operations director asked his question in the first minute of the video call, and Naomi answered it in the fifth.

The question was "What does it cost?" Naomi is a data consultant who works alone from Seattle. In March, Veldhaven, the Rotterdam food wholesaler, hired her to predict when trucks would reach its three warehouses. Early on this June morning, already afternoon in Lyon, she was offering the same kind of forecast to Sarnik, which distributes chilled and frozen food from four warehouses near Lyon. Its operations director had her one-page description open, and a budget that had just been cut.

"Good question," Naomi said. "Before the number, let me explain what goes into it, because otherwise it will sound like a lot."

She explained that every warehouse needed six weeks of its own gate logs before she trusted a forecast there. Then she said it again: "So basically, it's not one model for everyone." She described how she checked each forecast against the log herself, every week. She said what a truck that arrived an hour before or after its slot cost a dock, and what larger firms charged for less. She said she had no office and no staff, so none of that was in her price. "What I mean is," she said, reaching the same point a third time, "your warehouse gets its own forecast." Once more she said she knew the number would sound like a lot.

Four minutes after his question, she said it: "So it would be three thousand euros a month per warehouse."

The line went quiet. She could hear him typing. She filled the silence: "Roughly. But I'm flexible, so tell me what works for your budget."

The typing stopped. "Flexible how much?"

## A defense nobody asked for

Of everything Naomi said in four minutes, the director kept one word, and it came in her last sentence.

Most of those sentences would have served her well later, once he asked how the forecast worked. Said before the number, they became a defense, and a defense told him there was something to defend. The two warnings agreed with a complaint he had not made. "Roughly" turned a price she sets into a guess. And "tell me what works for your budget" handed him the job of pricing her work. Leaving the price open sounded generous, and it left him to finish her proposal.

The four minutes also pushed out the one fact he most needed. At the one cold warehouse Naomi had measured, her forecast was less accurate than at the others, and she did not yet know why. Every one of Sarnik's warehouses is cold.

## Where to stop

Say your point once, at the size the facts allow, and then stop. The end comes when the first four questions of the second-question test have their answers: *What is the point? What does it rest on? Where does it stop? What do you want from me?* Aloud, that is about fifty words, a target this book sets. Any sentence after your ask repeats an answer or argues with one. Of all the skills in this book, this is the easiest to start, because you start it by deleting.

Naomi's answers fit on four lines:

- **The point.** Three thousand euros a month per warehouse, starting with one.
- **What it rests on.** A check he can run on his own gate logs.
- **Where it stops.** The one cold warehouse she has measured, where it is less accurate.
- **What she wants.** A start date.

The first line comes from her point sentence, built as in *Know what you think*. "The director should start with one warehouse at three thousand euros a month, because his own logs will show him within a month whether it works." When the point is a price, the price goes in the sentence.

"Roughly" is gone from the four lines, because a price you set is a decision, and a decision has nothing to size. The cold-warehouse limit is in, because it rests on her own measurements and he can't decide without it. That is the sized claim from *How sure are you? Say that*, used for cutting: a hedge stays only when it has a basis.

In the first minute, she could have said: "It's three thousand euros a month per warehouse. I'd start with one: in the first month, your own gate logs show you how often it was within thirty minutes, before you pay for a second month. At the one cold warehouse I've measured, it's less accurate, and I don't know why yet. When could we start?"

> **Line to keep:** Stopping tells the listener you meant it.

## Leave out the apology and the repeat

An apology in front of your point tells the listener how you expect it to be heard. "I know this will sound like a lot" asks them to treat the number as a problem before they have weighed it. Save apologies for real faults; *The hard conversation* covers how to make one.

Then the repeat. Naomi made her per-warehouse point three times without being asked, and the second and third each opened with a filler: "So basically," "What I mean is." A second try is fair when the first one missed, as long as it is shorter and different. Before a third, stop and ask which part didn't arrive, and say only that part.

Fillers are saying more at the smallest scale: words that add nothing, such as *um* and *basically*. As in *Start here*, the count is optional. If you want fewer, start with those that open a repeat, like Naomi's "So basically": catch one and you catch the repeat behind it.

| Instead of | Say | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "Three thousand. Roughly." | "Three thousand." | A hedge on a number you set makes it sound open |
| "So basically, what I mean is..." | "Which part should I say again?" | A question shows you where the gap is |
| "There are a few options, each with trade-offs, so it depends, but..." | "I recommend the second option." | The trade-offs are your answer to their "Why?" |

## The pause you chose

Decide before you speak that your ask will be your last sentence, then wait after it until the other person replies.

Naomi got that pause after her number and filled it. The quiet after "three thousand euros a month per warehouse" was the director typing the number into his budget sheet. To her it sounded like a verdict, so she ended it with "roughly" and an open offer.

For the listener, a quiet like that may be working time: the number against the budget, and against what they will say when someone asks about it. Leave them that time.

> **From practice:** Make your ask the last line of your notes, written as a question. Your notes then end where your answer should, and the question hands the turn to the other person.

## Practice: the rate, written once

**Situation.** Sarnik's operations director had asked "Flexible how much?", and Naomi had promised him a figure in writing that evening.

**First draft (what a careful consultant writes).**
"Thank you for your time today, and sorry again for the long answer. Before I confirm a figure, I'd like to explain a little more about how the forecast is built, as I realize the number may seem high at first. Each warehouse needs its own fitting, so I start with six weeks of your gate logs, and I check every forecast against the log myself. As a one-person business, I have no overhead to pass on. All in, the cost would be around three thousand euros a month per warehouse, but I'm happy to discuss whatever works for your budget."

**What's wrong.** It is the call again, on paper: two apologies in front, the defense before the answer, a hedge on her own price and an open offer to finish. It still has no limit and no date, and it never answers his question.

**Better.**
"The forecast is three thousand euros a month per warehouse. Where I can be flexible is the start: one warehouse, for three months. In the first month I fit it to six weeks of your gate logs, and you see how often it was within thirty minutes before paying for a second month. It is less accurate at the one cold warehouse I've measured, for reasons I don't know yet; your first month will show whether that holds for you. Can we start on 1 July?"

She sent it that night. His reply came the next morning: "One warehouse from 1 July. Who on my team do you need in the first month?"

**For Veldhaven's finance lead.** The same week, Naomi sent the same rate to Veldhaven. Its finance lead approves her next contract; Claire, who runs operations there, decides when site three joins.

"From July to September, keeping the forecast running at sites one and two is three thousand euros a month per site, eighteen thousand euros for the quarter. Claire's go-live plan includes it at both sites. Site three joins at the same rate once its numbers catch up; Claire will decide when, from my weekly note. Could you approve the eighteen thousand by 30 June, when my current contract ends?"

**Why it works.** Each message answers the first four questions once, then stops. The listener sketch from *Who is listening* shows why they differ. The director decides whether to try the forecast at all, so he gets the rate first and a start date last. The finance lead decides how much to approve and for how long, so that message opens with the total and the months. The message to Sarnik answers "Flexible how much?" by moving the flexibility from the price to the start.

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Take a message you must send this week that carries a price or a date. Draft it, then mark the four answers in it, one sentence each, and delete everything before the first and after the last. If one is missing, *Words to use* below gives you a start. Then look for an apology in front of the number, a hedge on a number you set and an open offer at the end. **Done means** a colleague who reads only your first sentence can tell you the number and what it covers, and nothing follows your ask.

## Practice: hold the stop

**If you do only one, do this one.**

**Timed drill (30 seconds).** Ask a colleague to put to you the question your work gets most often: what it costs, when it will be ready, or what you recommend. Give your answers in 30 seconds or less, then stop; the silence after them is not timed. Constraint: the number, the date or the recommendation goes in your first sentence. Run three rounds. In each, your colleague makes one of these moves, in an order you don't know:

1. Say nothing after your ask, for as long as they like. Wait until they speak.
2. Cut in once before you finish: "That's more (or later) than we planned." Answer in one sentence, finish, and stop.
3. Wait until you stop, then say: "Sorry, I don't follow." Ask which part, and say only that part again.

**Untimed form.** Write your answers and a one-sentence reply to each move, then read it all aloud once.

**Done means** your colleague can repeat your number and its one reason, and you said nothing after your ask until they spoke.

## Words to use

- **To give the price.** "It's [amount] a month for [what it covers]." "The rate is the same for every customer." (Only if it is.)
- **To give what it rests on.** "You'll see [the result they can check] before you pay for [the next step]."
- **To give the limit.** "What I can't promise yet is [the limit]."
- **To ask.** "Can we start on [date]?" "Could you approve it by [date]?"
- **When they push back.** "I understand it's more than you planned. The rate stays the same, and the start can be smaller."
- **When they don't follow.** "Is it the price that's unclear, or what it covers?"
- **To take back a "roughly" or an open offer.** "Let me correct one thing I said earlier: [the correction]."

### Phrases you will hear

- "That's a big number." The price surprised them. It is not yet a no.
- "Walk me through the number." They want the reasons now.
- "Is there any wiggle room?" They are asking whether the price can move.

## When it backfires

**When they ask for the reasons.** Then the reasons are the answer: give them in order, and stop when the questions do. Most of Naomi's reasons were answers to questions he had not asked yet; they did harm only because they came first.

**When the other person holds the power.** A buyer with other options, or a client who can end your contract, may hear a bare number as abrupt. Put the warmth around the number and keep the number itself bare: no apology, no "roughly". If they push, hold the rate and the stop: one sentence, then quiet.

**When money comes up another way.** In some companies nobody names a price until the work is agreed; in others the first price is only a starting point. Ask someone who works there how prices are usually raised. If they expect yours to move, say once that it is the same for every customer, but only if it is.

**When you cut too much.** Cutting the limit to sound sure is saying less of the wrong thing: where it stops is one of your answers. And with someone thinking aloud, one clipped line per question can sound unwilling. Think aloud with them: give the point, then your reasons as their questions come.

**When the silence becomes pressure.** Held to make the other person uncomfortable, the pause you chose becomes a tactic. The check is whether you could say aloud what you are doing: "I'll stop there so you can think." If someone uses silence on you, your number was complete when you stopped. A silence before you answer "Is that your best price?" is different: it can sound as if the price is still moving, so answer at once. *Thinking on your feet* covers the pause before an answer.

**In a second language.** A short sentence leaves less to go wrong when you are nervous, so write the number sentence before the call and say it as written. Leave out the apology for your English. It is one more apology in front.

# Easy to hear

Fifteen or fifty?

Nobody asked it at Tolva's stand-up on a Tuesday early in June. Two days later a test answered it, with a door that stood empty for forty minutes.

Tyler, the delivery lead, runs Tolva's stand-ups, planning and retrospectives. English is one of the languages he grew up with. He is the fastest speaker on the call, and nobody has ever told him so.

That Tuesday he passed on a request from the manager of site one, the first of Veldhaven's three warehouses due to go live with Tolva's dock scheduler, in September. "They want a late truck to lose its slot after fifteen minutes, so let's set that before Thursday's replay." An engineer in Montevideo heard fifty and typed it into the test configuration.

On Thursday the team replayed a busy morning at site one on the test copy of Veldhaven's warehouse system. Diego, the engineer Tolva placed in Rotterdam, reported back in the team channel. "Door nine has been empty for forty minutes, held for a late truck, while two trucks that arrived on time are waiting. The configuration says fifty minutes. Is that what site one asked for?"

At Friday's stand-up the engineer said, "Tyler said fifty." Tyler said, "I said fifteen." Both were sure. "It doesn't matter who said what," Tyler said. "We set fifteen and run it again on Monday." He moved to the next item.

It was a generous thing to say, and it settled nothing: the team never decided how the next number would travel from a site manager to the configuration. Tyler is growing toward the problem-solver, one of the six thinker types: the habit of taking a mess with people in it to a decision that lasts.

## Tyler's sheet

Tyler couldn't prove what he had said on Tuesday. He could find out which words his calls were losing. For two weeks he wrote down every word someone asked to hear again, and every number or name someone acted on in the wrong version. Most were his own. One was Diego's: a sentence about site two's door list that Bianca, Tolva's product manager, asked him to repeat. By the third week of June Tyler had a page, one line per habit, each in his team's own words:

| Said | Came back as | The habit |
|---|---|---|
| "after fifteen minutes" | "fifty" | Numbers and names at half speed, then another way |
| "can't send it before Friday" | "Can or can't?" | Finish the ends of words |
| "By six, forty trucks" | "Six-forty?" | Pause where a comma would be |
| "The replay moves to Monday" | "What moves?" | Stress the one word that carries the point |
| "so we test on Thursday" | "Test when?" | Breathe before the sentence that matters |
| "Morning, Tyler here, quick one" | "You cut out at the start" | Slow the first sentence |

Half speed is the pace this book sets for numbers and names. The first line is Tuesday's sentence, so start there.

### Practice: one number, heard the first time

**Situation.** Tuesday's stand-up. Tyler passes on site one's rule for late trucks before Thursday's replay.

**First draft (what a fluent speaker says at full speed).** "They want a late truck to lose its slot after fifteen minutes, so let's set that before Thursday's replay."

**What's wrong.** Every word goes at the same speed, so nothing tells the listener which one to keep. The number sits in the middle, just before "minutes". Said alone, "fifteen" has its weight on "-teen". Before another stressed word, the weight can move to "fif-", and "fifty" has its weight there too. The final "n" that would still tell them apart is a quiet sound at the end of a word, and quiet sounds are the easiest to lose. And the number exists only in the air.

**Better.** "One rule from site one, for Thursday's replay. A late truck loses its slot after fifteen minutes. That's one-five. I'll put it in the chat." Pause and breathe after "replay". Say the number at half speed, with the weight on "-teen" and the "n" finished.

**Why it works.** The first sentence says what is coming before it comes. The rule gets a short sentence of its own, and the weight stays on "-teen" even before "minutes". Said another way, as "one-five", the number can't be heard as fifty. The chat holds it for anyone whose line dropped.

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Take one sentence with a number from tomorrow's update and fit it to this pattern: `[the number, in a short sentence]. That's [the same number another way]. [Where it is written].` The last three sentences of the better version fill it in. Say yours aloud three times, slowing down only for the number. **Done means** a colleague who hears it once writes the number down correctly.

## Six drills, five minutes

Each line has a drill of its own. They are optional, and together they take five minutes, a target this book sets. Tyler did all six before every stand-up; your own sheet, below, drills one line a week:

- **Fifteen (one minute).** Count from thirteen to nineteen with the weight on "-teen" and every final "n" finished, then the tens, thirty to ninety, with the weight up front. Take three numbers from your week, a door, a version, a price, and say each at half speed, then another way. Say a name the listener hasn't met at half speed. Your own name is the word you have said most often and your listener has heard least.
- **Can't (one minute).** Say pairs from your week, finishing the last sound of every word: "We can test Thursday." "We can't test Thursday." "We test the feed." "We tested the feed." Each pair differs at the end of a word. When a "not" decides something, don't trust it to one letter: say "cannot", or say what is true: "The door list comes on Friday at the earliest."
- **Six, forty (thirty seconds).** Read aloud: "By six, forty trucks." "By six-forty, four trucks." Pause at the comma long enough to breathe. Then mark the commas in tomorrow's notes, above all where two numbers meet.
- **Monday (one minute).** Say "The replay moves to Monday" three times, with the weight on "replay", then on "moves", then on "Monday". Each weight answers a different question. The listener who asked "What moves?" didn't know what was moving, so "replay" was the news; for someone who knew, it would have been "Monday". Before a call, underline the one word in each important sentence that is new to the listener, and give it the weight.
- **Thursday (one minute).** Find the sentence in tomorrow's update that carries the decision. Breathe in before it starts, not halfway through, and say it on that breath with the last word as strong as the first. If it won't fit on one breath, make it two sentences.
- **The first sentence (thirty seconds).** Say tomorrow's first sentence at half your usual speed, then at full speed, then somewhere between, and keep that one. Make it short: who is speaking and what is coming. Someone may still be unmuting.

None of the six says to slow everything down. Slow down where a lost word would cost the most: the first sentence, a number, a name, the word that carries the point. Everywhere else, your own pace is fine. Slow every word, and the ones that matter stop standing out.

At the last stand-up in June, Tyler passed on site two's version of the rule: "Site two wants thirty minutes. Three-zero. It's in the chat." Nobody had to ask.

## The one person who never hears it

On Tuesday Tyler said what he meant, and the engineer typed what they heard. Tolva's stand-up is a video call, at ten in the morning in Montevideo and three in the afternoon in Rotterdam, and everyone joins from their own screen. A video call is harder on words than a room is: sound arrives late and thinned, faces are small or missing, and someone may be unmuting as you start. A listener who loses a word may not stop you, because it is easier to fill the gap with the likeliest word and keep listening. Fifty was a likely word. So was fifteen. And the speaker is the one person who never hears the mistake: Tyler heard himself say fifteen.

Neither side catches the mistake as it happens, so the speaker has to prevent it. Being easy to hear is a handful of physical habits, used on the words someone will act on. They are small enough to train in five minutes a day, and they work with the accent you have. You can start before tomorrow's first call.

> **Line to keep:** Every word you rush, someone at the other end has to rebuild.

### Practice: your own sheet

**If you do only one, do this one.** It takes ten minutes today and five a day after that.

1. Write down the last words someone asked you to repeat, or acted on wrongly: numbers, names, dates, a "not", a term your team shortens. Then play one of your recordings from *Start here* to a colleague, and add every word they had to guess.
2. Give each word its habit from Tyler's sheet, and keep one line per habit.
3. Write each line as a sentence you will really say this month.
4. Each day before your first call, read the sheet aloud once (a minute), drill this week's line (three minutes) and say that call's first sentence (a minute). Change the line each week, and add a word whenever someone says "sorry?"
5. Once a week, record the sheet. Listen once for pace, once for a pause where each comma is, and once for whether every word can be heard. Record again the one sentence that didn't come through.

*Safe practice: record only yourself, or others only with their consent and within your employer's rules.*

**Done means** a colleague who hears your sheet's sentences once writes down every number, name and date in them correctly.

## Practice: sixty seconds, interrupted

**Timed drill (60 seconds).** Say your next update live to a colleague, who interrupts once, whenever they choose, with "Sorry, which number?" Constraint: you may not say any number the same way twice. Saying the same words louder only repeats the puzzle. Answer in another form, then carry on from where you stopped, not from the beginning.

**Written form.** Before your next call, write another form beside every number, name and date in your notes, and use it the first time anyone asks.

**Done means** your colleague writes down every number and name in your update correctly, including the one they asked about.

## Words to use

- **A number someone will act on.** "Fifteen minutes. That's one-five." "It's in the chat now."
- **A date.** "[day] [month name], a [weekday]." Use the month's name, because the order of day and month in figures depends on where your listener works.
- **A time, across time zones.** "[time], [city] time."
- **A version.** "[version], that's [the digits one by one]."
- **A letter that sounds like another.** "[letter] as in [word]." Use the same word every time.
- **A "not" that decides something.** "We cannot test on Thursday. The earliest is Friday."
- **The first sentence.** "[Name] here. One change to [what]."
- **A name.** "My name is [name]. I'll type it in the chat." "Could you spell that for me?"
- **When you didn't hear.** "Sorry, fifteen or fifty?" "Was that 'can' or 'cannot'?" "I missed the end of that sentence. Could you say it again?"
- **When someone asks again, or repeats it wrong.** "Let me say it another way: [the other form]. I'll type it now."

### Phrases you will hear

- "You're breaking up." Your sound is cutting out.
- "I didn't catch that." I didn't hear it.
- "I lost you there." Either your sound dropped or they lost the thread: ask which.
- "Loud and clear." I can hear you well.
- "A couple of days." Two days, or a few: ask for a date.
- "Half eight." In some varieties of English, half past eight. Someone translating word for word from another language may mean half past seven. Say "eight thirty".

## When it backfires

**Overuse.** Give every figure twice and you sound like someone reading out a phone number, and the listener may hear that you doubt them. Keep the second form for numbers someone will act on, and drop it once they say "got it".

**When they hold the power.** Someone senior and in a hurry may hear half speed as hesitation. Keep it for the number and the name, and say the rest at your normal pace. If a senior person repeats your number wrong, it is tempting to let it pass. Correct it at once: say it another way, and type it. A number needs no apology.

**Where asking feels rude.** In some teams people would rather guess than ask a colleague to say something again. Don't wait to be asked. The second form and the chat do the asking for them.

**When the line fails.** No habit survives a connection that drops every third word. After the second "You're breaking up", stop and type, or call back. Notes an assistant writes from a call transcript hold only what the transcript caught, so check their numbers before anyone acts on them.

**In a second language.** Start with the numbers line: it uses only sounds you already make. The stress drill may feel strange if your first language spreads its weight more evenly; stress only the one word that carries the point. If "can" and "can't" are hard to tell apart in your own mouth or ear, say "cannot" whenever it decides something. The drills never ask you to lose your accent; they ask whether a word arrived.

**If you stutter.** Nothing here asks you to be fluent. Skip any timing, and judge a take only on whether each number and name arrived.

# Voice, body and camera

Diego has just asked for the paper plan when Claire's face changes. Her eyebrows pull together and her mouth goes flat. Her eyes leave the camera, move to something on her left and stay there.

It is June. Diego works for Tolva, a software company in Montevideo. Tolva has placed him in Rotterdam with its largest client, the food wholesaler Veldhaven. Tolva's scheduler, which sends each arriving truck to a door, is due to go live at Veldhaven's site one on 14 September. Claire, who runs operations at all three of Veldhaven's distribution centers, has joined the call from site three, the cold store. On his laptop her face fills a window smaller than his hand. He can't see her hands, or whatever her eyes have gone to.

His request is small, and it costs her something. For the first two weeks after go-live, he wants her planners to keep printing the old paper plan every evening. If the scheduler stops in the night, the dock supervisors will still know where each truck goes.

He reads her face in under a second: no.

So he argues with it. "I know it's extra work for your planners," he says, leaning toward the lens. "But the first nights are when a new system is most likely to stop. If it stops at three in the morning, your supervisors need a plan in their hands, not a phone number in Montevideo." His voice has climbed and quickened. Between sentences his eyes drop to his notes.

"Diego." Claire is looking at the camera again. "Sorry. That was an alarm from one of the cold rooms here. Someone is going to check it." She pauses. "I haven't said no. Two weeks is fine. One of the planners is on leave the week of the 14th, so put it in writing for the site manager, with the day it stops."

He has spent his best argument on an objection nobody made. He has also told her, without meaning to, that he expected a refusal.

## The no that nobody said

Everything Diego saw was there. Claire's eyebrows did come down, and her eyes did leave the camera. The no was his. He took one change in one face, turned it into her answer and argued with the answer. In a window that size, a frown at an alarm and a frown at a request look the same.

A change in someone's face tells you that something happened on their side, and very little about what. Let it tell you which sentence to ask about, then ask in words, about the work. Your own face, voice and camera get read the same way, in a room or on a call. Most of what they send is yours to set, and the rest you can put words beside. Get this right and you stop arguing with faces.

Two tools from Part I do the reading. The observable version, from *The exact word*, asks what a recording would show: eyebrows down, eyes to the left for a few seconds, no words. Could two people who disagree about what the frown meant agree that this happened? Easily. Could they agree that Claire said no? They couldn't, because she hadn't.

The sized claim, from *How sure are you? Say that*, asks what a reading rests on. A face reaches you the way a message does, as something told. The frown told Diego that something was going on at Claire's end. What it was, the frown couldn't say, so Diego supplied it himself, and his basis word was *assumed*. The limit of any reading is everything else a frown can mean. Here it was an alarm on another screen. It might also be a picture running a moment behind the sound, arithmetic, glare from a window or a long sentence in a second language. Several signals that agree give you more to reason from, and still only a reading.

Then trade the reading for the one source that has the answer: her words. Her answer is still *told*, but by the only person who knows. Finish what you planned to say, at the size you planned it, and stop talking. Ask one question about what you just asked for, rather than about their face: "Does two weeks cause a problem for your planners?" She can answer that in a sentence. "You look concerned" asks a client's vice president to explain her face, and whatever is behind it, to a supplier.

> **Line to keep:** Only words can tell you what a face meant.

## The other side of the screen

When Claire looked back from her other screen, Diego was leaning into his camera, talking faster about trouble at three in the morning, his eyes dropping away from hers. She read him the way he had read her. That week she asked Lucía, Tolva's co-founder and chief executive, whether Diego expected the scheduler to fail in its first nights. Lucía passed the question on, and Diego wrote to Claire: "On the call I argued as if you had said no, and you hadn't. Nothing in our tests says the scheduler will stop. I want the paper plan so that if it does, nobody on the dock has to guess." Claire replied in one line, copied to site one's manager: "Agreed. Send her the plan with the day it stops."

However your words were prepared, the face and voice that carry them arrive live. None of this means your face matters more than your words.

> **Myth check:** The claim that 93 percent of a message lies outside the words is usually traced to two 1967 studies in which people judged the attitude behind one spoken word. Tone outweighed the word, a negative tone turned a positive word negative, and a face counted about one and a half times as much as a voice of matched strength. Nobody explained a plan or argued a case, so this book's advice is to let words carry the content, and keep your tone from contradicting them.

Each of your signals can look like something you didn't mean:

- **Where you look.** In a room, people can see what you are looking at; on a call, they see only that you have looked away. On a laptop the lens sits above the screen, so watching their faces makes you look slightly down, and looking into the lens means you can't see them. Neither is wrong. One way to choose: the lens for the sentence you most need them to take in, their faces while they answer.
- **In a room.** Sit or stand where the person who decides can see your face without turning when you reach the ask. Turning toward whoever is speaking can look like listening. A laptop open while they talk can look like email: close it, or say what it's for.
- **Your face while you read or work something out.** It can look like Claire's frown, aimed at whoever is speaking. You don't need to change it. When it matters, put words beside it. Claire did, but only after Diego had argued.
- **Your voice at the ask.** Diego's climbed and sped up the moment he thought he had to defend his request. Keep the ask, and whatever follows it, at the pace of the sentence before it. A sentence that rises at the end can sound like a question to some listeners. If yours does and you mean a request, say so in words: "That's what I'm asking for."
- **When you're muted.** Your face is all the speaker has. A nod, or unmuting to say "Go on," tells them you are still with them.

> **From practice:** Before a call that matters, drag the window of the person who decides to the top of your screen, as close to the camera as it will go. Looking at them and looking into the lens become almost the same thing.

## Practice: hold the claim when the face changes

**Situation.** A video call. You lead the move of a client's order history to a new system, and their finance director has asked when it will be finished. At the words "second weekend", her eyebrows come down and she looks off to one side.

**First draft (once the face changes).**
"It needs a second weekend. Well, possibly. It depends a bit on the invoices, and we could maybe run them on a weeknight instead, so it might not come to that."

**What's wrong.** Nothing about the move changed between the first sentence and the second. Her face did. The claim shrank to fit a guess about a frown: "possibly", "maybe" and a weeknight the engineer doesn't believe in. If she was only checking her calendar, she now has a weaker answer and a promise nobody can keep.

**Better.**
"It needs a second weekend. The first one moved every order. The invoices are the rest, and they can't move while your month-end close is running. They're smaller than the orders, so one weekend after the close should finish them. Before I go on: does that weekend cause a problem on your side?"

**Why it works.** The claim keeps the size the facts give it, with its reason attached. The question is about the work, so whatever the frown meant can arrive in words, whether it was her calendar or the cost. She never has to explain her face.

**Your turn (5 minutes, with a colleague).** Take something you will ask for this week, such as more time, a budget or a decision. Say it to a colleague, on a call or across a desk. Ask them to change their face once, at a moment you don't know in advance: for example, a frown or a glance at a phone. When it happens, finish what you planned to say, stop, and ask one question about the work. **Done means** your colleague can say your claim was the same size after their face changed as before, and could answer your question in one sentence.

**If you do only one, do this one.**

**Written form.** Write the answer. Under the sentence that asks for something, write what you would add if the listener frowned there. If it changes the size of the claim, cross it out and write a question about the work.

**Mistakes and fixes.**

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Arguing with a face | Stop and ask about the work |
| A claim shrunk to fit a frown | Keep its size and its reason |
| "You look concerned" | A question about what you asked for |
| A nod written down as a yes | Get the yes in words |

## Practice: the frame at your ask

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Sit or stand where you usually join calls or present. Record thirty seconds of a request you will make this week, with its reason. Play it to the moment you make the request and pause there. In one line, write what a stranger would read in that frame: eyes that left the screen while you thought, a frown as you asked. Then play the request itself once more and listen for a single thing: did your voice climb or speed up at the ask, compared with the sentence before it? Change one thing and record once more. **Done means** someone shown both takes can point to what changed.

**Without recording.** On your next call, look at your own window once while someone else is talking, and write down what a stranger would read in it.

*Safe practice: record only yourself, or others only with their consent and within your employer's rules.*

## Words to use

- **When a face changes at your ask.** "Before I go on: does [the ask] cause a problem on your side?" "What would you need to know before you decide?"
- **When your own face or eyes could be misread.** "I'm looking at your message on my other screen." "I'm writing that down." "Sorry, a message just came in. Please go on."
- **When you can't see faces.** "I can't see anyone, so I'll ask each of you: [name], does [date] work?" "Your picture froze just then. Does [the ask] work for you?"
- **To turn a nod into a decision.** "Can I write that down as a yes to [the ask]?"

### Phrases you will hear

- "That raised a few eyebrows": it surprised people, or made them doubt it.
- "I can't read her": I can't tell what she thinks.
- "She's putting on a brave face": she looks calm, but may not feel calm.
- "He gave me a look": his face showed he didn't like something, without a word.

## When it backfires

**When the frown is about you.** Sometimes it follows a remark that could hurt, such as a joke about their old system. Then a question about the work sounds as if you didn't notice. Repair the remark first: "That came out wrong. What I meant was [what you meant]." If it wasn't about you, the repair cost one sentence.

**Overuse.** A question after every flicker can sound unsure, and it breaks into their thinking. Keep it for a face that changes at a sentence that asks something of them.

**Who holds the power.** A client or a boss may move on before you can ask, so ask afterward, in a message about the work. Expect your own face to be read closely too, and put words beside it early: "I'm working out the order of the steps." With a peer you know well, naming what you saw can be quicker: "You frowned when I said Thursday. Is that a problem?" When the power is yours, your frown can shrink someone's estimate the way the practice's first draft shrank. Say what it means.

**Culture and habit.** How much eye contact or nodding feels polite differs between people and teams, and nobody's habit is the correct one. In some teams a nod means "I'm following", not "I agree". Get the decision in words before you write it down.

**Cameras off.** A dark window says nothing about attention. The connection may be weak, or the room shared. Ask for cameras only when faces would change what happens, and say why. Otherwise, ask each person by name: silence from a dark window is easy to write down as a yes.

**Looking away.** Some people think better without a face in front of them, or find holding someone's gaze tiring. Don't read honesty into where anyone's eyes go.

**In a second language.** Following a long sentence in English can look like disagreeing, on their face and on yours. Expect some frowns to mean "working", and when the frown is yours, say what it means: "I understand so far. I'm just checking the numbers."

---

# Steady under pressure

What do you do in the last ten minutes before a call you dread?

Lucía had three files open and was reaching for a fourth. In ten minutes, at eleven in Montevideo and four in the afternoon in Rotterdam, Veldhaven's chief executive would call. He had asked for twenty minutes on a Thursday in June to hear the date from her, not from a summary.

She is co-founder and chief executive of Tolva, a company of fourteen people in Montevideo whose scheduler tells each arriving truck which warehouse door to use. Tolva's largest client, Veldhaven, is a food wholesaler with three distribution centers run from Rotterdam. The first of them, site one, was due to go live in September.

The files were the contract, her notes from the last board call and Mateo's design note from May. Mateo, her co-founder and Tolva's chief technology officer, had written there what the date rested on. She closed all three. Anything new she read now, she would have no time to fit in.

She took a yellow note and wrote two lines on it:

"He should plan site one for September, because either result of his security review still lands in that month."

"Not the 14th without the 'if': the review decides it."

She stuck it under her camera, where reading it would look like looking at him. On her pad, for herself only, she wrote one more line: "This call decides what he tells his board about site one. It does not decide whether Veldhaven stays."

Then she stood at the window and said her first sentence aloud, twice. The first time it came out fast. The second time it came out whole. She also said aloud her answer to the push she expected. If he wanted the 14th with no condition, he would get the 28th as the date and the 14th as a chance. At a minute to eleven she drank some water, let one slow breath out and joined.

He came straight to it. "Claire tells me you have a date for me."

"Site one goes live on 14 September, if your security review passes in one round. If it needs a second round, the 28th. I'll know by 20 August."

"I can't take an 'if' to my board. Is it the 14th?"

The 14th was one word away, and saying it would end the silence. Her eyes went to the second line under the camera.

"Then take the 28th to your board," Lucía said. "If the review passes in one round, you get two weeks back, and you'll hear it from me first."

"In May your company told Claire the integration was on track," he said, "and nobody on your side could tell her what the date depended on. Why should my board believe this one?"

It was a fair question, and it stung. The May summary had been Lucía's, and Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, had waited a day for the answer to what the date depended on. Lucía heard herself begin, "That summary went out before Mateo had...", and the rest of the sentence was gone. For two seconds, perhaps three, she said nothing. Then she looked at the first line of the note.

"You're right about May," she said. "I sent that summary before I knew what the date rested on. This time I know. It rests mostly on your security review, and either result still gives you site one in September."

"And the exact day?"

"On 20 August. I'll call you myself."

"Then my board hears September, and I hear the day on the twentieth. I'll hold you to that."

The call took eleven of his twenty minutes, and that afternoon she sent him the date in writing, condition included. He had no way to check the review that day. What he could check was whether her date changed when he pushed, and it did not. Choosing a path while nobody knows the answer, and saying what would change it, is the strategist's habit, the thinker type Lucía is growing toward.

## Decide before anyone pushes

A steady call is mostly decided before it starts. Lucía lost no facts that morning. She nearly lost the size of her claim, and for a few seconds her place. Those were the two things the push went after, and you can protect both while nobody is pushing. In the last ten minutes, write down the sentence you will come back to, the one thing you will not agree to, and what the call can and cannot decide. Then say your first sentence, the answer they came to hear, aloud until it comes out whole. Ten minutes is a target this book sets: enough for three lines and one sentence said twice.

The point sentence, from *Know what you think*, is the way back when you lose the thread, the moment your next sentence is simply gone. The second line, what you will not agree to, is a decision made while you are calm, so that when the push comes there is nothing left to decide. The stakes line gives the call what a sized claim has in *How sure are you? Say that*, a limit: what the call decides, and where that stops. Lucía feared the call could cost Tolva its largest client. Written down, the stakes shrank to what one man would tell his board about one site.

None of this will steady your hands, and it doesn't need to. A voice that shakes can still carry a sentence it has already said twice. And if your attention keeps running to the worst version of the call, three short lines can give it somewhere better to go.

> **Line to keep:** Write it down while you are calm, and you can find it again when you are not.

## Practice: your last ten minutes

Run these steps before your next hard moment this week. It might be a price you must say aloud, a date someone will lean on, a no to someone senior or a review of your own design. **If you do only one, do this one.**

1. Close everything you were reading. There is no time left to fit anything new in.
2. Write your point sentence where your eyes will be during the call: on a note under the camera, or at the top of the page in front of you.
3. Under it, write the one thing you will not agree to, and why.
4. For yourself, one line on the stakes: `This call decides [one thing]. It does not decide [what I fear].`
5. Say your first sentence, the answer they came for (Lucía's was her date and its condition), aloud twice. If a colleague is near, ask them to say the push you fear most, at a moment you don't choose, and answer it. If you lose your place, look at the note and say the point again in plain words.
6. In the last minute, drink some water, let one slow breath out and read the note once more.

**Done means** a colleague who reads only your note can say what you are asking for and what you will not agree to.

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| The fear written as the stakes | Put the fear after "It does not decide" |
| A rehearsal of the whole call | Rehearse the first sentence and the hardest push |

If you won't have the ten minutes, write the note the evening before, stop reading early enough to sleep, and keep the last step for the minute before you join.

## When the next sentence is gone

The thread can go even with the note in place: a sharp line, or a word that won't come when you reach for it. When it goes, stop, look at the note and say the point again in plain words, as if for the first time. Then carry on from there, or ask what they need.

You can say what is happening while you look: "Let me come back to the point."

If your point sentence no longer answers what they just asked, don't force it back in. Say that you didn't prepare for that question, and say when you will have an answer.

## The sting can wait

A line that stings can pull you toward a reply about yourself. Lucía's began as one: the history of the summary, everything that would make May sound less bad. It answered a question he had not asked: whose fault was May? He had asked why this date should be believed. Her answer admitted May in four words, because he was right about it, and spent the rest on what the date depended on.

If a sting is unfair, you don't have to settle that on the call. Say "I see that differently, and I'll answer it in writing," and answer what was asked.

**Spar with an AI.** Rehearse the push and the sting before they reach you.

```text
Play the chief executive of a client company. I lead the vendor team building your new system, and I'm calling to give you [a go-live date / a price / a decision]. You want it firm, for your board. Each time I attach a condition, press me to drop it. Once, when I don't expect it, raise this past mistake of mine in one sharp sentence: [your mistake]. Keep your replies short. After six exchanges, leave the role and tell me whether my condition survived, which sentence I said only to end the discomfort, and where I lost my point.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Practice: a sharp comment, answered in the morning

**Situation.** 23:40 on a Tuesday, two days before a client's release. Their architect comments on your team's pull request: "Second broken build this week. Does anyone on your side run the tests before you merge?"

**First draft (written at 23:46).**
"To be fair, both builds broke because your team upgraded the date library on Monday and nobody told us. We run every test before we merge. I'll look into it tomorrow."

**What's wrong.** It answers the sting first: before he learns whether his release is blocked, he learns whose fault the week was. "We run every test before we merge" is bigger than the facts, because none of those tests ran against the upgraded library. "I'll look into it tomorrow" gives him nothing to plan around.

**Better (sent at 7:50).**
"Your release isn't blocked: I reverted our merge last night, and main has passed every build since. Both breaks had one cause: our branches still used the date library from before Monday's upgrade. So yes, we run every test before we merge, but only on our own branch. From today we also run them on the latest main. The fixed change passes there and can be merged once you approve it."

**Why it works.** It opens with his release. The revert went in that night; the reply went out in the morning. The cause takes one sentence and blames nobody. His question gets a true answer at its real size: every test, but only on the branch. Who upgraded what can wait for the review of both breaks. The sting gets no reply at all.

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Take the last work message that stung you. Write the reply you wanted to send. Cross out every sentence that defends you or answers the sting, then add the answer to the question inside the message, or to the need behind it. Read what is left the next morning before you send anything like it. **Done means** a colleague who reads your new reply can say what happened and what happens next, and can find no sentence whose only job is to defend you.

## Words to use

**To hold a condition.** "I'd rather give you the condition now than an apology in August." "The date and the condition come together."

**When the thread goes.** "I've lost my place. The point is this: [your point sentence]."

**When a line stings.** "You're right about [what was true]. Here is what's different this time." "I see that differently, and I'll answer it in writing. On your question: [the answer]."

**To close.** "If you hear anything new about [the review], tell me, and I'll tell you what it does to the date." "I'll send you the date and its condition in writing today."

### Phrases you will hear

"Put a stake in the ground" (commit to one date or one position). "I'll hold you to that" (I expect you to keep this promise, and I will check). "Don't sugarcoat it" (tell me the bad part plainly).

## When it backfires

**When the note becomes a script.** Read aloud word for word, the point sentence can sound read, and coming back to it again and again can start to sound like dodging. Use the note to find your place, then say the point in your own words.

**When they can overrule you.** Veldhaven held the contract, and Lucía could still keep her condition, because the date was hers to give. If someone above you says "Tell them the 14th," say the condition once, in writing, to the person who decides, and let them decide with it in view. *Saying no and pushing back* has the rest of that route.

**When saying you lost your place costs more than it should.** In some rooms "Let me come back to the point" is ordinary; in others it can sound unprepared. If you can't tell which room you're in, skip the announcement and say the point again.

**When there is no time at all.** A senior person stops you in the corridor with the hard question. The routine shrinks to one step: say your point sentence to yourself once, then answer.

**When it is more than nerves.** Nerves that stop you working, before every hard call or for days ahead of one, are beyond what a book can fix. Take them to a professional you trust.

**In a second language.** Pressure may thin out a second language first, and numbers, dates and names are the words you can least afford to build on the spot. Put the ones you will need on the note, written the way you will say them, so that under the push you read them instead of building them.
