# Thinking on your feet

Bianca, Tolva's product manager, was ten minutes into a roadmap call when site two's manager stopped her.

14:12, site two's manager: "Sorry, before the next slide. The one thing I asked you for, texts to my drivers, is after the peak. Then our systems team tells me my printers need new firmware, and my labels move three weeks. So why do I hear about my own site from them, and never from you?"

14:12, Bianca: "The new label interface needs newer firmware than the printers at your site have. Site one's printers already had it, so our test there passed. Your systems team can update a site in about half a day, and Diego is agreeing the dates with them this week."

14:13, site two's manager: "I know about the firmware. That's not what I asked."

The roadmap showed what Tolva would build next, for which warehouse, and when. Tolva's software sends arriving trucks to warehouse doors. On the video call were the managers of Veldhaven's three distribution centers and Diego, the engineer Tolva placed with Veldhaven, its largest client.

Earlier in June, Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, had chosen between the two changes her managers asked for most, because Tolva could finish only one before September. She chose the override, which lets supervisors move a truck to another door from the dock screen. The texts would wait until after the December peak.

## 14:13: the right facts, the wrong question

Bianca told him nothing new: his own team had already explained the firmware. She heard "why" as a question of fact, what had made the date move, and gave him the cause. He was asking whether Tolva listens to site two and keeps it informed. His request would wait until after the peak, and news of his printers had come from someone else. That is a challenge, and no cause settles it.

Bianca got the step before the answer wrong: deciding what she had been asked.

Before you answer a hard question, decide what kind it is, because each kind is settled by something different. Then answer the kind you were asked, even when it arrives hostile or in the middle of your sentence. Take about two seconds to decide, a target this book sets. Those two seconds turn the hardest question in the room into one you know how to answer.

> **Line to keep:** Facts settle only one kind of question.

## Sort first

The tool for those two seconds is **sort first**. Before answering a hard question or joining a disagreement, say to yourself what kind it is, so you know what would settle it. A question is a **fact**, a **judgment**, a **commitment** or a **challenge**.

| Kind | At 14:12 it might have sounded like | What settles it |
|---|---|---|
| Fact | "Which firmware do our printers need?" | The fact and how you know it; if you don't have it, when you will |
| Judgment | "Was the override the right choice?" | Your view, what you weighed, and whose decision it is |
| Commitment | "Will site two get the texts before the peak?" | Yes or no, with its condition, from someone who can keep it |
| Challenge | "Why do I never hear it from you?" | The true part, said first; then sort what is left |

To catch a wrong sort, imagine giving the answer you have in mind: would it end the question? A "why" can ask for a cause, for a reason, or for you to defend yourself. In a design review, "Why a queue?" can mean any of the three. If you hear "That's not what I asked," sort again.

A challenge asks whether your word holds, or whether you listened, and the person asking may already have the facts, so more facts can sound like a defense. Say first whatever part of it is true, with no "but" after it. If none of it is true ("Why did you hide the delay?" when nobody did), say once what did happen, and how you know. Then sort what is left, because a challenge can carry another kind of question inside it. His carried a commitment: will you tell me yourself next time?

A disagreement is about **what is true** (agree the test before anyone argues the answer) or **what to do** (agree the goal). Or it is about **who gets something limited** (agree a fair rule and name who decides). The override against the texts was the third kind: one change before September, and Claire to decide which. *Arguing well* takes disagreements in full.

## Say that you are thinking

In a room, people can watch you think; on a call, a silent pause can look like a frozen screen. Either way, say what the pause is for, "Let me think," and sort.

One question gets no pause: a question about what you did or knew. "Did you test site one's printers?" needs no thinking, so a pause before it earns no credit for effort. A slow "yes" can sound less sincere than a quick one, so answer first.

> **Research says:** Across fourteen experiments, people judged slower answers as less sincere than faster ones, in settings from everyday conversation to police questioning. The effect was smaller when the delay could be put down to thinking hard, or when the answer was socially undesirable. The studies measured how answers were judged, not whether slow speakers lie, and saying "let me think" aloud is this book's advice, built on the effort result.

## 14:14: the same question, sorted again

Back on the call, Bianca said, "Let me think," and sorted again. Then:

"That's fair. You should have heard it from us, and before the date moved. From today, if a date for site two moves, I'll call you myself, the same day. And by tomorrow, every date on this slide will say whether we checked it or are still assuming it."

He was quiet for a moment. "Which of mine are you assuming?"

"Your label date. The old one assumed your printers matched site one's, and nobody checked. The new one assumes your systems team updates them by mid-July. They told us they can; nobody has done it yet. The others will be marked tomorrow."

She made it easier for him to hear and changed none of the content: nothing on the roadmap moved. His follow-up was a fact question: he had stopped asking whether Tolva would tell him anything and started testing what it told him. Her answer was a sized claim, with its basis (told) and its limit.

## 14:17: a judgment, then an interruption

Site three's manager unmuted. "Honestly, was the override the right choice? The texts would help all three of us."

It was a judgment, and Bianca gave her view first. "Yes, for September. Site one goes live first, and when a door breaks, a supervisor has to be able to move a truck at once. The texts save each driver a walk to the window. The override keeps one broken door from blocking a whole morning. Claire made the choice, and I—"

"So my drivers walk to the window all through the peak." Site two's manager again.

Treat an interruption as a question that won't wait its turn, and sort it like any other. This one was a commitment question in the form of a complaint: can you do anything for site two before December? If it carries what matters most to the person asking, take it now, after one finished sentence. If it jumps to something you will cover anyway, say when, and keep that promise.

Bianca took it. "One sentence to finish site three's answer, then yours. Claire made the choice, and I'd make the same one." Then, to site two: "I can't promise texts before the peak. I can find out whether texts at your gate alone would fit before November, and you'll have a yes or no from me by the end of July."

## 14:26: a missing number

Site three's manager asked how long drivers wait at her gate on a normal morning. Bianca didn't know. Diego answered: "That's in the gate log. I'll pull last month's mornings for all three sites and send them tonight." A fact nobody has on hand is settled by a source and a time.

The session ended at 14:31 with site two's manager still unconvinced. Only July would settle his challenge: whether the next news about site two came from Bianca. At 14:12 Bianca had answered the question she was ready for; after that, she decided before each answer what she had been asked. That is the habit of the framer, the thinker type she is growing toward.

## Practice: sort, then answer

**Situation.** A video call with an investor you have met twice. You have just shown your pricing, and she says: "Has anyone actually signed at this price, or is that a hope?"

**First draft (what a careful founder says).**
"We priced it from the hours it saves. A team of ten saves about a day a week, and we charge less than a quarter of what that day costs them."

**What's wrong.** None of it answers her. She asked whether anyone has signed at this price; the draft argues that the price is fair and leaves her to work out that the answer is no. Her challenge carries a fact about what you did, and that answer comes first, with no pause.

**Better.**
"No, not at this price yet. Our two customers pay about two-thirds of it, on contracts we signed last year. The first quote at this price goes out on Monday, and I'll send you their answer, whatever it is."

**Why it works.** It answers the fact her challenge carried, then gives it a size. The last sentence turns her doubt into a test she can watch, with a date, and promises the result either way.

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Write down the question you would least like to hear about your work this week. Sort it, and if it is a challenge, sort what is left and write that question underneath. Then write a first sentence whose first words answer it. **Done means** a colleague who reads only that sentence can tell which kind of question you heard and what your answer is.

**Timed drill (60 seconds).** **If you do only one, do this one.** Hand a colleague your question. They ask it, then cut in once, without warning, with "That's not what I asked" or a question of their own. Sort before you begin, and say "Let me think" only if you need the pause. If the question is about what you did or knew, answer at once. When they cut in, sort again, then answer now or say when you will. Constraint: no reason before the answer, either time. **Done means** your colleague can name the kind you took each question to be and repeat both answers in a sentence each.

**Written form.** Write the question, its kind and your first sentence. Your colleague writes an interruption under it, and you reply in one written sentence.

**Mistakes and fixes.**

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| A judgment answered with all you weighed and no view | Your view, then what you weighed, then who decides |
| A plain fact question heard as an attack | The fact, in the voice you would use for any other |
| A promise someone else must keep | Name who decides, and promise an answer by a date |
| A "but" after the true part | A full stop, then what you will do |

**Spar with an AI.** Rehearse against someone whose request was left out.

```text
Play a [client or user] whose request was left out of my next release. Here is the plan I am presenting: [three lines]. Ask me four questions, one at a time, in any order: a fact, a judgment, a commitment and a challenge, without saying which is which. Interrupt one of my answers once. At the end, list each question, the kind you meant, the kind my answer treated it as, and where I could have answered sooner.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

- **To sort before you answer.** "Let me think."
- **When you can't tell the kind.** "Do you need a date from me, or the reason it moved?"
- **A challenge.** "That's fair: [the true part]. From [when], [commitment]." "That's not quite what happened. Here's what did, and how we know: [what]."
- **A judgment.** "My view is [view], because [the one thing I weighed]. The decision is [name]'s."
- **A commitment you can't make.** "I can't promise that. I can promise you an answer by [day]."
- **An interruption.** "One sentence to finish this, then yours."

### Phrases you will hear

- "On the spot": asked a hard question in public, with no time to prepare.
- "With all due respect": usually comes just before a disagreement.
- "That's a loaded question": the question assumes something you may not accept.

## When it backfires

"Do you need a date from me, or the reason it moved?" after a plain question sounds like stalling. Sort silently whenever the kind is clear, and ask only when you can't tell.

Some challenges outlast the meeting. If the record behind one is bad, nothing you say in the room will settle it; only a kept commitment will, so make the commitment small enough to keep.

When they hold the power, never name the kind aloud: "That sounds like a challenge," said to a client's chief executive, turns a question into a contest. If they interrupt, they have the floor; give them the answer first and put the rest in writing afterward. When you hold the power, your fact questions can land as challenges, so say which you mean: "I'm not testing you. I really don't know."

A hard question may show respect in one team and sound close to an accusation in another. Before you sort one as hostile, ask a colleague who knows the room how sharp questions are meant there.

In a second language, sorting while you translate is a lot for two seconds, so take longer and say why: "Let me make sure I understood the question." The asker's English can mislead you too. When someone is upset in a second language, the softening words may be the first to go. Check whether the edge is in the question or only in the English.

---

# With a machine in the room

*On a call: put your own lines first*

The script was a hundred and forty words long, and Diego had written none of them.

Diego is the engineer Tolva placed with Veldhaven, its largest client. Late in June he needed one thing from Veldhaven's systems team: the label printers at sites two and three updated in the same week.

Earlier that month he had taken a frown from Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, for a no. So he asked Tolva's approved assistant how to ask politely. Its draft thanked, apologized, told the labels' story in order and ended hoping the team "could potentially consider" both sites, "ideally within the same week". Read aloud, one sentence took two breaths, and the fact that mattered came last, as a wish.

He kept the thanks and wrote his own three lines on a card under the camera. On the video call he told the systems lead: "Thanks for making time. I need the printer updates at sites two and three in the same week. Then our label work fits the three weeks we announced. A week apart, it takes four. Can you do that?" He put the weight on "same" and stopped.

She looked away. He didn't guess why. He waited.

"Why does the week matter? It's half a day per site."

The script had no answer to that. Diego did. "We test our labels again on the new firmware. Same week, one round of tests for both sites. A week apart, two rounds, one after the other."

"Then both in the same week, before mid-July. You'll have the day by Friday."

## From the page to the call

An assistant can prepare what you will say. Everything this part trained comes after: saying less, being easy to hear, your face and camera, staying steady, and the next question.

Give it the jobs that end before you speak. Ask for speech; unless you do, assume it writes for a reader. Speech means short sentences, numbers as you will say them and your ask last. Put your own lines where your eyes will be, and keep the script off the screen. Then let it play your listener: one interruption, then the two hardest questions it can find. The question you get may be a third, and you will answer it from what you know of your own work.

> **Line to keep:** There is no script for the second answer.

## Practice: a draft for the ear

**If you do only one, do this one.**

**Situation.** Tomorrow, on a video call, you tell a prospective customer when their pilot can start.

**First draft (what an assistant writes).** "Following our kickoff on 3 June, we resolved two formatting issues in your sample data. Based on current capacity, we anticipate commencing the pilot as early as 15/07, contingent upon receipt of the signed data agreement by 01/07."

**What's wrong.** It reads well and is hard to say: history first, a date in figures, and the customer's one task hidden in "receipt of", never asked for.

**Better.** "The earliest we can start your pilot is the fifteenth of July. That date needs your signed data agreement by the first of July. Can your team sign it by then?"

**Why it works.** The date comes first, in words; the condition and the ask get a breath each.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Get an assistant's draft for your next call that needs a decision. Read it aloud, cut every word you wouldn't say in conversation, and say your version from three lines on a card. Then have the assistant interrupt you once and ask the question your listener would ask next, and answer it. **Done means** a colleague who hears your version once can repeat your number and your ask, and you answer the question without notes.

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## When it backfires

**When the words aren't yours to change.** Read an approved incident statement as written, and say so. Answer questions in your own words, or say who will.

**When you rehearse every call.** You may answer the question you practiced instead of the one asked, so sort it first, as in *Thinking on your feet*.

**In a second language.** Keep the assistant's sentence if you can say it whole; swap any word you trip on for an everyday one.

## Record again

Record sixty seconds on what you are working on and why it matters, with only your point sentence in view. Slow your first sentence and stop after your ask. Score it:

1. **Sentences before the point.** Count the sentences before the first one that says why your work matters, or write "never".
2. **Hedges with no basis.** Each *probably*, *I think*, *should* or *hopefully* with no reason after it.
3. **One example.** One case that shows why it matters; background doesn't count. Yes or no.
4. **The ending.** An ask or a next step: yes or no.
5. **Said back.** Before anyone hears it, write your point in one sentence. A colleague or a friend hears it once and writes theirs, or an assistant given the transcript stands in. Theirs should name your point and your ask.

The filler count is optional. Pauses, restarts and searching for a word never count; if you stutter, work in a second language or pause to think, skip it. The written form: three minutes without stopping. Put it beside your earlier takes.

*Safe practice: record only yourself, or others only with their consent and within your employer's rules.*

# Part 3. Clear connection

---

# Listening people can feel

Listening makes no sound. On the first Tuesday in July, Diego did a great deal of it, and the dock supervisor beside him had no way to know.

Diego is Tolva's engineer inside Veldhaven, whose first warehouse, site one, starts running on Tolva's dock scheduler in September. After the morning trucks had gone, he laid two plans side by side on the desk in site one's dock office. One was the paper plan Veldhaven's planners had printed the evening before; the other, the plan the scheduler had made overnight from the same bookings. He had asked the supervisor, who had run site one's morning shift for eleven years, to show him where the scheduler was wrong.

The supervisor ran a finger down the scheduler's plan and stopped at 6:10. "This one. A container from the port, on door four. Then your system puts the next truck on door four at 6:50."

Diego had stopped at "your system". He was already shaping his answer.

"That container came floor-loaded," the supervisor went on. "No pallets. Boxes stacked to the roof, and two of my people take them off by hand. Two hours. Your 6:50 truck waits over an hour at the gate. Not every container is like that. Some come on pallets, and those are quick. I see which ones on the packing list the night before."

"It doesn't use a fixed time," Diego said. "It takes the length of the slot from the booking."

"And the carrier books forty minutes for everything." The supervisor glanced at his radio. "Fine."

Diego wrote "container times" in his notebook, said, "Okay. This is useful. Thanks," and left.

## Two words in a notebook

Diego had listened, and he was right about the booking. From the supervisor's side of the desk, a visitor from the software company had written down two words, corrected him once and called it useful. Until your listening comes back to people in words, they are taking it on trust. Part of the conversation had not reached Diego either. While he held his correction ready, the supervisor had told him which containers mattered and how to spot them the night before.

Your listening counts for the other person once they can check it. So give them something to check: say what you understood, what you will do about it and what you are still unsure of, then let them correct you. The moment they correct you is the moment they know they were heard, and the correction can carry the one fact you missed.

> **Line to keep:** To feel heard, people need something to correct.

On the dock, Diego told when he should have asked. "When you know the answer, say it" is right when a question is put to you and the answer is in your head, because people rely on whoever knows. A supervisor who asks whether a new rule is live wants a yes or a no. "Ask more than you tell" brings out what you don't know, and it is right on the dock, where every missing piece was in the supervisor's head. The rule for choosing: tell when the missing piece is in your head. Ask when it is in theirs, when you need them to commit, or before you decide they are wrong. Diego had decided the supervisor was wrong before the supervisor finished.

## The read-back

The tool for this is **the read-back**, in three parts: what I understood, what I will do, what I am unsure of. Use it when you receive, and ask for it when you give ("tell me your plan before you start"), with people and with agents. Skip it when the stakes are low and the other person wants speed.

- **What I understood.** Their point, in their words wherever you can: "floor-loaded", "by hand", "the packing list". People can correct only what they recognize. Give back the part you will act on, and leave the rest.
- **What I will do.** One action, and when. Repeating their words shows you heard them; this part shows that what they said changed something.
- **What I am unsure of.** One real question. It gives them the easiest way in to correct you, and it is where a missing fact can surface.

Knowing you will say it back also changes what you do while they talk: you collect their words instead of shaping your reply.

None of this is new. A pilot reads an instruction back before acting on it. In some hospitals, whoever takes over a shift sums up what they heard, asks questions and restates the key actions: the same three parts. This book adds their words instead of yours, one action with a time, and a question you can't answer yourself.

> **Research says:** In nine hospitals, the rate of medical errors fell 23 percent after a program had resident doctors hand patients over in a set order, aloud and in writing. A later independent review rated the evidence for fewer errors as moderate, but one randomized trial of a version of the program found no drop in preventable harm. The program changed several things at once, so it cannot single out one habit; giving your own handovers a fixed shape is this book's reasoning from it.

## The next morning, line by line

That evening Diego began his note to Mateo, Tolva's co-founder and chief technology officer, and stopped halfway through a sentence: "The scheduler needs to know which containers". He did not know how it would know. At ten the next morning he called the supervisor.

**Diego:** "It's Diego, from yesterday. Do you have two minutes? I want to check what I wrote down about the containers."

He asks for the time and gives the reason, which makes the supervisor the judge of his notes.

**Supervisor:** "Go on."

**Diego:** "What I understood: containers from the port come floor-loaded, boxes stacked to the roof, and two of your people unload them by hand. That takes about two hours, but the carrier books forty minutes, so the next truck on that door waits."

The first part, in the supervisor's own words. Nothing about slot lengths or booking fields, the words Diego would use with Mateo.

**Supervisor:** "Not all of them. Some come on pallets. Those are quick."

The correction is the sentence Diego missed on the dock while he held his own ready. It is also the first sign the supervisor has had that the rest went in: only one detail needed fixing.

**Diego:** "Only the floor-loaded ones, then. What I'll do is write this up today for Mateo, who builds the scheduler, so those containers get a longer slot. What I'm unsure of is how the scheduler would know which ones they are before they arrive."

The second part shows that the call will change something. The third is a real question, and the supervisor has already answered it once.

**Supervisor:** "The packing list. It comes the night before. I told you that yesterday."

**Diego:** "You did, and I missed it. Does the packing list reach Veldhaven's warehouse system, or only your inbox?"

He owns the miss in one short sentence and moves on. The question after it is one the supervisor can't answer, which tells Diego where the next fact lives.

**Supervisor:** "I don't know. Ask the office." Then, after a moment: "Come on Friday at six. Two containers are due. You can watch one come off."

Diego hadn't asked him for that. The call took under three minutes. Diego's note to Mateo that afternoon held two facts he did not have when he left the dock, and one question for Veldhaven's office. What the dock knew reached Mateo intact, which is the translator's habit.

> **From practice:** End a read-back on a question that makes correcting you easy. A question that a polite yes can answer may get only the yes. "What did I miss?" asks for the gap itself.

## When you hand the work over

The read-back turns around when you are the one giving the work. The next week Diego gave a coding agent the job of writing tests for the container rule. Before it wrote a line, he asked: "Tell me your plan before you start: what you understood, what you will do, what you are unsure of." Its plan gave every container two hours, and its third part said it was unsure of nothing. That empty line was the warning. The packing list, the one thing that decides which containers get the longer slot, was missing from the plan. An agent's read-back shows you its guess while one sentence can still fix it. With a colleague, ask for the same three parts in plain words.

## Practice: say it back in their words

**Situation.** A video call. A customer's head of support has spent four minutes on why her team stopped trusting your product's ticket routing. One morning it sent two billing complaints to the technical queue, and nobody noticed until one of those customers called back angry. Since then her agents sort every ticket by hand before they start.

**First draft (what a founder who knows the product says).** "Got it. So the classifier's confidence threshold is too low, the misroutes eroded trust, and you've fallen back to manual triage. We'll tune the threshold this sprint."

**What's wrong.** It is a read-back in the founder's language. She can't correct "confidence threshold" or "manual triage", so the safe reply is "I suppose so." The part that hurt, nobody noticing until a customer called, is missing. And it names a cause nobody has checked.

**Better.** "Two billing complaints went to the technical queue, nobody saw it until a customer called back, and now your team sorts every ticket by hand. I'll find out why those two went wrong and tell you by Thursday. What I can't tell yet is which hurt more: the wrong queue, or not seeing it."

**Why it works.** Her words come back to her, so she can correct them. One action has a day on it. The last sentence is a question only she can answer, and her answer decides what to fix first: the routing, or the fact that nobody could see it fail.

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Take the last time someone explained a problem to you at length. Write your read-back in three sentences, one for each part, using at least two of their words for the problem and none of your field's words they would not use. Say it aloud once. **Done means** someone outside your field, hearing it once, can tell you what the problem was and what you will do.

## Practice: one read-back this week

**With a person.** This week, when someone explains a problem to you or hands you work, say back the three parts before you act. End on a question that makes correcting you easy. Then watch the reply: look for a correction, something they add, or a point they stop repeating. A quick "yes" with nothing after it means your third part needs asking again, more plainly. Once this week, turn it around: when you hand someone a task, ask for their plan before they start.

**Done means** your notes hold one thing the other person corrected or added after your read-back, in their words. If they changed nothing, your notes hold the question you asked and their answer.

**If you do only one, do this one.**

## Words to use

- **To start a read-back.** "Let me say back what I took from that."
- **The three parts.** "What I understood is [their point, in their words]." "What I'll do is [one action] by [day]." "What I'm not sure of is [one thing]."
- **To make correcting you easy.** "What did I miss?" "Which part did I get wrong?"
- **When they have to repeat something.** "You've said that twice, so I haven't shown you I got it. Here's what I have: [your read-back]."
- **When you hand over work.** "Before you start, tell me your plan in two sentences: what you'll do first, and what you're not sure of."

### Phrases you will hear

- "I hear you." (I heard what you said. It doesn't say what they will do about it, so ask.)
- "Point taken." (Your point is fair. It may still change nothing.)
- "Let me play that back." (A read-back is coming. Correct anything that is off.)
- "I'm all ears." (I'm listening. Go ahead.)

## When it backfires

**When they want speed.** Two weeks after the call, at five past six, a container stood at door four and trucks were lined up at the gate. The supervisor called across the dock: "Is your container rule in yet?" Diego began, "So what I understood is that you want the floor-loaded ones to—" "Diego. Yes or no." "No. It's still in testing." The tool was right and the moment was wrong. A quick question in a rush, with nothing new at stake, gets the answer and nothing else.

**When it turns into a script.** A read-back that hands back every sentence, in the order it was said, can sound like a technique being used on someone. Give back only the part you will act on, in plain words, then your action and your question.

**When power is uneven.** With a client or someone senior, a full read-back can sound as if you doubt they were clear. Lead with what you will do: "So I get this right: I'll [action] by [day]. Is that what you need?" When you hold the power, asking for a read-back can sound like a test. Put the reason on your own side: "Tell me your plan, so I know my brief was clear."

**When the team has its own habit.** In some teams a spoken read-back can sound as if you didn't trust the speaker. There, send it in writing after the call.

**In a second language.** The read-back is the cheapest check you have, because it catches a misheard word on either side before anyone acts on it. Use their words for the thing, even when yours would be more exact, and keep each sentence short.

# Questions and common ground

The man in front of Lucía in the coffee queue was marking the fair's floor plan with a pen, and he had crossed out more stands than he had circled. It was July, the second morning of a logistics trade fair in Rotterdam. Lucía had stayed on after visiting Veldhaven, a food wholesaler there and Tolva's largest client, to look for the next one. She is co-founder and chief executive of Tolva, fourteen people in Montevideo.

His badge said Hugo, operations director, Sarnik: a distributor of chilled and frozen food with four warehouses outside Lyon.

Lucía nodded at the floor plan. "Anything worth the walk so far?"

"Not yet." He read her badge. "Tolva. What do you sell?"

"Software that decides which truck goes to which door. At our pilot dock last year, the average truck waited about twenty minutes less, by the client's own gate log."

"Everybody in this hall saves me twenty minutes." He tapped the crossed-out names. "What does it cost?"

There was an easy answer, a figure low enough to keep him talking, and Lucía had nothing to base a figure on. "It depends on your doors and your trucks, and I'd be guessing at both. What does your busiest warehouse look like at six in the morning?"

"Six is the middle of it. From five to seven, more trucks than doors."

"What happens to the trucks that don't get one?"

"They wait in the yard with the cooling running. The driver calls his dispatcher, the dispatcher calls my shift lead, and on a bad morning my phone rings before I've had coffee." He looked down the queue. "Like this one."

"We got that problem wrong at first," Lucía said. "Our first version booked every truck a slot at the gate. The trucks came on time and waited anyway, because nobody had planned the doors. We rebuilt most of it."

Hugo folded the plan. "My engineers want to build a scheduler themselves, with a coding assistant. Since my budget was cut in June, I listen to them more."

Lucía let that sit. "Once a truck is through your gate, how long does it wait for a door?"

He started to answer and stopped. "I know when they arrive. From this month a consultant forecasts when they will arrive." Lucía had a good idea which consultant, and where else that forecast ran. Neither was hers to say. "How long they wait inside," Hugo said, "nobody writes down."

It was the first question at the fair he could not answer, and he did not look at the floor plan again.

## A claim he had heard all morning

Lucía's best fact did nothing. Twenty minutes was true, measured and hers, and to Hugo it was one more vendor's number in a hall full of them. He could not check it in a queue, so he asked for the one figure every stand would have to give him: the price. She answered that as far as she honestly could, then asked, because what the price depended on was in his head.

Her questions did what the number could not. Each one handed him the subject he knew best, and each answer told her which of her facts, if any, mattered to him. They reached a problem they both had: trucks that come on time and still wait. Then came a question neither could answer.

Small talk becomes real talk when each question follows the other person's last answer further into their work, and you meet them there with something true of your own. Do that, leave with a next step, and a stranger in a queue can become someone who takes your call.

Lucía asked Hugo a second question about his own yard, and it was Hugo who went home to find out.

> **Line to keep:** Common ground is a question you both want answered.

## Fill in the sketch out loud

The listener sketch from *Who is listening* is three lines about one person: what they know, what they have to decide, what they stand to lose. With a stranger all three are blank, and the conversation is how you fill them. By the time the coffee came, Lucía could have written Hugo's:

- **Knows** when his trucks arrive, and from this month when they will.
- **Has to decide** what a smaller budget pays for, and whether his engineers build it instead.
- **Stands to lose** his mornings: the call that reaches him when the yard fills.

She asked for none of it directly. Open with one line about where you both are. Then ask about their work in the words they would use with a colleague: what they are working on, what they must choose this year. For the third line, ask what happens when the thing goes wrong, and who gets the call.

The follow-up does most of the work. Take the most concrete word in their answer, a time, a number, a place or a person, and ask what happens there. Hugo said "more trucks than doors", so Lucía asked about the trucks without one. A follow-up is built from their words, so it can only come from someone who heard them.

You may hear "never ask why": it can sound like an audit. Keep the rule narrower. A why about the work opens a story: "Why five to seven?" A why about a choice someone made asks a stranger to defend it, so give your reason for asking first: "I ask because we chose wrong the first time. What made you go with a forecast?"

None of this is a discovery call yet. It is the conversation that earns one.

## Answer with something of your own

A question opens the subject, and something of your own shows what kind of answer is safe to give. Hugo's ringing phone was a small admission. Lucía answered with a bigger one, a first version built for the wrong problem. He answered that with something he had held back: his own engineers want to build a scheduler themselves.

Among peers, say something of your own before you ask for theirs. With a client, an investor or a boss, show that you know the work before you say what went wrong, as Lucía's pilot number did. Upward, admit the limits of what you know, never a list of your weaknesses.

## Prepared questions or your own words?

One piece of advice says to prepare your openers, because nerves, a second language or an executive with four minutes leave no time to invent one. The other says never to use lines, because people can hear a canned question. "What keeps you up at night?" tells a buyer he is the tenth person to hear it today.

Prepare what the question does, and let the moment choose its words. Lucía had decided before the fair to ask each operations person about their busiest hour, and for Hugo that meant six in the morning. Then test any move by whether you could name it to the person while you use it. Said aloud, "I ask everyone about their busiest hour, because that's the hour our software is for" would have cost her nothing. A shared hobby you invented fails that test at once, and so does any move that works only if they never notice it.

## Practice: a short answer, then one question back

**Situation.** You are the engineer your company placed with a client. In the elevator after a review, the client's chief operating officer, whom you have never spoken to, asks: "So, how are you finding it here?"

**First draft (an honest status report).** "Good, thanks. We finished connecting your order system on Monday, the test data came in on Tuesday, and we should start on returns next week if nothing else comes up."

**What's wrong.** She asked how you are finding it, and got a status report. It ends without a question, so the ride ends in silence, and she knows you only as the integration.

**Better.** "I like it. Your support team shows me exactly where the old system slows them down, and that makes my job easier. Can I ask you one thing? When the new system is live, what's the first number you'll look at?"

**Why it works.** Her question gets a true answer in plain words, with one thing about her people she can be glad to hear. Then one question about what she will judge the work by, which gives her the next sentence. Whatever she answers goes into her listener sketch.

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Pick someone senior you will meet this week without an agenda. Write a one-sentence answer to "How's it going?" that someone outside your field could repeat, then one question about what they will decide or watch this year, in their words. Say both aloud once. **Done means** a colleague who hears them can repeat your answer and say what the person would have to talk about to answer your question.

## Leave while it is still good

The coffee came while Hugo was still thinking about his yard. The conversation was going well, which was Lucía's reason to end it.

"Let me check I have it," she said. "More trucks than doors before seven, a forecast for when they arrive, and nobody who knows how long they wait. I'll send you one page on how we measure it, by Friday. What I don't know is whether your gate log can show it."

"Send it. And put a price in it."

"I'll put in what the price depends on. The number needs your doors."

"Then call me in August. By then I'll know how long they wait."

That ending is the read-back from *Listening people can feel*, used as a goodbye. Its last sentence held the question they now shared. Then she left, before either of them had to look for a way out.

Don't wait for the right moment to stop.

> **Research says:** In two studies from one paper, people reported afterward when they had wanted a conversation to end, some after talking with someone close to them, some with a stranger. An ending that suited both people was very rare, one that suited either was uncommon, and neither could tell well when the other had wanted to stop. None of this was tested on clients or buyers, so carrying it into work is the book's reasoning: you can't feel the right moment, so choose one.

Hugo had queued with one question for every stand in the hall. He left with one about his own yard. That is a first step toward the framer, who decides what the question is before anyone answers it.

## Practice: from their title to their work

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.** Use your next conversation with someone you don't know well: a new client's first call, a dinner, a fair.

1. Before it, write one question about their work at its busiest or hardest hour, in words they would use.
2. After their first answer, take its most concrete word and ask what happens there.
3. When you reach a problem you also have, say one true thing of your own about it, one step deeper than they went.
4. Look for a question you both want answered, then end it yourself: the read-back from *Listening people can feel*, and a day.

Watch their second answer. If it has a time, a place or a person the first one lacked, they have moved from their job title to their work.

**Done means** that evening your page holds their three lines, each built on something they told you, and a next step with a day they agreed to.

## Words to use

- **To open, after one line about where you are.** "What are you hoping to find here?" "What does your busiest [hour or day] look like?"
- **The follow-up.** "[Their word]. What happens then?" "Who gets the call when that happens?"
- **To go first.** "We had the same problem. [One true thing that happened.]"
- **A price you can't know yet.** "It depends on [what], and I'd be guessing at yours. What does [that] look like?"
- **To leave with a next step.** "I'd rather talk about this properly than in a queue. Can I send you [one thing] by [day]?"
- **To leave without one.** "I'll let you get to the next stand. It was good to hear about [one thing they said]."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Let's touch base." Let's talk again; ask when.
- "I'll let you go." They would like to end the conversation, politely.
- "We should grab a coffee sometime." A friendly close that is often not a plan; ask for a day if you want one.

## When it backfires

**When the price is all they came for.** Some people come to a fair to compare prices, and questions about their mornings can feel like a sales move. Answer what they asked as far as you honestly can, offer one question, and if they don't take it, let them go with your card.

**When the other person sets the depth.** With a client's executive or a buyer, let them. Ask about what they decide and watch, not about them, and keep your admission to what you don't yet know. When the power is yours, with a candidate or a new engineer, your questions can sound like an assessment, so go first.

**When the room opens differently.** How soon talk turns to work, and how directly someone's problems can be asked about, differs from one room to the next. Watch how respected people there open a conversation, and go deeper only after they do.

**When you only ask.** Question after question with nothing of your own is an interrogation, and a first conversation steered into discovery is a sales call nobody agreed to. When you notice you have only asked, tell them something.

**When small talk costs you a lot.** Skip it. One line about where you are is enough before the question about their work.

**In a second language.** Small talk can be harder than a technical answer, because its words don't come from your work. A follow-up is easier: it is built from words the other person has just used. Prepare your first question and one true thing about your own work, and let the rest come from theirs.

# Story for people who think in systems

"What would you tell site two's manager about the texts?" Bianca, Tolva's product manager, wrote to Mateo at lunch on the first Monday in July.

Mateo, Tolva's co-founder and chief technology officer, wrote back: "That his drivers hate the walk. Texts are after the peak, though." Tyler, the delivery lead, remembered "something about the window".

That morning, on Tolva's weekly call, Bianca had shown them a number on a slide, in large type. It read: "Site two, June mornings: a truck waits 19 minutes between the gate and its door. 8 of them are the driver's walk to the window and back." She said it once, clearly, with its source. The call moved on without a question, and by lunch the eight minutes were gone.

Tolva was putting its dock scheduler into Veldhaven's three warehouses, one site at a time from September. Diego, the engineer Tolva placed there, had pulled the number from site two's gate log, which also times each driver at the window. In June, site two's manager had asked for one thing: a text telling each driver which door to use, so nobody walks to the window to ask. Bianca had promised him a yes or no by the end of July on whether texts at his gate alone could be ready before November.

## What the room kept

The number failed for two reasons, and neither was the way Bianca said it.

Nobody on the call had stood at site two's window, so eight minutes of walking counted something none of them could see. They kept the part they could picture: drivers who dislike walking.

It also counted the wrong thing. Mateo decides what Tolva's engineers build and when, and a driver's eight minutes doesn't tell him whether texts are worth an engineer before November. Bianca had started from the request she was passing on, so her number measured the request.

To carry a number into someone's decision, let them see one case of what it counts. Then show that the case was ordinary, in the units they decide in. If you think in systems, you have good reason to distrust a story: one truck proves nothing, and a vivid one can push a decision further than the data allow. Keep the distrust, and build it into the story. Done well, your number becomes what they repeat to the next person who decides.

> **Line to keep:** It is the count that turns an anecdote into a reason.

## The working story

The tool is **the working story**: under ninety seconds, a limit this book sets, built backward from what the listener must decide.

- **The decision**, written first, never told first.
- **One moment**: a time, a place, a person, one thing said or seen.
- **The count**: the number that shows the moment stands for a pattern, or the honest statement that it is one case.
- **The handover**: the decision you ask for, in one sentence.

Never in place of the answer to a direct question.

Write the decision first, because it chooses the moment and the count. Put it at the top of a card as the listener's choice: "Mateo: one engineer for texts in October, yes or no?" Mateo decides about engineers and doors, so his story needs a door.

Then keep it to yourself until the end. Almost everywhere else in this book the point comes first; here it waits, because nobody asked, and the moment can make the listener want the answer. Said first, the decision can turn the moment into your argument, and a careful listener may start looking for what you left out.

Give the moment one detail the listener could check, and cut the rest. It can come from someone who was there, or from one row of your data, told at the speed it happened. Either way, it must have happened.

> **From practice:** Before you build a story on one row of a log, find where that row sits in the whole set: near the middle, at the edge, or alone. Then say which. A worst case later found posing as a typical one gives the listener a reason to doubt the rest of your table.

Put the count in the units your listener decides in. If you have only one case, say "one": that is a count too, and it keeps the moment honest.

The handover asks for the decision as a question they can answer, and then you stop. If the story runs long, cut words from the moment. Never cut the count.

## One truck, three decisions

Bianca wrote Mateo's decision on a card and asked Diego for a moment. On Thursday he stood by site two's window from five to seven and sent her one message: "6:04, a truck through the gate, door eleven free. The driver walked past door eleven to the window, waited behind four others and came back with 'eleven'. Nine minutes on foot to carry one number."

The gate log could have given her a row. Diego gave her the detail no log holds: the driver walked past the free door on the way to ask for it.

On Monday Bianca asked Mateo for three minutes and told it:

"Last Thursday at 6:04, a truck came through site two's gate. Door eleven was free. The driver walked past it to the window, waited behind four others, was told 'door eleven' and walked back. The truck reached the door at 6:15. For nine minutes, a free door and a waiting truck were a hundred meters apart, and the only link between them was a driver carrying a number on foot. That was an ordinary truck: in June's log, the walk takes eight minutes. At about sixty trucks a morning, it's as if two of site two's doors were shut from five to nine. Texts would put the number in the cab at the gate. Can one engineer have the first two weeks of October to build them?"

Mateo asked one question, and it was about the count: "Eight minutes across all of June?"

"Every morning in Diego's log."

"Then it's two doors, every morning, and in December we'll need every door we have. If Claire wants texts at go-live, you can have the engineer."

Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, decides something else: whether site two takes one more new thing on its go-live day, 9 November, a few weeks before her December peak. Her version kept the truck to one sentence and answered the risk she would raise:

"Last Thursday at 6:04, a driver at site two walked past door eleven, which was free, to your window, and came back nine minutes later with the number eleven. June's log says that was an ordinary truck: every morning the walk leaves about two doors' worth of time unused, and those are doors you'll want in December. Mateo can have texts ready for site two's go-live, and if they fail, the window still works. Do you want them from 9 November, or after the peak, as planned?"

"From the ninth," Claire said, "for carriers who send you their drivers' numbers. The window for everyone else."

Site two's manager got no story at all. In June he had asked for a commitment, and the answer was due. Bianca's message on the last Thursday in July began: "Yes. Texts start at your gate on 9 November, when the scheduler goes live there, for every carrier that sends us drivers' numbers by 15 October. Drivers without one still use the window. What moved it was your doors: the walk keeps about two of them idle every morning."

Each telling began from a different decision, so each kept a different count: doors for Mateo, the peak for Claire, the manager's own doors, after the answer. Bianca had started the month passing on site two's request with a number attached. She ended it saying which problem the request solved and for whom.

## When a story is the wrong answer

"Lead with a story" suits a room that hasn't asked you anything and needs something to see before it will weigh a number: that was Bianca's Monday call. "Answer first" suits a person who asked a question and needs the answer before anything else: that was site two's manager, who had lived a hundred of those mornings and was owed a yes or no.

The rule: a question gets its answer first. Tell the story when nobody has asked, there is time and you want to be remembered.

## The company's story

A company's story is a working story too, with the listener's decision at the top: whether to join, to buy, or to look closer. The founding moment is tempting. The moment that serves their decision is usually a customer's: one morning when your product changed something a person could see.

Then give the count you can stand behind, however small. Tolva's is still one: at a single pilot dock the year before, the average truck waited about twenty minutes less over six weeks, by Veldhaven's own gate log. Until a whole site is live, "one dock, six weeks" is the honest count, and saying so lets a careful listener believe the rest.

## Practice: the build that failed on Thursday

**Situation.** You are an engineer on a small product team. On Friday your head of product decides whether next sprint goes to fixing flaky tests in the build or to a feature the sales team wants. Nobody has asked you yet; you have two minutes at the start of planning.

**First draft (in the engineer's own numbers).** "Our pipeline fails about one run in six on flaky integration tests. Each failure takes around forty minutes to get back to green, so last month that was roughly sixty engineer-hours of reruns. I'd like us to prioritize test stabilization."

**What's wrong.** All the numbers are in the team's own units: runs, green, engineer-hours. Your head of product can't see any of them, and none measures what she decides about: what reaches customers, and when. "Prioritize test stabilization" is a topic, not a decision she can say yes to.

**Better.** "Last Thursday at five, the fix for the checkout error was ready. The build failed twice on a test that has nothing to do with checkout, and the fix reached customers at seven, after the evening orders it was meant for. Thursday was ordinary: one build in six fails like that, and last month the reruns took about a week and a half of one engineer. Can next sprint go to the tests, and the sales feature to the sprint after?"

**Why it works.** She can see a finished fix waiting while orders came in. The count, in her units, shows that Thursday was an ordinary day. The handover is a choice she can answer in one word.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Take a number you want someone to act on this month. Write their decision at the top of a card. Under it, write one moment the number counts, then the count in the units they decide in, then the handover as a question. Say it aloud once, decision last, in under ninety seconds. **Done means** a colleague who hears it once can tell you the moment, the number and what you asked for.

## Practice: tell it this week

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.** Pick a decision someone must make this week who hasn't asked you about it, and put your working story for it on a card. Tell it once, in the meeting or the message, then watch the first reply. A question about the count ("Is that every week?") means they are weighing it. A question about the moment ("Was that a bad day?") means the count came too late or too weakly, so next time put it right after the moment. "So what do you need?" means the handover didn't land: say it again as a question. **Done means** your listener, asked that evening what they would tell the next person who has to decide, names the moment and the number.

## Words to use

- **To open with the moment.** "Last [day] at [time], at [place], [one thing someone did or saw]."
- **To give the count.** "That was close to an ordinary [day]: [the number, in their units]." "This is one case. I haven't counted the others yet."
- **To hand over.** "If that's worth [the cost] to you, I'd like your decision by [day]."
- **When they ask a direct question halfway through.** "[The answer]. The morning behind it takes a minute, if you want it."
- **When someone tells you a story.** "Was that a typical [day]?" "What are you asking me to decide?"

### Phrases you will hear

- "That's anecdotal." It's one case, and they want the count.
- "Put a face on it." Show me one person or case it affects.
- "Don't cherry-pick." Don't choose only the cases that help you.
- "What's the takeaway?" What should I remember, or decide?

## When it backfires

**When the moment outweighs the count.** A vivid case can carry a decision further than its count can. If your count is weak, or only "one", say it before the moment, or leave the moment out.

**When they hold the power.** Someone senior and short of time may hear a story as a delay. Give the handover first, in one sentence, and offer the moment after it. With a client, tell their own mornings, and never tell one client's morning to another without asking.

**When the room distrusts stories.** In some teams a story in a decision meeting sounds unserious. Lead with the count and keep the moment to one sentence.

**When every update becomes a story.** Listeners may learn to wait for the ending. A weekly status gives the answer first; keep the working story for decisions people have to care about before they choose.

**When the moment gets improved.** If you build a typical morning from the log, say that you built it. A composite told as one real morning works only if nobody checks, which is what makes it manipulation.

**In a second language.** A moment needs only a few kinds of sentence: what happened, where, and what someone saw. If telling it feels harder than giving numbers, write the moment as three short sentences and say them as written.

---

# With a machine in the room

*After you listen: keep their words*

Hugo put it this way: "On a bad morning my phone rings before I've had coffee." The assistant put it this way: "Peak-hour dwell at inbound sites drives avoidable escalations."

Hugo runs operations at Sarnik, a chilled-food distributor near Lyon. In July, at a trade fair, he said the first one to Lucía, co-founder of Tolva, a dock-scheduling company. She had promised him a page by Friday on how Tolva measures a truck's wait.

On Thursday night she gave her notes, without his name or Sarnik's, to the assistant Tolva had approved for client work. The page came back finished. Its headline was the twenty minutes every stand had promised to save him. His phone had become an escalation. A driver shivered through a frozen dawn, and the last line asked for half an hour to discuss a pilot.

Then she asked the question Hugo would ask next: which driver? There wasn't one. Nor had she said what Hugo had to decide, so the assistant had assumed he was choosing whether to buy. Before that, he had to find out how long his trucks wait. She closed the page and wrote her own:

"You told me a truck without a door waits in your yard with the cooling running, and on a bad morning your phone rings before you've had coffee. You said nobody writes down how long it waits. Two clock times per truck, at the gate and at the door, would show it. Which warehouse could write both down for a week?"

Tolva's method went underneath, with what a price would depend on. The assistant corrected her spelling and nothing else. Hugo replied on Friday evening: "Gate times we have. Door times from Monday, one warehouse." He had corrected her, and there would be a count.

## Whose words, whose morning

You were there; the assistant wasn't. Unless you name what they said, assume it will trade it for something smoother and guess whose decision the page serves. So put it in your request:

`[Reader] has to decide [what]. Keep these words exactly: [theirs]. Use only this moment: [what happened, who saw it]. The count is [number, or "none yet"]. Before you draft, tell me what you understood and what you're unsure of.`

Lucía's, filled in: "An operations director has to decide how to count his trucks' wait. Keep these words exactly: my phone rings before I've had coffee. Use only this moment: the bad morning he described. The count is none yet." Correct the read-back before it drafts. Then ask each sentence of the draft where it came from: them, you or nobody. What came from nobody goes, however good it sounds.

> **Line to keep:** Keep what they said, even when the machine says it better.

## Practice: the note after the call

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.**

**Situation.** You manage a product. A customer's finance manager told you, "At month end two of us stay until nine, matching invoices by hand." You promised a note.

**First draft (what an assistant writes from your notes).** "Thanks for a productive call. We covered invoice formats, user access, export timing, month-end workload and training."

**What's wrong.** Five topics, none chosen. "Month-end workload" hides two people staying until nine, and nothing is asked.

**Better.** "You said that at month end two of you stay until nine, matching invoices by hand. I don't know yet whether that's every month, or how many invoices it takes. Before I propose anything, can I sit with you on the 30th and count them?"

**Why it works.** Her words, so she can correct them; an honest gap where the count will go.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** After your next conversation about someone's problem, write one sentence in their words before an assistant sees your notes. Fill in the request and get a draft. Beside each sentence write *them*, *me* or *nobody*, and delete every *nobody*. Send it, and watch what the reply corrects or adds. **Done means** every sentence you sent has *them* or *me* beside it, and one of theirs matches your notes word for word.

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## When it backfires

**When they didn't expect to be quoted.** A sentence said at a fair may not be meant for someone's boss. If others will read your note, ask first.

**When an assistant takes the notes.** Even where everyone has agreed, people may say less. Read its summary for the words it traded away.

**In a second language.** Keep a phrase said in another language as they said it, beside the English. A translation is a draft too.

## Record again

Record sixty seconds on what you are working on and why it matters, for one listener you can name. Make your example one moment that happened, with its count. Then check:

1. **Sentences before the point.** How many come before the first one that says why it matters? If none does, write *never*.
2. **Hedges with no basis.** How many *probably*, *I think*, *should* or *hopefully* have no reason after them?
3. **One example.** Is there one case that shows why it matters? Background doesn't count.
4. **The ending.** Is there an ask or a next step?
5. **Said back.** Before anyone hears it, write the point you meant. This time, find a person, who hears it once, writes the point in one sentence and asks you a question. Their sentence should name your point and your ask.

The filler count is optional; skip it if you stutter, work in a second language or pause to think. In writing, take three minutes without stopping. Keep it with your earlier takes.

*Safe practice: record only yourself, or others only with their consent and within your employer's rules.*

# Part 4. The rooms

---

# The meeting

Tyler: "Good morning, everyone. Two weeks of work, forty-five minutes, two decisions. The first one is..."

Lucía: "Sorry, Tyler, one thing before that, because it changes the plan. On Monday I told Claire her supervisors will have the override on their phones from the first night. So phones go to the top, and the rest moves down. Any problem with that?"

Tyler: "Okay. Let's see what we can move."

By the end of minute one, the plan had changed. This was planning at Tolva, a video call on the last Wednesday in August, run by Tyler, the delivery lead. Bianca, the product manager, decides the order of the work, and four engineers do it. Lucía, co-founder and chief executive, doesn't usually come.

The week before, she had told Veldhaven, Tolva's largest client, that its first warehouse, site one, would go live two weeks late, on 28 September. On Monday Claire, who runs operations there, asked what her supervisors would get for the wait, and phones were an easy yes. The override lets a supervisor move a truck to another door. For now it runs on a screen they have to walk back to.

In the silence after "any problem with that?", one engineer unmuted, and muted again.

## The plan that changed by silence

Tyler's answer kept the call calm, and it let a plan change without anyone deciding it. He didn't ask whether the override was ready for phones, what would wait, or whose choice it was. One engineer had the answer to Lucía's question and did not say it.

Sort each item before anyone argues it, hear the person who knows before the person who decides, and close with each owner saying the decision back, with a date. Each takes one sentence, and you can say it without running the meeting. Learn the three, and you are the person people want in the room when something has to be settled.

> **Line to keep:** A decision is only as real as the name beside it.

## Minute four: what kind of item is this?

Tyler had opened the list to see what could move. Nothing on it was his to move. He closed it.

"Lucía, if phones go first, I'd like us to decide it. Bianca, is the order still yours?"

"The order is mine," Bianca said. "The promise is Lucía's."

Tyler typed three questions into the shared notes, where everyone could see them. Is the override ready for phones? What does the first night need? Two engineers: phones, or what was on top before?

This is *sort first*, from *Thinking on your feet*, used on an agenda. What sounded like one item was three, and each is settled by something different.

| An item about | Is settled by | In Tyler's notes |
|---|---|---|
| What is true | A test, agreed before anyone argues the answer | Try it the way site one will use it |
| What to do | The goal, said aloud | What the first night needs |
| Who gets something limited | A fair rule, and the name of who decides | Two engineers; Bianca decides |

Take them in that order, because a choice made on a wrong fact has to be made again. An item that fits no row is news: send it beforehand and drop it from the list. For the rest, write each item as a question with the decider's name after it. "Phones" is a topic. "Do phones go first? Bianca decides" is something a room can finish.

## Minute nine: the person who knows, then the person who decides

"Question one," Tyler said. "First anyone who worked on the override this week, then everyone else. Bianca and Lucía last."

The newest person on the call spoke, an engineer on contract in her second week. "This may be a basic question. What happens if two supervisors move the same truck?"

"It gets two doors," said the engineer who had unmuted in minute one. "I did it on Monday, on the test copy, from two screens. I've seen it once. With phones, everybody has a screen."

"Why didn't you say so when I asked?" said Lucía.

"You had already told Claire."

Lucía's question had come after the promise, from the person who made it. Any reply had to begin by telling the chief executive, in front of her own team, that she was wrong. That is how the most senior person in a room can be the last to hear what it knows. If that person is you, ask before you announce, ask for facts instead of objections, and speak last, which is an old practice in many teams.

Hear, too, the engineer's "everybody has a screen". It says what the change would set off next, and it came from someone who had run it.

The contract engineer could ask because nobody expected her to know. While you are new, the basic question is yours, so use it. Once you aren't, invite it from whoever is.

> **Research says:** One paper reports two studies of diverse groups in which higher-status members tended to have more influence on the group's decision. That gap narrowed when the leader looked more at lower-status members; with influence more even, the groups worked through their information better and did better on the task. No independent repeat was found, and the finding is about where a leader looks, so calling on people first by name is our extension.

On a video call nobody can tell where you are looking. Use names, and tell people before the meeting that you will.

## Minute twenty: a rule, a decider, a sentence

By minute sixteen two engineers were deep in how to lock a record. "Do we need that to choose, or to do it?" Tyler asked. "To do it," one of them said, and they took it to the chat.

"Question two. What does the first night need?" Lucía made her case: a supervisor with a truck at the wrong door shouldn't have to walk to a screen to fix it. She was right, and Bianca said so. Bianca added one thing: no truck with two doors. The goal they agreed on included both.

That left the limited thing, two engineers for two weeks. Tyler asked for the rule before the choice. "Whatever the first night can't run without goes first?" Bianca and Lucía both said yes. Then Bianca decided, in a point sentence: "We fix the double move first, because a truck with two doors is worse than a supervisor who has to walk."

"I'd have tried to do both," said Lucía. "But the order is yours, and the promise is mine to move."

The group didn't vote, and it didn't wait until everyone agreed. One person decided, named before the discussion, by a rule agreed before the answer. Lucía could repeat the reason to Claire without sharing the view. In June Tyler would have smoothed all this over; now the disagreement had a kind, a rule and a name, which is the problem-solver's habit taking hold.

Choose that way when one person has to answer for the result. Ask for everyone's agreement when everyone has to keep the decision, as with a team's working rules. And keep out of the meeting whatever one person can decide and undo alone: say in advance that whoever sees it first decides, then tells the rest.

## Minute forty-one: the owners, one by one

Tyler didn't summarize. He asked each owner for a *read-back*, from *Listening people can feel*: what I understood, what I will do, what I am unsure of.

"Phones are not in this plan," Lucía said. "I'll call Claire today, before six her time. I'm not sure what date to give her."

"None yet," said Bianca. "Ask me at the next planning, on 9 September. By then the fix will have run for a few days."

"I'll fix the double move and show it from two screens by 4 September," said the engineer. "I'm not sure who reads the tests if an agent writes them."

That was Tyler's other decision: who reads what the coding agents write before it merges. Two minutes were left; Lucía's item had used the rest. "Mateo and I will settle that," said Lucía. Mateo, her co-founder, was not on the call. Tyler typed both names. He could see that the line had no date, and he could see the clock, and he let it go.

A chair's summary, or an assistant's, would have said "Lucía to update Claire", and nobody would have known she had no date to give. The unsure part is where an owner tells you what the plan still lacks. In the shared notes, every line with one name and a day was done by that day. The line with two names wasn't, because each of them could wait for the other.

## The other three meetings

The same moves run the rest of an agile team's calendar. Give each meeting one question, and end it when the question has its answer.

| Meeting | The question | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| Stand-up | Who needs whom before tomorrow? | Everyone who is stuck has a name and a time |
| Review | Does it work for the person it was built for? | That person has used it while you watched, and said what they'd change |
| Retrospective | Which one thing do we change? | It has an owner and a day to check whether it helped |

In a stand-up, yesterday matters only where it changes someone's today. In a review, hand over the screen and stay quiet, because applause settles nothing. In a retrospective, start from *the observable version*. A room can argue all afternoon about "the handover was a mess". It can fix "the ticket waited from Monday to Thursday".

## Practice: the message that gets you the floor

**Situation.** Minute two of a planning call. The chief executive has just moved an item to the top. On Monday you saw it fail. Nobody is leaving a gap, so you type in the call's chat.

**First draft (what a careful engineer types).**
"Sorry to jump in, and it may just be the test copy, but I was trying a few things with the override on Monday and saw something a bit odd. Happy to go through it later if useful!"

**What's wrong.** What happened is missing. "Later" gives the room permission to go on.

**Better.**
"On the override: Monday, on the test copy, I moved one truck from two screens and it got two doors. I've seen it once, so I don't know how often it happens. Can we look at that before we add phones?"

**Why it works.** It names the item the room is on and gives one checked fact with its limit. Then it asks for a place in the order, which the chief executive can grant without having been wrong.

**Your turn (5 minutes).** Write yours for a meeting this week: `On [the item]: [what I saw, and when]. [Its limit]. Can we [what you want] before we [the next step]?` Keep it under forty-five words, a target this book sets. Send it in the chat, or say it aloud, item first. **Done means** a colleague who reads it once can say what you saw and what you want the room to do first.

## Practice: one item, said back

**If you do only one, do this one.** Choose one item in a real meeting this week. If you don't run the meeting, tell whoever does what you plan to ask.

**With a person.** Ask three questions, each at its moment:

1. Before the discussion: "Who decides this one?"
2. Before that person speaks, to whoever is closest to the work: "What have you seen that we should know first?"
3. Before the next item, to the owner: "What will you do, by when, and what are you unsure of?"

Watch the third part of the reply. If the owner is unsure of nothing, ask what they will do first tomorrow. **Done means** an hour later you and the owner each write down the decision, the name and the date, separately, and the two match. **Written form.** Send the owner question three after the meeting, and compare their answer with your notes.

## Words to use

- **To sort an item.** "Are we deciding this, or hearing about it?"
- **To hear whoever knows.** "Who worked on this last?" "[Name], you ran it on Monday. What did you see?"
- **To ask what everyone else skipped.** "This may be a basic question. What happens if [it goes wrong]?"
- **When you are the most senior.** "I haven't promised this yet. What should I know before I do?" "I'll go last."
- **To bring the talk back.** "Do we need that to choose, or to do it?"
- **To decide.** "Before we choose: is [rule] a fair way to choose?"
- **To leave it open.** "We can't decide this today. [Name] will bring [the missing fact] by [day]."

### Phrases you will hear

"Let's take this offline" means talking later, without the group: ask who, and by when. "Let's park it" means leaving it for now: ask what would bring it back. "We're aligned" may mean agreement, or only that nobody objected: ask who does what.

## When it backfires

**When they hold the power.** Tyler's questions worked because Lucía let them. Had she said "It goes first", sorting her item aloud would have been a correction in public. Ask once: "Before it goes in, may I tell you what we saw on Monday?" If the answer is no, write the decision down with her name, put the fact beside it, and send both to everyone as the notes. Better, reach her before the meeting, while nothing has been announced.

**When going first is a risk.** Being called on before your manager can feel like a trap, and in some teams it is rude. Ask people privately beforehand, let them write it, or carry the fact yourself with their permission.

**When a decider comes too early.** If the people who must keep a decision haven't been heard, each will decide again, alone, after the meeting. A quick decision the team doesn't follow is slower than another half hour.

**When everything gets sorted.** A choice you could undo by lunch needs no rule and no round. Do it every time and a meeting sounds like a courtroom. Save the read-back for owners: twelve people reciting is a ceremony.

**In a second language.** A fast meeting can close an item while you are still building your sentence. Write it before the call, and ask for each decision to be typed where everyone can see it. If you run the meeting, read the chat aloud before you move on.
