# The explanation

Mateo drew for forty minutes.

It was a Tuesday in the first week of August, and he had flown from Montevideo to Rotterdam for this meeting. Mateo is co-founder and chief technology officer of Tolva, whose scheduler tells each truck which warehouse door to use. Veldhaven, a food wholesaler and Tolva's largest client, was opening its security review of Tolva's access scopes: what the scheduler's login may read and change. When he capped the pen, the whiteboard held eleven boxes, nine arrows and the lifetime of a login token. In red, at the bottom left, was why a scheduler has to change bookings at all. Nothing on it was wrong, and nothing on it was bigger than anything else.

Two people had to decide from it. Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, had a date to plan for. Site one, the first of her three warehouses, would go live on 14 September if the review passed in one round, and on the 28th if it took two. Otávio, Veldhaven's head of information security, had to put his name under the access. If anyone ever came in through it, the breach would be his to explain.

"Does that make sense?" Mateo asked.

"Clear," Otávio said. "Very thorough. Thank you."

Claire took a photo of the board.

Otávio's email came at 7:52 the next morning, copied to Claire. "Under our vendor security policy, an outside company may not change live bookings without a documented need. I cannot approve the access as presented."

The need was on the board, in red. "As I explained yesterday," Mateo typed, and stopped. He deleted it and sent a question: "When someone asks why you approved our access, what do you have to be able to answer?"

Otávio took four minutes. "What it can change. At which sites. How fast I can cut it off."

Mateo went to find Claire. She held up her photo. "Which part of this is my date?"

## What a decision needs

Otávio hadn't changed his mind overnight. He had gone back to his desk with one thing to decide and nothing he could check, so he opened the policy. "I can't tell yet what this login could change" would have helped more, said in the room. But a founder had just drawn for forty minutes, and "Does that make sense?" asks for a polite yes.

Mateo had explained how the connection works to two people who will never build one. Someone who must decide needs to know what each choice does to the thing they answer for, how sure you are, and what would change your advice. Give them that, and people with twice your rank and none of your background can choose well on your word. Keep the rest ready for the second question.

> **Line to keep:** Until they can say what they gave up, all you have is a nod.

One test sorts your material. Take each part and ask: if this worked some other way, would they choose differently? If not, it stays in your notes. Most of Mateo's boxes belonged there. An assistant will draw all eleven on request. Which ones matter depends on what Otávio and Claire answer for, and you learn that by asking them.

> **Research says:** One laboratory study looked for what predicts how far people overrate their understanding of a device. The best predictor: the more of its parts showed, the more they overrated. The study used everyday devices, not diagrams, so treating a nod at a full whiteboard as a weak sign is this book's reasoning.

## One choice, two people

Mateo made a listener sketch of each (*Who is listening*): what they know, have to decide and stand to lose. Otávio knows access controls better than Mateo does. He has to decide whether to sign, and he stands to lose the trust that lets him sign anything. Claire knows what it costs to move a go-live. She has to choose a date, and she stands to lose her word to a board, with the peak coming in December.

Seen from there, the design held one real choice. The login Mateo had drawn could change any booking at all three sites. It existed, and it did far more than the scheduler needs. A smaller login, a separate one for each site, could change one thing: the door. It would take four days to build, in the middle of the round, and Otávio's team would have to read the change.

A choice like that fits a pattern with four slots:

`I recommend [choice], because [its effect on what you answer for]. You give up [cost]. I'd change my mind if [one fact].`

Filled in: "I recommend the small login, because nobody who steals it can cancel a booking. You give up four working days, and perhaps the 14th. I'd change my mind if a login can't be limited to one field."

Say the cost right after the benefit. It is tempting to skip, because it can lose you the argument, and it is what makes the decision theirs.

## Thursday, two rows

On Thursday the whiteboard held two rows, the big login and the small one, with the same truck in both. Mateo said his four slots, then pointed at the truck.

"A truck of canned tomatoes checks in at site one," he said. "Our scheduler picks door two, and the login writes 'door two' on the booking. Either login can do that. Now someone steals the login. With the small one, they can write 'door ten'. A supervisor sees tomatoes at the wrong door and moves them. With the big one, they can cancel bookings at all three sites, and the first person to know is a driver at the gate of your cold store."

That is an architecture explained: one case walked through twice, first working, then with the part in question failing. Engineers already test designs with scenarios; this one is for the person who decides. Mateo's last line says who would feel the failure first: the habit of the system reader, the thinker type Mateo is growing toward.

There he stopped. In next-question order, you stop when the next question is theirs to ask.

"Why only perhaps the 14th?" Claire asked.

"The four days fall inside Otávio's round. If his team can read the change in what's left of it, the 14th holds. If not, the 28th."

"How sure are you?" That was Otávio, in the room.

"What the big one can change, I checked on the test copy yesterday. That a login can be limited to one field, your warehouse-system team told me. The four days I reasoned from the work we did in the spring. How fast you can cut either one off, nobody has tested. We'll test it on Monday, and it's the likeliest reason for a second round."

Each part is a sized claim with its basis word, and the unknown comes with a day and a cost. A decider can plan around that.

"And if I insist on the 14th?"

"Then it's the big login, and we narrow it in October."

"I wouldn't sign that one," Otávio said.

Claire looked at the two rows. "The small one. If it needs a second round, it needs one. I'd rather move a date in September than lose a morning in December."

"Let me check how I explained it," Mateo said. "Otávio, what would you tell your chief executive we chose, and what we gave up?"

"One login per site. It reads that site's bookings and changes one thing, the door. We gave up four days, and maybe two weeks." He was writing as he spoke. His file had its documented need.

On Monday they switched a login off at nine, and at ten it was still working. The reason was the token's lifetime, written on Tuesday's whiteboard in the same ink as the rest. The written result asked for a second round, to see that hour gone. On 20 August Lucía, Tolva's chief executive, told Veldhaven: the 28th. Neither Claire nor Otávio needed to ask why.

## Plain or precise?

"Use plain words" is good advice: a term your listener doesn't know can hide the one thing they would object to. "Stay precise" is good advice too: a simplified claim can be false, and whoever decides on it will hold you to it.

The rule from *The exact word* decides it: plain words for the listener, precision for the claim. If simplifying makes it false, keep the precision and add an example.

Mateo nearly told Otávio that the small login "only touches doors". That is plain, and false: the login also reads bookings. So he kept the claim exact and put the tomatoes in it: "It reads that site's bookings and changes one thing, the door. Someone who stole it could see that tomatoes are due at six. They couldn't cancel them."

| Instead of | Say | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "It runs with admin rights." | "It can change any booking at all three sites." | Reach is what they sign for |
| "It's eventually consistent." | "The stock count can be ten minutes old." | Says how wrong it can be |
| "It scales." | "We tested three sites, never four." | Says where the claim stops |

## Practice: what the model means for Monday

**Situation.** You built a model that ranks customers by how likely they are to cancel. The head of customer care, who has four people on the phones, writes: "Is it good enough to use?"

**First draft (the model builder's answer).**
"It performs well: the area under the curve is 0.87 on the holdout set. At a threshold of 0.5, precision is 0.60 and recall is 0.75, but it's tunable, so it depends on your appetite for false positives. Happy to go through the methodology."

**What's wrong.** It uses a vocabulary her job has never needed, and it answers "How good is the classifier?" She has to decide whom four people call on Monday, and "tunable" hands that back with the choices taken out.

**Better.**
"Yes, for choosing whom to call. I recommend calling the 50 customers it ranks highest each morning, which is what your team can reach by noon. I ran it on the last three months and checked it against the records. On an average day, 30 of those 50 went on to cancel, so 20 calls would go to people who were staying. You would also miss 10 who canceled from lower in the list. Calling 100 reaches 7 of those 10 and takes the whole day. I don't know whether a call changes anyone's mind, because nobody has measured it. If your team leaves 10 of the 50 uncalled, picked at random, two weeks will give us a first answer. If calls change nothing, I'd stop. Fifty or a hundred, from Monday?"

**Why it works.** Her question is answered first, in calls and customers. The cost sits beside the benefit, and the unknown that could reverse the choice comes with a test.

**Your turn (10 minutes, in writing).** Take a choice on your desk that someone else must make. Write it in the four slots, add how you know, then cut every sentence that would leave their choice the same. **Done means** a colleague outside your field reads it once and can say what you recommend, what it costs and what nobody knows yet.

## Practice: ask for the cost back

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.** This week, explain one real choice to the person who decides it, starting with what each option does to what they answer for. Then, in place of "Does that make sense?", ask for a read-back, as Mateo did: what would you tell your boss we chose and gave up?

Watch for the cost in their reply. If only the benefit comes back, walk one case through the failure and ask again. **Done means** they have said the cost in their own words and you had nothing to correct. **Written form.** Send the four slots and ask for the one line they would forward.

**Spar with an AI.** Rehearse the second question before you meet it.

```text
Play the person who must decide this: [role, what they answer for]. You have no
technical background. I will explain a choice in under two minutes. Stop me once,
at the first word only my team would use. When I finish, ask the two questions you
would need answered before signing. Then, as that person, write the sentence you
would forward to your boss: what we chose and what we gave up. Last, list anything
I said that would not have changed your choice.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

- **Before you prepare.** "When someone asks why you approved this, what do you have to be able to answer?"
- **To open.** "There are two ways to do this. Here is what each one does to [what they answer for]."
- **The unknown.** "Nobody has tested [what]. If it goes badly, [what it costs you]. We'll know on [day]."
- **When the detail doesn't change the choice.** "I can show you how that works. It doesn't change what you're choosing."
- **When agreement comes too fast.** "Before you agree, what would you still need to see?"

### Phrases you will hear

- "under the hood": how it works inside
- "at a high level": the main points only
- "What's the catch?": what do we give up?

## When it backfires

**When the decider knows more than you.** Plain words can sound like a lecture to an expert. Otávio needed exact reach, sites and minutes, and no tour. Ask first: "Which part do you want in detail?"

**When they outrank you and want one answer.** "Just tell me which." Give the recommendation and its cost in one sentence, then in writing the same day. If they choose the other way, note the cost of that once, without arguing.

**Where a recommendation comes last.** In some companies people weigh the options before they hear yours. Ask beforehand, and put it where they expect it.

**When one option is there to lose.** A weak option placed beside yours so that yours wins is steering. If there is an option you would rather they didn't see, put it on the board.

**When the last question sounds like an exam.** Make it about your explaining, as Mateo did, or ask in private.

**In a second language.** Pick one word for each thing and repeat it. A "login" that becomes an "account" and then a "credential" sounds like three things. Write the options on the board before you speak so nobody has to remember them.

# The update

Renata: "Someone at Veldhaven says site one is the 28th now. True?"

Lucía: "Yes. I told their chief executive this morning. You'll have it in the August update."

Renata: "He also says the label work for sites two and three slipped three weeks. In June. Your July update says on track."

Renata: "Why am I hearing this from someone else?"

It was 20 August. Lucía is co-founder and chief executive of Tolva, fourteen people in Montevideo whose scheduler decides which truck goes to which warehouse door. Renata, in São Paulo, was its first investor and holds the third seat on its board. Veldhaven, a food wholesaler in Rotterdam, is Tolva's largest client. The first of its three warehouses had been due to go live on 14 September.

Lucía had a defense. The printers at sites two and three had been updated in July. Both sites had kept their November dates. So "on track" had been right about every date Renata knew. She typed half of it and read Renata's question again. None of it was an answer.

In June she had given Veldhaven's chief executive a whole date. It was the 14th if his security review passed in one round, the 28th if it needed a second, and she would know by 20 August. The review needed a second round, and that morning she had phoned him, as promised. Renata had heard the "if" once, on the May board call. In July Lucía gave her two words.

Renata had turned the two words into a date. At the start of August she told her partners that Veldhaven would be live on the 14th. All that morning, people in Rotterdam had known her sentence was wrong, and she had not.

## A date travels without you

A date leaves your hands when you say it. Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, builds shifts on it. Renata takes it to her partners. They speak on your word, and they can't see it move.

So an update has one job: keeping what those people say true. Put the answer first. Send every date with the thing it depends on. When it moves, tell whoever has repeated it that same day, whenever the next report is due.

> **Line to keep:** A date you move in silence is still being repeated.

People can stake their own word on yours, because your dates arrive with their conditions and your bad news arrives from you.

Two habits get you there.

**Write the names.** Before you announce a change, list everyone who has repeated the old version. Lucía's list that morning would have had four lines: Veldhaven's chief executive; Claire; Bianca, the product manager whose Friday report goes to both companies; and Renata. Whoever has to act on the change, or holds your promise, comes first, so the chief executive was the right first call. Next comes whoever will be asked about it soonest. Renata was the next call, and Lucía had planned to tell her in the August update.

**Let the report carry the month and the phone carry the change.** A monthly update is a good place for what you built, spent and learned. A moved date can't wait there for its turn.

## The test becomes the shape

Lucía left the defense unsent and phoned.

"You should have heard both from me. Site one goes live on 28 September if the second review round passes. I'll know by 4 September. If it fails, I don't have a date yet. The November sites need the same review, with two months of room. Your cash number counts no Veldhaven money. Who have you given the 14th to?"

That is the second-question test from *Start here*, answered in order:

1. **What is the point?** The answer, with its date.
2. **What does it rest on?** The one thing the date depends on, and what moved since they last heard.
3. **Where does it stop?** What isn't affected, and what you don't know yet.
4. **What do you want from me?** A decision, one question, or "nothing today".
5. **Who answers for it?** A name, and the day they will hear next.

Answer-first is old advice, and incident reports have long said what broke, what is affected and what comes next. The test insists on two more: what you don't know yet, and a name. The date inside it is a sized claim, from *How sure are you? Say that*: the date, what it depends on, the other date, and when you'll know. Lucía had no other date. She said so instead of inventing one.

Now test it. A busy executive may leave after the sentence with the date. If they left the call there, would they repeat something true? "We're on track for September" fails. "28 September if the second review round passes" survives, because the "if" is inside the sentence.

The shape holds from room to room, and the first sentence changes:

| Who hears it | Start with | Have ready |
|---|---|---|
| Your team, on a status call | What moved since last time | Who it blocks today |
| An executive with two minutes | The date or the decision, with its "if" | The cost of each choice |
| Someone who can decide what you can't | The decision, and by when | What happens if nobody decides |
| An investor | The date or number they repeat to others | What you got wrong since the last update |

## What they can see before the date

"My partners," Renata said. "All of them. And the labels?"

"I left them out because no date had moved. You should have had that in July, to judge for yourself."

Then Renata asked the second question: "How will I know, before the 28th, if the 28th is moving?"

"On two days," Lucía said. "Their policy gives each round ten working days, so by 4 September you'll know whether it passed, in Veldhaven's words. On 18 September the scheduler plans a full day at site one beside their paper plan, and I'll send you how many doors the supervisors changed. If either day goes by without that, I'll call you before you have to ask."

"Write me that. I'll forward it as it is."

> **From practice:** Slow work is quiet between its start and its date, and people fill the quiet with the last thing they heard. Before you begin, agree on points along the way that an outsider could see pass or fail: a result in somebody else's writing, a count, something that ran. "Nearly done" is no use as a point, because only you can see it.

A missed point is bad news while there is still time to plan around it. That evening Renata wrote again: "Sent as it was. They asked what happens if the review fails. I pointed to your fourth sentence."

## Practice: the July paragraph

**Situation.** The last day of July. Lucía writes the Veldhaven paragraph of her monthly update. The security review starts next week.

**First draft (what a careful founder writes).**
"Veldhaven: a strong month, and we remain on track for September. Integration tests at site one are nearly finished, and the printer updates at sites two and three went smoothly. The site teams have been great partners throughout. At the Rotterdam trade fair we had several very promising conversations. More next month!"

**What's wrong.** "On track" drops the condition Renata last heard in May. "Went smoothly" is the last scene of a slip she never heard about. She can't tell which piece of the good news she will be asked to defend.

**Better.**
"Site one goes live on 14 September if Veldhaven's security review passes in one round. If it needs a second, the 28th. I'll know by 20 August and call you that day.

"What moved: the label work for sites two and three slipped three weeks in June. We assumed their printers matched site one's, and nobody had checked. The printers are updated, and Diego, our engineer there, has since printed our labels at both sites. Their November dates still hold; they need the same review, with room for a second round.

"Cash still runs to late April, counting no Veldhaven money.

"Have you given your partners a date for site one? If so, tell me which, and I'll keep it right."

**Why it works.** The date she will repeat comes first and is hard to repeat without its "if". The slip arrives from Lucía, with its cause and its limit. The question at the end puts a name on the list.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** **If you do only one, do this one.** Take the last status you sent and underline the one date or number a reader would repeat. Rewrite that sentence with its condition, and add a line that begins "What moved:". **With a person.** Send it to someone who speaks on your word, then ask, "If [name] asks you about this tomorrow, what will you say?" Listen for the "if". **Done means** their answer has your date and its condition, and you corrected nothing.

## The bad part first

You may want to warm someone up before bad news. The warm-up mostly serves you, because a listener who senses bad news may hear nothing else until it comes.

> **Research says:** In one paper, not directly repeated, people giving mixed news and those receiving it preferred different orders; receivers wanted the bad part first. Hearing it first eased worry, and the relief left them less motivated to change their behavior. Applying that to a slipped date is this book's reasoning: open with the bad part, and when they need to act, put the request right behind it.

One sentence of ownership is enough at the top: "You should have heard both from me." The apology, if you owe one, is a conversation of its own (*The hard conversation*).

## When someone above you has to decide

An escalation is an update whose fourth answer is a decision you can't make. It needs one more rule: the person it is about reads it before it goes. Knowing they will read it takes the complaint out of your draft, and their reply often brings the fact you lacked.

### Practice: the escalation

**Situation.** You are the engineer on a client project. The client's network team has to open one test connection, and acceptance testing starts on the 24th. You write to the project's sponsor, a vice president.

**First draft (what a patient engineer writes).**
"Just flagging that we're still waiting on the network team. I raised it on the 3rd, followed up on the 7th and asked again on Monday. I know they're busy, but it's becoming a real blocker on our side. Any help appreciated."

**What's wrong.** It is a record of the writer's patience. The sponsor can't find a decision, a date or a cost, and the network lead will be asked about a message she has never seen.

**Better.**
"I need a decision from you by Thursday noon: open our test connection this week, or move acceptance testing from the 24th to the 31st. We need five working days between the open connection and the first test. Nothing else is waiting on it. The network lead has read this. Her team is moving the data center until the 21st, and our connection would stop that for half a day."

The sponsor phones: "So whose delay is this?"

"The connection is theirs. I asked three times without saying what it would cost, and that part is mine. What I need is which one moves: the data center by half a day, or the testing by a week."

**Why it works.** She can decide from the first sentence. The network lead's reason is there because the network lead read it. Asked about blame, you give two sentences, your own part included, and go back to the decision.

**Your turn (10 minutes, written).** Take one thing you are waiting for. Write the decision, its deadline and the cost of each choice, and send it first to the person it is about: "Is any of this wrong?" **Done means** they have corrected it or agreed to it, and whoever decides could answer in one line.

## Words to use

- **When a date moves.** "You'll hear this from others today. I wanted you to have it from me." "[New date], if [one thing]. I'll know by [day]."
- **When there is no other date.** "If that fails, I don't have a date yet. I'll have one by [day]."
- **To write the names.** "Who have you given the old date to?" "Who will ask you about this first?"
- **At the start of slow work.** "Before [date], you'll see two things: [one] on [day] and [one] on [day]."
- **Before you escalate.** "I'm asking [name] to decide this. Here is what I'll send. Is any of it wrong?"
- **When someone wants "on track".** "I can send the date with its condition. Without it, people would repeat something we don't know."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Just a heads-up": early notice. Ask whether you need to do anything.
- "Keep me in the loop": tell me when something changes. Ask which changes count.
- "It's green": the report says all is well. Ask what would turn it red.

## When it backfires

**Too many changes.** If you report every wobble, the one that matters looks like the rest. Break the rhythm only when something a listener has repeated stops being true, or a point along the way is missed.

**News that isn't yours.** Lucía could tell Renata her own date. What the reviewers found belonged to Veldhaven. A contract or a confidence comes before speed.

**When the other person holds the power.** If your boss punishes bad news, send it in writing, early, with a choice attached. If someone senior wants "on track", offer the sentence with its condition; they can send another one under their own name. If you can't refuse, keep your version, with its date.

**When going up is read as going around.** Teams differ on who may tell whom. Ask when the work starts: "If this date moves, who hears first, and from whom?" Showing someone the message first is for blocked work; harm or misconduct goes by a formal route (*Difficult people*).

**A second slip.** When the same date moves twice, a clear sentence is no longer enough. Say what you assumed both times, and what you now check before you give a date.

**In a second language.** An "if" at the end of a long sentence is easily lost on a call. Put it first: "If the review passes, the date is 28 September."

# The presentation

One colleague typing question marks can show you the slide where your talk loses the room.

"Type a question mark in the chat whenever you don't know why I'm telling you something," Naomi asked Diego on a Monday late in August. She is a data consultant who works alone from Seattle, and Veldhaven buys her forecast of when trucks will reach its warehouses. On Wednesday she would present it by video to Veldhaven's operations review: fifteen minutes, nineteen slides. Diego is the engineer Tolva has placed at Veldhaven, and Tolva's dock scheduler will plan doors on her forecast. He gave her half an hour to rehearse.

The first mark came on slide five, while she explained how she cleans the gate logs. Eight more had come by slide thirteen. Then they stopped. On slide eighteen she reached her ask: that seven of the carriers serving site three, the cold warehouse, report when each truck leaves its last stop.

"It got better after thirteen," she said.

"No," Diego said. "On thirteen I started answering email. I came back when I heard you ask for something, and by then I didn't know what it was for."

## A quiet room

Diego told her because she had asked him to. The review might never have told her. A bored room doesn't object, and its silence is easy to take for a yes.

Slides five to seventeen, the middle of the talk, showed the forecast in the order Naomi had built it. They answered a question only another data scientist would ask: how is it made? The people on Wednesday's call run warehouses. Once they heard her ask, they would want to know whether they could plan a shift on her forecast.

Build the middle out of the room's questions, one to a section. Decide your ask first. Give people a reason to care about it in the first minute, then answer the questions it will raise, in the order this room will raise them. An assistant can turn your notes into nineteen tidy slides. It can only guess what site three's manager will ask on Wednesday, and you can find out. Get those questions right, and a talk you used to survive becomes a conversation you have prepared for.

> **Line to keep:** A room keeps listening for the answer it is still waiting for.

## The first minute

Naomi's old first slide was an agenda. Her new opening is a working story (*Story for people who think in systems*): one moment, its count and the decision handed over. It runs under ninety seconds, a limit this book sets.

"Two weeks ago, at half past three in the afternoon, your shift lead at site three had two people in freezer jackets beside an empty door. A truck was booked for that time, and my trial forecast agreed. It was still being loaded, at a supplier an hour away, and its carrier knew. Since July, two of your nine carriers have sent the time each truck leaves its last stop. Before I used those times, I missed half their trucks by more than thirty minutes, and two in three of those had left late. Should the other seven send theirs? That's what I'll ask you to decide."

The moment gives the room someone to picture. The handover tells people what they will be asked for while there is still time to think about it. It also starts a question in their heads, and an opening that starts one has done its work.

## The middle, one question at a time

From there, the middle runs on next-question order (*Give it a shape*), with a whole section in place of each sentence. Start from the ask. After each section, answer what this room would ask next.

You can guess some of the questions. Ask someone for the rest. Naomi wrote to Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven and would chair the review: "When I ask you to go to the carriers, what will site three's manager ask first?" Claire answered in one line: "What it costs them, and what we do if they won't." Two guesses and one reply gave Naomi her middle:

1. Could we plan a shift on it?
2. Are two carriers enough to believe that?
3. What does it cost the other seven?
4. What do we do if they won't?

Nineteen slides became six: the moment, the four questions and the ask. Everything about how the forecast is made went behind the ask, where a question can call it up. Each slide that stayed holds only what the room must look at to check the answer. Words she was going to say came off it.

The last two answers were short. It costs one message a trip, and only site three can say how the carriers will take it. If they refuse, the forecast stays out of site three's plan and go-live doesn't move.

> **From practice:** Ask the next question while the old slide is still up. When a slide changes, people start reading, and a question asked into their reading is easy to miss. Say it, give it a breath, then show the slide that answers it.

The tool also tells you when to stop: when the next question is theirs to ask. Naomi cut a fifth section, on the December peak. If December mattered to them, they would ask.

### Practice: one section, with a question in it

**Situation.** The operations review. Naomi reaches the figures for site three, and its manager comes in with a question. The first draft is from the nineteen slides.

**First draft (what a careful data scientist says).**
"This chart is absolute error by site, in minutes, median and spread. Site three has the longer tail. We added departure timestamps as a feature for the two carriers that have them, and you can see the tail come in."

"So can I plan a shift on it?"

"I'm coming to that on slide fourteen."

**What's wrong.** The words belong to her field, so the manager has to turn "tail" into trucks while Naomi keeps talking. Then the manager asks the very question the section exists to answer and is told to wait for a number on a slide.

**Better.**
"Could you plan a shift on it? At site three, not yet. With the leaving time, the forecast is within thirty minutes for about seven arrivals in ten. Without it, the same trucks: about five. That's the two carriers who send it, over seven weeks."

"Two carriers. I have nine. Why would the others be the same?"

"I don't know that they would. Those two bring about a quarter of your trucks, and I checked every one against your gate log. None of the seven weeks was a peak week. Six weeks of the others' times would tell us."

**Why it works.** The section opens on the room's question and answers it before explaining anything. The manager then asks the next question on Naomi's list, and a room that asks your next question before you do is following you. Her second answer stops where two carriers and seven weeks stop: the calibrator's habit.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Take a talk you have to give. Write its ask at the top of a page, and under it the four questions your ask will raise, in the room's words. Message one person who will be there: "When I ask for this, what will they ask first?" Then answer your second question aloud, question first, in about fifty words, a target this book sets. **Done means** a colleague who hears the answer once can say which question it answered and where the answer stops.

## A room you can't see

On Wednesday the review would reach Naomi as six small figures at the far end of one camera. She couldn't read their faces from Seattle, so she arranged for words.

- Diego sat at the table in Rotterdam, and she said why: "I can't see all of you, so Diego will tell me when someone wants to speak."
- The ask and the four questions went to everyone on one page the evening before. If her line dropped, the room would lose the charts and keep the decision.
- She said the slide's number each time it changed, because a shared screen can run behind the voice.
- She stopped sharing her screen before the ask, so the room saw a person asking.

## Rehearse what must be right

"Know it by heart": the first minute comes when nerves are loudest, and a wrong number is hard to take back. "Don't rehearse too much, be natural": a memorized text has no place for a question, and one forgotten word can take the paragraph with it.

They are right about different parts of the talk. Rehearse the parts that must be right: the first minute, the point sentence, the numbers and the two hardest questions. Improvise the surface, which is every sentence in between. In the middle, that means you know your questions by heart, in order, and find the words of each answer on the day. Forget a sentence, and the question is still there to answer.

Naomi rehearsed her point sentence until she could say it anywhere in the talk. "Claire should ask the other seven carriers for leaving times, because without them I can't test my site-three forecast before November."

### Practice: a question mark in the chat

**If you do only one, do this one.**

**With a person.** This week, ask a colleague for fifteen minutes on a call and present the middle of your next talk. They type one question mark whenever they can't say which question you are answering. Don't stop and don't explain.

Afterward, go to the slide where the first mark came and ask, "What did you want to know there?" The reply is often the question your section is missing. Put it first, cut what doesn't answer it, and give that section once more. Watch for marks that stop halfway, and ask whether your colleague stopped too. Writers ask early readers to mark where they got lost; this is the same mark, live.

**Done means** a second run with no question mark between your first minute and your ask.

**Untimed form.** Send the slides with your notes, and your colleague marks them in their own time. In a room, they mark paper.

## When the questions come

Naomi gave the ask, with its date: the leaving times from 7 September, six weeks of trucks, and her yes or no on site three by 23 October. Then she stopped. Site three's manager asked which hours were worst. That was a fact, so she gave it first, "Two to five in the afternoon," and then the slide behind it. Diego wrote to her that the manager wasn't finished.

"Every autumn somebody asks my carriers for one more thing," the manager said. "In December I'm the one asking them for favors."

Naomi **sorted first** (*Thinking on your feet*): a fact, a judgment, a commitment or a challenge? No slide would settle this. It was a challenge, and it was right.

"Those are your favors. Which of the seven would you spend one on?"

"Three of them. They bring half my trucks."

"Then three," Claire said. "I'll phone them before Friday."

Naomi had asked for seven and got three, with a name and a day. The test would be smaller, and the plan was one site three would stand behind. The manager's reason came out because a question met it instead of a defense.

Keep one sentence back for after the questions, because otherwise the last question becomes your ending. Hers was the decision as it now stood. "So, three carriers from 7 September. You'll have my yes or no on site three by 23 October, with a smaller test behind it."

## Words to use

- **To promise the ask early.** "By the end I'll ask you to decide one thing: [the decision]."
- **Between sections.** "That leaves the next question: [the question]."
- **When someone asks early.** "I'll answer that now." Then: "Back to [the question we were on]."
- **When the room has gone quiet.** "I'll stop on this one. What would you want to know before you decided?"
- **When your time is cut.** "I'll skip to the decision and the one risk in it."
- **When you present remotely.** "I can't see the whole room. [Name] will tell me when someone wants to speak."
- **To close after the questions.** "So the decision is [what it is now], and I'll [your part] by [day]."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Walk us through it": explain it step by step. Give your first question, then the answer.
- "I'm conscious of time": please finish soon. Go to the ask.

## When it backfires

**The room breaks your order.** A chief executive says, "Go to the number." Go there. Your order was a guess about their questions, and they have corrected it. The more power they hold, the faster you leave your slides; offer the rest on the page you sent. Defending the sequence costs you more than losing it.

**You save the answer for later.** Once someone has asked, making them wait serves you, not them. A question you raise and answer helps them; an answer you hold back is a trick, and people may notice.

**You do it on every slide.** A question before each chart sounds like a school quiz. Ask between sections only.

**Nobody has to decide anything.** A safety briefing or an audit has to cover every item, whether or not the room is curious. Give the full list, in its own order, and hand it out. If your whole talk answers one question, send a page and use the meeting for what it raises.

**Two rooms in one.** An engineer and a finance lead can want different next questions. Follow the person who decides, and tell the other where theirs will come.

**The quiet means something else.** In some rooms questions go through the most senior person, or wait until afterward. Ask your host beforehand how this room asks, and don't read silence as boredom, or as a yes. Diego could be frank because he was asked; a junior colleague may type no marks at all for someone who signs their review.

**A second language.** Learn the questions between your sections as whole sentences; they carry the talk if an answer comes out roughly. Invite questions in the chat as well as aloud, and take your time with one: "Let me read that once more."

---

# The demo

Two minutes into the demo, door seven stops moving.

On the screen in Veldhaven's boardroom in Rotterdam, one morning at site one is playing back: fourteen trucks at the gate between 5:40 and 6:00, and twelve doors. Tolva's scheduler is sending each truck to a door. A moment ago Lucía, Tolva's chief executive, said "Watch door seven", and the board did. Now the truck above door seven hangs where it is, and a small circle turns in the corner of the screen.

Site one, the first of Veldhaven's three food warehouses, went live two days ago, on 28 September, two weeks late. The board approved the project on the word of Claire, Veldhaven's vice president of operations, who has stopped looking at the screen. She is looking at her chief executive, who in June told this board "September" on Lucía's word.

Diego, the engineer Tolva placed with Veldhaven, types at the laptop, then says to Lucía, "The test feed timed out. Live is fine. I'm watching it now."

Lucía lets eight seconds pass in silence. That is too long: the room has begun to guess how bad it is. Then she steps back from the laptop and turns to the room.

"The screen has stopped. Our test connection to your warehouse system has timed out. Site one's live scheduler runs on a separate connection, and Diego has just checked it: it is assigning doors normally. I can restart, which takes about five minutes, or show you yesterday's rehearsal of these same minutes. That one is a recording, and I'll say so. Either way, you'll have the cause in writing from me tonight."

Veldhaven's chief executive asks what the room is thinking. "Does it stop at three in the morning too, when nobody is watching?"

"Once since go-live," Lucía says. "On its first night, the live scheduler stalled for forty minutes. Your dock supervisors went back to the paper plan, and we had the cause by seven. It was in that morning's report. This is a different fault, in the test copy, and I would rather show you the recording than guess."

He chooses the recording: the same twenty minutes, one morning earlier, with the same late truck. She says "recording" as it starts, and again when the truck reaches door seven. The last slide holds one line: "Keep 9 and 23 November for sites two and three?" The board decides two days later, after reading her note on the cause, and keeps both dates.

## What a demo is for

A demo has one job: to let the person who decides watch their own problem being solved, so the decision you need becomes easy to make. Everything else is a tour.

Build it backward from the decision, and show one real moment in the first two minutes, a target this book sets. Say plainly what is real and what is staged, and rehearse the failure as carefully as the success. Then the demo can break without taking the decision with it.

> **Line to keep:** When the screen stops, the room starts watching you.

## Build it backward from the decision

The first two minutes are a working story, from *Story for people who think in systems*, with the product showing the moment. In Lucía's demo:

- **The decision**, written first, never told first. Her card opened with "Keep 9 and 23 November for sites two and three." Every other line had to serve it.
- **One moment**: one real morning at one site, with one late truck added.
- **The count**: the pilot's shorter wait per truck, from Veldhaven's own gate log, at its real size: one dock, six weeks. Site one, she said, had run two days, too few to count.
- **The handover**: the decision, asked in one sentence, on the last slide.

Over the moving trucks, before the freeze, she said only this:

"It's twenty to six: fourteen trucks, twelve doors. This one is an hour late, so under site one's own rule it lost its door after fifteen minutes. Watch door seven."

It is the board's own gate and a rule its own site manager asked for; the product shows up as a door for one truck.

Showing the result before the features is old advice; the working story adds the decision that chooses the moment. The ask waits until the room has seen it, unless someone asks a direct question or time is short. Then the decision goes first.

### Practice: the demo card

**Situation.** Tomorrow you show your product to a client's leadership team. You have thirty minutes and, so far, an agenda.

**First draft (what a busy founder writes the night before).** "Agenda: platform overview; dashboard and door view; carrier rules and time windows; reporting; roadmap; questions."

**What's wrong.** It is the product in the order it was built, every screen at the same volume. Nothing on it says whose problem gets solved or what the room should decide.

**Better.** Lucía's card for the board, six lines, its moment filled in that morning:

- Decision: keep 9 and 23 November for sites two and three.
- Moment: site one this morning, 5:40 to 6:00, fourteen trucks, twelve doors. Watch door seven.
- Real or staged: real arrivals, replayed on a test copy of their system. One late water truck is ours.
- Count: pilot dock last year, average wait per truck down from about fifty minutes to about thirty, from their gate log.
- Handover: "Do we keep both dates?"
- If it breaks: what broke, what we checked, where it stops, the choice, who sends the cause. Fallback: yesterday's recording, labeled.

**Why it works.** Every line has to earn its place against the first, and the breakdown is planned before anything breaks.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Write the card for your next demo: six lines, the decision first. **Done means** a colleague who reads only your card can tell you what you will ask the room to decide and what it will watch first.

## Say what is real

A working story's moment must have happened. A demo often adds something that didn't, and a demo is a claim: this is what the product does. Size it as in *How sure are you? Say that*, with its basis and its limit. Before the first click, Lucía said:

"Everything you'll see is this morning's arrivals at site one, replayed on a test copy of your warehouse system. One truck is ours: a water delivery that arrives an hour late. We added it so you can watch what happens when a truck misses its slot."

It cost her a little magic and bought her the rest of the meeting. If a board member learns afterward that something was staged, they may wonder what else was, and the doubt can run backward over everything they saw.

Staging a truck is fine. Letting the room believe it was real is where persuasion ends. Keeping a recording in reserve is a common habit, and the label keeps it honest: said aloud and shown on the screen. Passed off as live, it works only if nobody notices, and that is the line this book does not cross.

## When it breaks

The first move is physical: step back from the keyboard, face the people, and let someone else fix it if anyone can. Then answer the room's next question before anyone asks it. The second-question test, from *Start here*, fits a frozen screen exactly:

1. **What is the point?** What broke, in one sentence.
2. **What does it rest on?** How you know, and whether you checked it or were told.
3. **Where does it stop?** What is not affected, and what you don't know yet.
4. **What do you want from me?** The choice you are putting to the room.
5. **Who answers for it?** Who will send the cause, and when.

Lucía's recovery took about thirty seconds and answered every question in the test. In May, one question from Claire had drawn two minutes of history from her. The difference was her card's sixth line, written while nothing was wrong.

Diego did his part. In June he had answered "It should be fine" about label printers he had only partly tested. Here he said "Live is fine" while looking at it, and she passed the check on with his name.

Look at what she left out: no "this never happens", no stack of apologies, no blame. The feed belongs to Veldhaven's own test system, and the people who answer for it were at the table. "Our test connection to your warehouse system" is true and names the side Tolva answers for, so nobody had to defend a team in front of the board.

Then she went back to the decision. A recovery is a detour; the handover is why you came.

> **Myth check:** You may have heard that a failure handled well wins a more loyal customer than no failure at all. Pooled studies of hotels, restaurants and other services found that a good recovery left customers more satisfied than those with no failure, but no more inclined to return or recommend. One field study saw no such lift after a second failure, and none tested demos, so our advice: recover well and never count on a failure to help.

### Practice: the recovery

**Situation.** Twenty minutes into a demo for a client's finance team, the screen freezes.

**First draft (the defense before the answer).** "Oh no, sorry, sorry. This never happens, it worked perfectly this morning. Honestly, I think it's your network, it's been slow all week. Let me just try refreshing. Sorry, one second."

**What's wrong.** Three apologies and a defense arrive before a single fact. "Never happens" has no basis, and blaming the network makes the client's own people defend themselves in front of their boss.

**Better.** "The screen has frozen, and I don't know why yet. Your data and your live system are safe: this demo runs on a copy. I can restart, which takes about three minutes, or show you yesterday's run as a recording. You'll have the cause from me by tomorrow morning."

"Has this happened to your other customers?" asks their finance director.

"Not that I know of, and I haven't checked. Tomorrow's note will answer that. Shall I restart, or show you the recording?"

**Why it works.** The first answer covers the whole test in under fifty words, with what you don't know in the first sentence. The second admits what you haven't checked, adds it to the promise and hands the choice back.

**If you do only one, do this one.** **With a person.** Take ten minutes to prepare and five to rehearse. On three slips of paper, write the three things most likely to break the next time you share your screen, such as the test data or an expired login. On a fourth, write "It stopped, and nobody knows why." For each, plan two lines that answer the test, and a fallback. Then start the demo for a colleague. Two minutes in, they turn over one slip (on a call, they pick a number), and you act as if it had happened. Ask them to listen for what stopped and what is safe, before you touch the keyboard. **Done means** your colleague can write down, after hearing you once, what stopped, what is not affected and what you asked the room to choose.

In the real demo, watch the first question after anything goes wrong. If it is about the decision, your recovery worked; if it is "So is it fixed?", one of your answers was missing.

**Spar with an AI.** Rehearse the worst minute first.

```text
You are the head of finance at a client company, watching my product demo. I will tell you, step by step, what is on the screen. Interrupt once with a failure: a frozen screen, a wrong total or a refused login, and no cause. After each answer I give, ask the one question it leaves open. When none is left, list your questions in order and mark any answer that claimed more than I could know.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

To open:

- "Here is one real morning at [place]. Watch [one thing]."
- "Everything you'll see is real data from [when], except [one thing], which we added so you can see [what]."

When it stops:

- "The screen has stopped. Here is what I know."
- "Your live system is not affected. [Name] has just checked."
- "I can restart, which takes about [time], or show you yesterday's run. That one is a recording."
- "You'll have the cause in writing from me by [time]."

To close:

- "We're out of time, so here is the one thing to decide."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Smoke and mirrors": it looks as if it works, but it is staged.
- "Kick the tires": try it yourself before you trust it.
- "The happy path": the route through the product where nothing goes wrong.

## When it backfires

**Technical audiences.** To engineers and evaluators, one polished moment can look like a trick. Hand them the controls after your two minutes, and show one known failure on purpose, announced as one.

**When the product is what broke.** The test still holds, but the honest answer to "where does it stop?" may be "I don't know yet." Then ask for time to find the cause before the room decides. Pushing the handover right after a real failure turns a recovery into a sales move.

**Power.** Whoever decides controls the clock, and a board can cut thirty minutes to ten without warning. If that happens, say the decision first, then show the moment and give the count.

**Culture.** In some rooms, leaving out a short apology sounds cold; in others, the apology sounds weak. Ask your host beforehand how this room handles a problem in a meeting. Claire told Lucía the board wanted facts first, so Lucía kept her apology for the note she sent that night.

**In a second language.** Under stress, you want a first sentence that is ready. Write it on the card word for word, with the names of the parts most likely to break, and practice those names slowly.
