# The pitch

"So, what does your company do?"

The candidate had read the job ad, and the question was fair. Investors and customers ask it too. An assistant had drafted the ad, and it could have described almost any company. One Tuesday in the middle of August, Mateo, who runs technology at Tolva, a small company in Montevideo, was asking her to become its first support engineer.

He had a sentence ready, the one his co-founder, Lucía, used with investors. "We're a dock-scheduling platform for food distribution," he said, "and before the December peak we go live at three warehouses with our largest client."

She took a moment. "So three warehouses start in three months, and I'd be all of support."

"Yes," said Mateo. Then he explained, for eleven minutes, how the scheduler re-plans when a truck is late.

"Thank you," she said. "I should tell you that I have another offer, in a team of nine. I promised them an answer on Friday."

Nothing Mateo said was wrong. He had given her the news investors like best, and for her it was the worst news.

## A sentence that stays, a reason that moves

A pitch has two jobs. It lets a stranger picture what you do, and it gives this listener a reason to decide. Build the two separately. The sentence that says what you do stays the same for everyone. The reason after it is the one this listener needs, so it changes with each person.

> **Line to keep:** Of all your reasons, lead with theirs.

Start with the sentence that stays. "Dock-scheduling platform" shows nothing, so the candidate pictured the only thing she could: three start dates. Write what a recording would show (the observable version, from *The exact word*). Tolva's recording shows trucks, doors and a clock: "We decide which truck goes to which warehouse door, and when."

| Instead of | Say | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "A patient-engagement solution" | "We text clinic patients the day before, and refill the slots they cancel." | A company: a message, a slot, a day |
| "Predictive arrival insights" | "I forecast when a warehouse's trucks will reach its gate." | One person's work, and who uses it |
| "An onboarding initiative" | "A new engineer will release a change in their first week." | A project, as someone will see it |

Saying what a customer can see is old advice. The harder part is leaving the sentence alone once it works: learn it, and use it in the ad, on the site and on the call. If your company does three things, choose the one a customer would miss first. The other two can wait for a question.

Then find the reason that moves. Fill in the listener sketch for one person: what they know, what they have to decide, what they stand to lose. Write your point sentence, `[this listener] should [believe or do this], because [the one reason]`, and take the reason from the last two lines of the sketch.

Don't take it from what convinced you. Mateo has stayed with Tolva's problem for three years because one late truck can undo a whole morning's plan, and he finds that beautiful. It explains why he is there. It gives a support engineer no reason to turn down a team of nine.

## What a bad week looks like

That evening Mateo could fill in two lines. She knew the ad, three dates and a team of one. She had to choose between that and a team of nine, by Friday. The third line he left blank. He might have written "her evenings". He sent her a question instead: "Before we talk again: what does a bad week look like where you are now?"

"I open a ticket," she wrote back. "The customer asks every day, and every day I apologize. I've been apologizing for one export since March."

Ask about the work, and listen for the loss. She could carry three warehouses; she was tired of apologizing for faults she wasn't allowed to fix. So the reason that was hers, *you can fix what you hear about*, was easy to write, and at Tolva it was false. The ad said support would "triage and escalate". Mateo had to make it true before he could say it, so he gave the job the same access to the code that every engineer has, under the same review. When the reason they need is false, you have two honest choices: change the work, or leave the reason out.

On Thursday he called. "We decide which truck goes to which warehouse door, and when. You'd be the first to hear when we decide wrong, and you'd have the access to fix it."

Then a working story, built backward from her decision:

"In July, a shift lead at our client wrote to me: 'Your nightly email says the flour comes at one in the morning. It comes at six.' The email showed Montevideo time. The fix took me ten minutes. She waited four days for it, and by then her shift had stopped opening the email. That month the client's sites sent me twenty-six messages. Nine needed a change in the code, and those would be yours. The other seventeen needed a clear answer. No site is live yet, so I can't tell you what a live month looks like. Would you want those nine?"

"What happens when two sites go wrong on the same night?" she asked. It was her second question, and no ad had an answer to it.

"You take one and I take the other, until we hire a second person. I don't know when that will be, so I can't give you a date. My nights I can put in the offer."

"Put the access in the offer too," she said. On Friday she signed it.

Mateo used one proof, his strongest, with its limit attached. A second, weaker one can feel like more support. Cut it.

> **Research says:** In two experiments about everyday causes, people given weak evidence for an outcome judged it less likely than people given none. In a later online experiment, this happened to listeners who expected the speaker's strongest evidence, and not to those who expected hedging. That a pitch audience expects your strongest, and that a weak proof hurts beside a good one, is our reasoning, untested here.

## Words Renata can carry

Late in August, Renata, Tolva's first investor, offered Lucía an introduction to a partner at another fund: "Send me something I can forward."

Renata couldn't say yes for that fund. She could only carry the words. Before you pitch, ask whether this listener can decide. If they can't, get to the person who can, or write lines that hold up when someone else delivers them. And size the request: before a first meeting, an investor decides only whether an hour is worth it.

"Tolva's software decides which truck goes to which warehouse door, and when. Three warehouses start on it between September and November, so if the dates hold, their December logs will show whether it works at full size. An hour now lets you say what you'd need to see in them. So far: one pilot dock, six weeks, average wait per truck down from about fifty minutes to about thirty, by the client's gate log. No whole warehouse has run on it yet. The first starts on 28 September, if a second security review passes."

The partner wrote back: "The three peak weeks, by site, from the client's own log. When could I have those?" She had started deciding.

Change the reason for each listener as often as you like, as long as they could meet and agree on the facts.

## What to admit, and when

You have been told to be open about what is hard, because people trust someone who admits things. You have also been told never to show doubt to a person who is judging you.

The first is right about anyone who will live with the flaw. Mateo's four days would have met her in her first week, and hearing it from him let her weigh it. The second is right about someone with few facts and someone else to convince: one confession can become most of what they know, and all of what they repeat.

So choose by who is listening. With people who will work beside you, say something of your own early, the flaw included. With investors, clients and bosses, show competence first, then the admission, and make it a limit of what you know. Lucía gave the gate log, then "No whole warehouse has run on it yet." A partner can check that, and watch for the day it changes. "We're honestly a little overwhelmed" gives her a worry about Lucía, with nothing to check.

## Practice: the request to finance

**Situation.** You lead a platform team. On Friday the head of finance closes next quarter's budget, and she has asked every team for one short message: what, how much, why this.

**First draft (what a careful engineer writes).**
"We'd like a read replica for reporting. Analytics queries currently hit the primary database, which isn't how anyone would design it today. A replica is the standard pattern, it's low risk and easy to reverse, the team knows it well, and it sets us up for growth. The cost is modest, about 1,400 euros a month. Glad to go through the design."

**What's wrong.** Every line is accurate, and it answers a question she didn't ask: is this good engineering? Hers was: why this, out of everything on my list? Six reasons, and none of them touches her month. "Modest" is hers to judge.

**Better.**
"On the last day of each month, the finance reports and our customers' orders share one database, and the orders wait. At the last three month-ends, checkout took more than ten seconds for two to four hours; I read that from our logs. I'd like a second copy of the database, for reports only: 1,400 euros a month, from October. It would take the reports out of checkout's way. Whether your reports would also run faster, I haven't tested. Can you give me a yes or no by Friday?"

She replies: "And if it's no?"

"Then I'd run the reports overnight. That costs nothing, and your team would have them at seven instead of on request. If you can live with that on the last day of the month, no is a good answer."

**Why it works.** It opens with something anyone at the checkout could see. It gives the one reason that falls in her month, with one proof and its limit. The price has no adjective. A budget holder is always choosing against something else, so the second answer tells her what a no would cost and who would pay it.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Take something you need money, people or time for. List your reasons and cross out each one you could give only to a colleague. Write the message with one reason, its proof and its limit, then your answer to "And if it's no?" **Done means** someone outside your field reads it once and can say what is being bought, what the claim rests on and what a no would cost.

## Practice: one sentence, one listener

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.** Say the sentence that stays to someone outside your field and ask: "If you stood there, what would you see?" Change it until their answer is right.

Then choose one person whose yes you need this month. Write their three lines, leave the last one blank, and ask them one question about their own work to fill it in. Say your sentence and their reason in under thirty seconds, a target this book sets. **Untimed form.** Send both in a message.

Now listen for the next question. "What is it, exactly?" means the sentence failed. "Why would I?" means the reason was still yours. A question about cost, dates, proof or limits means they have started deciding. **Done means** you have their next question written down, word for word, and it is one of that last kind.

## Words to use

- **What you do.** "If you stood in [place], you'd see [what]."
- **To find their reason.** "What does a bad week look like where you are now?" "What else are you choosing between?"
- **To find who decides.** "Who else has to agree, and what will they ask you?"
- **The proof.** "The strongest thing I can show you is [proof]. It doesn't cover [limit]."
- **An admission, upward.** "We haven't shown [what] yet. We'll know by [when]."
- **The graceful exit.** "If this isn't yours to take on, who should I ask?"

### Phrases you will hear

- "What's your moat?" (What would stop someone from copying you?)
- "What's the traction?" (What shows that people want it: contracts, use, renewals?)
- "Give me the elevator pitch." (Say it in half a minute.)

## When it backfires

**When you have no proof.** Say so, and offer the test: "Nobody uses it yet. Here is what we'd measure in the first month, and what would make us stop." A weak proof dressed as a strong one fails at the second question.

**When two listeners share the room.** Use the reason of the person who decides, and tell the other one afterward what it means for them. Two reasons at once sound like a list.

**When they hold the power.** If a senior person cuts in, give the request and stop; the reason can wait for their question. If the answer is no, a second reason sounds like pressure. Ask what would have to change, and when you may ask again.

**When asking is read as haste.** In some companies a request in the first meeting is welcome; in others it costs you the second one. Ask whoever introduced you how decisions get made there, and put the request in writing afterward.

**In a second language.** Learn the sentence that stays word for word, and say it until it needs no attention. Then all of your attention is free for the question that follows it.

---

# The sale

Hugo: "Thirty-four minutes. Gate to door, between five and seven, over three weeks. After seven it's nine."

Lucía: "Then five to seven is where we start. The scheduler re-plans the doors every time a truck checks in."

Hugo: "Can it show the temperature in the trailer?"

Lucía: "Yes. We can add that."

Hugo: "Does it know where each truck is standing in the yard?"

Lucía: "It can. We'd build you a map."

Hugo: "Texts to the drivers?"

Lucía: "Yes, those too."

Hugo: "Good. Send me a proposal."

The video call, on a Tuesday late in August, stayed friendly to the end. Lucía is co-founder of Tolva, which makes dock-scheduling software in Montevideo. Hugo runs operations at Sarnik, a distributor of chilled and frozen food near Lyon. In July he had told her that Sarnik didn't know how long a truck waited for a door. He had gone and counted, and she had answered his count with three yeses.

That evening an assistant turned her notes into eleven pages: a temperature module, a yard map, a messaging service, four warehouses, 8,400 euros a month for each. Hugo replied the next morning. "I asked if it could. I did not ask for it. Those questions were my engineers' list. What does five to seven cost?"

## Questions, heard as orders

Hugo was right: the proposal priced features he didn't need. Each of his questions had a short, true answer ("It could. We haven't built it."). Lucía answered three questions with three promises, because a yes kept the call pleasant. The questions that would have set a price went unasked: what he was deciding, who would sign, and what thirty-four minutes cost them.

Selling well is mostly finding out what is true and writing it down so someone else can check it.

A sale is a decision another person has to make and then explain. The second question may come from someone you never meet, and your buyer will have to answer it for you. So fill in their side of the decision with them, and say it back before you price it. Write a proposal whose every line they can check, say the price as something you have decided, and sort the objection before you answer it.

> **Line to keep:** Sell a decision they can explain without you.

## The call that should have come first

On Thursday Lucía phoned. "You're right. I priced your engineers' list. May I ask three things before I write another line?"

Her questions were the listener sketch from *Who is listening*, filled in aloud: what Hugo knew, had to decide and stood to lose. Asking before offering is among the oldest advice in selling. The sketch tells you what to ask, and when you have asked enough.

| The sketch | Lucía asked | Hugo said |
|---|---|---|
| **Know** | "What have you tried for five to seven?" | "Earlier slots. Carriers ignore them. Now I'm getting another quote." |
| **Decide** | "What do you decide, by when, and who signs?" | "Next year's budget, in October. I recommend. Our finance director signs." |
| **Lose** | "When you show her the number, what will she ask first?" | "What she asks me now. Why we pay carriers to wait." |

The third question never mentions losing. It asks what happens to your answer next, and the loss comes back in the reply: every month, Hugo explains a cost he can't yet bring down.

Look at her second question. Hugo could stop this purchase alone; he could not start it alone. Whoever signs may care about something your contact has never had to count, so ask to meet them before you price anything. Lucía asked: "Could I have ten minutes with her first?"

> **Research says:** In three experimental and field studies, people underestimated by as much as half how likely others were to agree to a direct request for help. A separate lab later found the same kind of underestimate. The requests were for help, so asking for the introduction, in person where you can, is our step; they say nothing about the order.

The finance director gave them ten minutes on Monday. Hugo had counted minutes; she had been paying for them. At the warehouse he had timed, carriers had billed 4,100 euros for waiting in July.

Then Lucía used the read-back: what she understood, what she would do, what she was unsure of. "At your busiest warehouse, trucks wait thirty-four minutes from five to seven, and you're billed for it. I'll write one page about that and leave everything else out. I'm not sure whether you'd start with one warehouse or four."

"One," said Hugo. "And it's not the busiest. It's the one with the fewest doors."

Tolva's price depends on doors and trucks. One wrong word would have put a wrong number on the page.

## A page they can check

Every claim in a proposal is a sized claim, from *How sure are you? Say that*: the claim, its basis, its limit. On a call you can add the limit when someone asks. On paper nobody can ask, so print it.

### Practice: the proposal

**Situation.** On the last day of August Lucía writes again, for Hugo and for the finance director who signs.

**First draft (what went out on Tuesday, shortened).**
"We are pleased to propose a complete dock-management platform for Sarnik's four warehouses, combining real-time scheduling, trailer-temperature monitoring, a live yard map and driver messaging. Clients report significant reductions in waiting time. The investment is 8,400 euros per warehouse per month, all modules included. We look forward to a long partnership."

**What's wrong.** It answers questions asked in passing and skips the one he came with. "Significant" has no count behind it. Nothing says what Tolva hasn't shown, and the finance director can't tell which part of 8,400 euros would shorten any wait.

**Better.**
"To decide in October: should next year's budget include our scheduler at the one warehouse you timed?

"The problem, as you corrected it: between five and seven, a truck there waits thirty-four minutes for a door (Hugo's count, three weeks). In July, carriers billed 4,100 euros for waiting (your invoices).

"What we have shown: at one client's dock, the average wait fell from about fifty minutes to about thirty, over six weeks, by their own gate log. What we haven't shown: a whole warehouse, cold or not. Our first is due to start in late September, if a security review passes.

"The price: 5,000 euros a month for that warehouse. July's waiting charges wouldn't cover it, even if every one disappeared. Whether the rest is worth it (the cooling units running in your yard, the calls before seven) is yours to judge.

"Left out, because you didn't ask for them: trailer temperature, the yard map, driver texts.

"To check us: send your three weeks, and we'll replay them truck by truck before you sign anything. Questions about any line come to me. Lucía"

**Why it works.** It opens on their decision and uses their numbers, each with its source. It prints the limit and does the subtraction the finance director was going to do anyway. Either of them can repeat the case from this page.

**Your turn (12 minutes).** Take a proposal, a quote or a budget request you've sent. Rewrite it on one page: the decision, the signer, the problem in their numbers, what you've shown and haven't, the price, what you left out, one check they can run. **Done means** a colleague who reads it once can tell you the price, what it buys and the one thing you haven't shown.

## Say the price

Two pieces of advice about saying a price each have a good case. Soften it: a number can threaten someone's budget and their standing, and a person who feels pushed may stop weighing it. Project it: say it flat, because "only" and "roughly" announce that it can move.

Use both, on different things. Soften what the price costs the person, and leave the content alone. Tell them before their boss hears it, give them the page that explains it, and let them say no without embarrassment. Then say the number at full strength. The same goes for a limit, and for any point the room keeps passing over.

Lucía said it on the Monday call: "It's five thousand euros a month, for that warehouse." She stopped there, as *Say less* teaches. She had a lower number in her head and left it there. If four thousand was possible, Hugo would have been right to ask what the other thousand had been for. A price should move when what it covers moves: a shorter term, a narrower scope, less support.

## The objection, and a no

On 10 September Hugo called. "Your page is clear. The other company quotes two and a half thousand. And my engineers say they can build it themselves in six weeks, with a coding assistant. So tell me your number again."

Treat an objection as a disagreement and sort first: say to yourself which kind it is, and you know what would settle it.

| You hear | It may be about | What could settle it |
|---|---|---|
| "You're twice their price." | What is true: is it the same job? | One test, agreed first, run on both |
| "My team could build it." | What to do | The goal: what must still work in two years |
| "There's no budget." | Who gets something limited | A fair rule, and who decides |

Lucía took the price first. "Five thousand euros a month, for that warehouse. I haven't seen theirs run, so I can't tell you it's worse. Give us both the same three weeks and count the trucks that would still have waited past thirty minutes. If theirs does as well, buy theirs."

Hugo wrote that down. "And the build?"

"They can build a first version. Ask them who answers for it at five in the morning, in its second winter."

"That I will ask." He read something on his screen. "Five thousand is clear. And it's no. One dock, six weeks: your own page says it. I can't put that in front of her."

Everything in this chapter was done well, and it failed. The price was clean, the objections were sorted, and the reason he gave was the limit she had printed. A rounder claim might have got past him that afternoon. It would have left Hugo to explain the first bad night to the person who signed.

Lucía didn't cut the price or argue with her own sentence. She asked, "What would you need to see?"

"A warehouse running on it, nights included. My budget closes in October."

"Then I'll call you when I have one, and I'll tell you how the nights went. The price will be the same."

"Call me, then."

### Practice: three lines before the price

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.** Before you next send a price (a quote, a day rate, a request for budget), send the person three lines. First, the problem in their words, with their number. Second, what they decide, by when, and who signs. Third, the one thing you're unsure of.

End with "What did I get wrong?" and hold the price back for their answer. Watch for the word they change: it may be the one you were about to price. **Done means** their reply corrects or confirms each line and names whoever signs.

**Spar with an AI.** Paste this in, and expect a no.

```text
Play the head of operations at a company that may buy from me.
Another vendor quoted half my price, and your engineers want to build it.
Ask what I sell and what it costs. Raise both objections, one at a time.
Interrupt me once. Whatever I answer, end with a no and one honest reason.
Let me reply to the no. Then stop playing and tell me: the price you heard,
any point where I lowered it or apologized for it, and whether I found out
what would change your answer.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

- **When they ask "Can it...?"** "It could. We haven't built it. What would you use it for?"
- **To find whoever signs.** "Who else will read this?" "What will they ask first?"
- **The price beside their cost.** "It's [amount] a month. [What they counted] alone doesn't cover it. The rest is yours to judge."
- **A lower quote.** "I haven't seen theirs run. What test would you trust for both of us?"
- **To hold the price.** "I can change what's included. For what's on this page, the price is the same."
- **A no.** "That's clear, thank you. What would you need to see?"
- **To leave.** "Then I won't follow up before [the thing they need]. You'll hear from me when it happens."

### Phrases you will hear

"What's the ballpark?" (roughly how much?) "Can you sharpen your pencil?" (can you charge less? Ask what they would take out.) "That's above my pay grade." (someone else decides. Ask who.)

## When it backfires

**When they only want a number.** Someone who has asked your price twice and received questions has a reason to leave. Give the number, or the range and the one fact it depends on, and then ask.

**When they hold the power.** A large buyer's process may forbid calls or ask for a figure in a box. Send your questions by the route it names, and put your limit in the one free-text field.

**When "who signs?" embarrasses.** In front of a team, or where rank is sensitive, it can sound like "so you don't decide". Ask in private, and ask who else will read the page.

**When you need this sale to pay salaries.** Holding a price is harder with nothing behind it. Decide your lowest number, and what comes out at that number, before the call (*Negotiation* has the preparation).

**When the count says they don't need you.** Say so and stop. You will have lost an order and kept someone who believes your next number.

**In a second language.** Type the price in the chat as you say it. If an objection arrives as an idiom, ask for its figure: "What number did they give you?"

# The brief

Mateo: "Write the migration that adds site two's doors. Same as site one."

The agent, six minutes later: "Done. Site two's doors are in, with site one's settings: sign numbers, door types and the fifteen-minute rule for late trucks. I wrote 28 tests, and all of them pass."

Mateo read it twice. He is co-founder and chief technology officer of Tolva, whose software decides which truck goes to which warehouse door. On that last Thursday in August its largest client, Veldhaven, was a month from going live at site one, and site two would follow in November.

Fifteen minutes is site one's rule; in July, site two's manager had asked for thirty. Site one also has a problem of its own. The sign above a door there shows one number and Veldhaven's system uses another, so Tolva keeps a list that matches them. The agent had copied that list to a building where nobody at Tolva had checked a single sign. The 28 tests had passed because they came from the same guess.

Mateo typed, "What did you have to assume?" The answer ran to nine lines. He deleted the migration.

That morning he had handed a person a job in nearly the same words. "Set up the morning replay for site two," he wrote to a junior engineer. "Same as site one." The reply: "Before I start: I think site two asked for thirty minutes, and site one has fifteen. Which do you want? And which morning should I replay?"

## Four words, nine guesses

"Same as site one" felt exact to Mateo, because he carries all of site one in his head. The junior engineer had been at the stand-up in July when somebody said thirty, so he could see a gap and ask. The agent had never been at a stand-up. Unless told to ask, an agent usually guesses, and the guess comes back looking finished.

When work comes back wrong, read your instruction before you judge whoever followed it.

A brief hands over decisions. Whatever you leave out still gets decided, by a question, by a guess or by the experience of whoever you asked. Leaving something out is often right, because that is how you give an able colleague room. So decide what only you can decide, say what is theirs, and hear their plan while it is still easy to change. Then you can hand work to a person or a machine and get back what you meant, starting this afternoon.

> **Line to keep:** Every gap in a brief gets filled, so choose the ones you leave.

## Decide it on one page

The brief combines tools you have. Write a line or two for each of these, whoever receives it.

- **The point.** A point sentence from *Know what you think*: what you need, and the one reason. The reason lets them handle the case you forgot.
- **Done.** The observable version: what a recording would show or a number would state when the work is finished, and what must stay as it is.
- **Known and assumed.** The facts they need, each with its basis word: checked, told, reasoned or assumed.
- **The read-back.** Their plan, before the work starts: what they understood, what they will do, what they are unsure of.
- **The name.** The last question of the second-question test: who answers for it? One person, who reads the result before it goes further.

Tickets have long carried an aim and acceptance criteria, and careful teams list their assumptions. I'd add the basis words, the read-back and the name, all before anyone starts.

Mateo's second brief to the agent took him twenty minutes:

"Add site two's doors to the scheduler, because testing there starts in the first full week of October.

"Done when three things are true on the test copy. Every door on Veldhaven's list for site two appears once, under the number on its sign. A late truck there loses its door after thirty minutes. Every door at site one keeps its number, its sign and its fifteen minutes.

"Checked: our sign list covers site one only. Told, by site two's manager: thirty minutes. Assumed: at site two, the signs and the system use the same numbers. Diego walks the dock on Tuesday, so leave the signs until then.

"Before you start, send me your plan: what you understood, what you will do, what you are unsure of. If a fact is missing, ask. Don't fill it in.

"Who reads it before it merges: Lucía and I will agree."

Under *what I will do*, the plan said it would rebuild the sign list as one list for both sites. Mateo asked, "What else reads that list?" The agent answered: "Site one's dock screens." He wrote, "Then leave site one's rows alone, and put site two's beside them." The correction took one sentence, because there was nothing to undo.

Under *what I am unsure of*, it asked which rule covers a truck already on its way when the rule changes. Mateo didn't know. The plan had found a gap he hadn't seen, and the question went to site two's manager.

On Tuesday, Diego, the engineer Tolva has placed at Veldhaven, wrote: "Every sign matches except three and four, which were swapped when the dock was painted. The drivers know. No file does." The word *assumed* had told Mateo where to send him.

## A colleague or an agent

The same lines serve both. What goes into them changes.

| Where they differ | With a colleague | With an agent |
|---|---|---|
| What they already know | Often more than you; ask | Only what you give it or let it read |
| What happens at a gap | They may ask, or wait, or use experience | It usually guesses, unless told to ask |
| What a wrong try costs | Their day, and some of their patience | Minutes to make; longer to notice |
| What to leave open | How they do it | Only what you could accept either way |
| Who answers | They can, if they agree first | A person, named before it starts |

The junior engineer's second brief was half as long, because he knew about the thirty minutes. He lacked the reason: "so site two's manager can watch one of his own mornings before he trusts our plan." He lacked the morning, and what done looked like: "every truck in that Tuesday's gate log, from five to nine, appears once." How to build it was his.

Mateo made asking cheap, too. The engineer had written his two questions at nine and sent them at twenty to ten. "I thought I should know already," he said. So the new brief ended: "Questions by noon, please. I don't expect you to know this already."

> **Research says:** A review of teaching experiments found that help which serves beginners well can stop helping, or even hurt, people who already know the subject. A later pooled analysis of sixty studies agreed, and found that giving beginners help mattered more than holding it back from experts. Both were about learning; applying them to a brief, and adding detail when you are unsure, is our reasoning.

## When the work comes back

A plan is a promise about the work. Before the result goes out under your name, check three things.

1. **Hold it against the done line, using something its maker didn't make.** Tests an agent wrote from its own guess show only that the code agrees with the guess.
2. **Ask, "What did you have to assume?"** People and agents can both answer; take an agent's list as *told*. Anything that wasn't in your brief is a gap somebody filled.
3. **Look for yourself at the part that would hurt someone first if it were wrong.** For Mateo's migration, that was site one's doors.

For the replay, Mateo counted the trucks in the gate log himself: fifty-eight. The replay had fifty-seven. The missing truck had checked in at 4:58 and was still waiting at five. Nobody had been careless; the brief said "from five." They added it, and the next brief said "everyone at the gate by five."

Then comes the name. You answer for what goes out under yours, however it was made, so settle who reads it while nobody is in a hurry.

> **Research says:** In one study, people made accountable for their results or their accuracy were less likely to miss what an automated aid missed, or to follow it against better information. When professional pilots were assigned accountability in another, it made no significant difference. So one name on the brief is our reasoning, and it doesn't replace the check.

The migration came back two days after Diego's message, with its tests passing, in the week Mateo was answering the second round of Veldhaven's security review. It wouldn't run until October, so it waited, unread. The last line of his brief still said "Lucía and I will agree," and he and Lucía, his co-founder and Tolva's chief executive, had set no day for it. It was the one gap still open, and he hadn't chosen it. In October, somebody would fill it by merging.

### Practice: the brief for Thursday

**Situation.** You run a small software company. On Thursday a customer decides how many seats to renew, and you ask a colleague who joined in May to prepare the numbers.

**First draft (what a careful founder writes).**
"Hi! So, we signed them last November, and the rollout was slow because of their login system. In June a whole team left and usage dropped. The renewal call is Thursday. Could you pull the usage numbers together and make them nice and clear? Whatever you think is useful. Thanks!"

**What's wrong.** The history comes in the order it happened, and the decision the numbers are for never comes at all. "Usage" and "clear" are labels. "Whatever you think is useful" leaves open the one choice only you can make.

**Better.**

- "Please make one page on how many people at the customer used the product each week since April, because on Thursday they choose between 40 seats and 20."
- "It's done when there is one line per week, up to last Friday, and beside each drop, what happened, or that we don't know."
- "Checked: they pay for 40 seats. Told, by their manager: a team of ten left in June. Assumed: signing in counts as using it."
- "Before you start, send me your plan and whatever you're unsure of, by noon tomorrow. The layout is yours."
- "I'll read it on Wednesday at four. I present it, so I answer for it."

**The read-back.** "I'd count people who ran a report, because sign-in happens by itself every morning. All right?" "Yes. Say so on the page."

**Why it works.** The reason lets your colleague judge every later choice. Done can be seen. The weakest fact is labeled, so she knew which one to question, and her answer cost one message.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Take the next job you'll hand over, to a person or an agent, and fill this in: `I need [what], because [the one reason]. Done when [what anyone could see], and [what must stay as it is]. Checked: [facts]. Assumed: [facts]. Send me your plan before you start. [One name] reads it before [the next step].` Then mark each gap you left: *theirs* or *forgotten*. Fill the forgotten ones. **Done means** someone outside the work can read it once and say what they'd look at to know the job is finished, and who answers for it.

### Practice: hear the plan first

**If you do only one, do this one.**

**With a person.** Hand over one real job this week, and ask for the plan before the work starts. Look for a step you didn't expect and a question you can't answer. Each shows you a gap. If the plan only repeats your words, ask, "What would you do first, and what could stop you?" Watch whether their next question is about the reason or a detail, and put more of that in your next brief. **Done means** you have the plan in their words, and you've corrected one step or answered one question before any work exists.

With an agent, do the same, and have it stop after the plan.

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

- **To hand it over.** "I need [what], because [the one reason]." "It's done when [what anyone could see]." "How you do it is yours."
- **To mark what you know.** "I checked this. I'm only assuming that."
- **To make asking cheap.** "Questions by [time], please. I don't expect you to know this already."
- **To an agent.** "If a fact is missing, ask. Don't fill it in." "Send the plan and stop there."
- **When it comes back.** "What did you have to assume?" "Which part are you least sure of?"
- **When the brief you get is vague.** "Here is what I think done looks like: [it]. What would you change?"

### Phrases you will hear

- "Take a stab at it": make a first try. Ask how finished it should be.
- "Run with it": decide the details yourself. Ask which ones are really yours.

## When it backfires

**When the job is small.** A name changed in one file needs a sentence. Write the page when a wrong result would be hard to undo or would reach a customer.

**When the receiver knows more than you.** Steps sent to an expert can sound like doubt. Give the point, done and the facts only you have, then ask how they'd do it.

**When the vague brief comes from above.** You can't make a client or a chief executive write the page. Write it yourself in four lines and ask them to correct it, in private.

**When the goal isn't decided.** Nobody can brief a result they haven't chosen. Brief the question instead: "Three rough options by Friday, none finished."

**When a question feels like weakness.** In some teams every plan comes back certain. Say first what you're unsure of in your own brief, and ask for one thing from them.

**In a second language.** Use one name for each thing and keep it to the end; a second word for variety can read as a second thing. Invite the plan in writing, so nobody has to find the English while you wait.

# On the page

Your page may reach its reader as two lines in a list on a phone.

On the evening of 30 September, Bianca's two were these:

"Subject: Incident summary, board demo, 30 September"

"Hi all, please find below an overview of the events before and after today's interruption."

Bianca is product manager at Tolva, whose scheduler sends trucks to doors at Veldhaven, a food wholesaler in Rotterdam. That day Tolva's demo to Veldhaven's board had frozen on a test connection. Lucía, Tolva's chief executive, had promised Veldhaven's chief executive the cause in writing that night, and had asked Bianca to write it up.

Under those two lines came a full page: every minute in order, from what Diego, Tolva's engineer in Rotterdam, had found in the logs that afternoon. The cause was in line nineteen. The page was going to three people: the engineer who would fix the fault, Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, and the chief executive.

Before she sent it, Bianca sent it to herself. In the list on her phone, between a calendar reminder and a parcel notice, it showed a date and "please find below".

She read it as each of the three. The engineer would find nothing to fix, Claire nothing about her docks, and the chief executive nothing about Friday. On Friday his board would decide whether to keep the November dates for sites two and three.

No single pair of lines could serve all three, so she wrote three.

## Written for someone who stops early

On a call, Claire would have interrupted to ask about her docks. A page can't be interrupted. Whoever opens it decides alone, from the top, whether to go on.

So write the first two lines for a reader who will stop there, and make sure that reader still does the right thing. Everything below them answers the second question, for the reader who wants to ask it. Two lines are a target this book sets: in a message, the subject and the first sentence; in a chat, the first two sentences. Line one is the front half of your point sentence, what this reader should do or believe. Line two is the day, the reason, or the news that you need nothing.

> **Line to keep:** Who reads your third line? The person your first two were written for.

Putting the news first is old newspaper practice. A newspaper has to choose the news for everyone; you can choose it for one person.

Get good at this and your work moves while you sleep. An engineer in another time zone starts the fix, a client answers her own team, a board decides, and nobody books a call to find out what you meant. If the two lines won't come, more page won't help. You haven't decided yet, and *Know what you think* is the way back.

| On the page | Line one | Line two |
|---|---|---|
| A message | What you want them to do or know | By when, or "nothing needed" |
| A document | The decision it asks for or records, as a sentence | Who decides, and by when |
| A spec | What someone will be able to do that they can't do today | What you will both see when it's done |
| A review comment | What you saw happen, and where | Must change, or optional |

## Three questions about one freeze

Bianca wrote one question beside each name. The engineer would ask, "What do I change, and how will I know it's fixed?" Claire would ask, "Does this touch my docks?" The chief executive would ask, "Does this change what I decide on Friday?"

Here are her three pages.

**To the engineer who looks after the replay program.**

"Subject: By Friday, please make the replay program renew its token"

"It froze today in front of Veldhaven's board because it never asks for a new one. Done when a replay that waits twenty minutes after connecting still runs to the end on the test copy."

"Why, from both logs: since August's security change, a token lasts ten minutes. Diego connected before the meeting, and the token ran out two minutes into the replay. The program kept asking with the old one and timed out. At yesterday's rehearsal we started right after connecting, so it never showed. The live scheduler already renews, so leave it alone. Not checked: two other test programs share that login. Could you look tomorrow?"

The history that buried the first version is exactly what this reader needs, so it stays, under an action and a done condition. "Done" is an observable version: two people can watch the same replay reach the end.

**To Claire.**

"Subject: Nothing changes on your docks after today's freeze"

"The fault was in our test program, site one's live scheduler kept assigning doors, and I need nothing from you."

"If a supervisor asks: the program's connection to your test system expired, and renewing it was our job. The live scheduler renews its own; Diego checked its log tonight. None of our dates moves. The stall on the 28th was a different fault, and that report stands. Lucía is writing to your chief executive tonight, and her page says the same."

No token, no logs. Line two tells her she may stop reading, and the rest hands her the sentence she will be asked for on a loading dock.

**To Veldhaven's chief executive, from Lucía.**

"Subject: The cause of today's freeze, which was ours"

"A test program let its connection to your warehouse system expire. Site one's live scheduler doesn't have that fault, and we have found nothing in it that touches 9 or 23 November."

"You asked about three in the morning. The live scheduler renews its connection by itself. Diego read its log back to the first night, and every renewal worked. That is two nights, so it says nothing yet about December. The stall on the 28th was a different fault; you have that report. One thing this did show: we changed those connections in August and never ran the test program long enough afterward. Two others share its login, and by Friday you'll hear from me what we found in them. I'm sorry it happened in front of your board. Lucía"

His own question comes right after the two lines, and the limits come before he has to ask for them.

Bianca's draft of that page had said "so this can't happen live." Lucía, whose name would go under it, called her. "What does 'can't' rest on?" It rested on Diego having read the program. In the basis words of *How sure are you? Say that*, that was *reasoned*, and the chief executive would have taken it as *checked*. So Diego opened the live log and read every renewal since the first night. "Can't" came out, and the two nights went in.

All three went out that night. The engineer started in the morning with nothing to ask. Claire didn't answer, which is the right reply to a page that needs nothing. The board had Lucía's page when it met on Friday, and kept both dates. Bianca's first version became the record, attached under all three.

## Below the second line

Below the two lines, use next-question order from *Give it a shape*: each part answers what this reader would ask next. On a page you can print those questions as headings. "Background" and "Considerations" tell a reader where you put your material. "What if the text doesn't arrive?" tells them whether to read on.

That Friday, with both dates kept, Bianca opened the spec for texting site two's drivers like this:

"From 9 November, a driver at site two gets the door by text instead of walking to the window. Done when a driver whose carrier sent a number by 15 October gets one text with the door, and a driver without a number can still ask at the window."

Her headings were what the engineer would ask next: *What if the door changes? What if the text doesn't arrive? What stays as it is?* Under the second she wrote, "Open. I decide by Monday." A question you haven't settled belongs on the page, with a name and a day.

A title can be line one. "Caching options" waits for a reader with time. "Cache prices for an hour; the checkout team decides on the 8th" has asked its question before anyone opens it. When one document serves several readers, give each a line at the top, by name: "Support: the old export stops on the 12th. Finance: nothing changes."

## A comment on someone's work

The reader of a review comment made the thing you are commenting on, and reads it alone. Line one is the observable version: people who disagree about "fragile" can still agree that this input gave that result. Line two is the weight. Leave it out, and the author has to guess which comment stops the release and which is taste.

> **Research says:** Across five experiments, people writing e-mail believed their tone, sarcasm or humor included, came across better than it did. Later studies by other groups, one of them on text messages, point the same way. The five were about tone and say little about facts; our step is to put a comment's fault and weight in plain words and keep the joke for a call.

### Practice: the comment on line 41

**Situation.** You're a data scientist reviewing a teammate's pull request, a query that counts active customers for Monday's report.

**First draft (what a careful reviewer writes).**
"Nice work! The join looks a bit fragile to me. Are you sure about the counts? The naming could be clearer too, and maybe we should think about caching at some point."

**What's wrong.** "Fragile" and "clearer" are verdicts with nothing to run. "Are you sure?" asks the author to defend everything. "A bit" and "maybe" protect the reviewer, and three points arrive at one weight.

**Better.**
"Please change before merging: line 41 counts a customer twice when they have two addresses. On last week's data, 1,131 customer numbers come out as 1,204 rows. Counting distinct numbers would fix it, if no two customers share one. I haven't checked that."

"Optional: `tmp2` would read better as `active`. Merge without it if you like."

The author answers: "Some do. Since June, families can share a number." You write back: "Then my fix is wrong for them, and the double count is still there. How do you tell two people on one number apart? I'm free at three if talking is faster."

**Why it works.** The author can run it, and the first words say what blocks the merge. Because the comment gave its limit, the author could correct the fix and leave the finding standing.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Take your last review comment, on code, a design, a document or a slide. Write line one as what you saw and where, and line two as *must change* or *optional*. Delete any question whose answer you already know. **Done means** someone who hasn't seen the work can say what the author must change, and what would show it's fixed.

## Practice: two lines on a phone

**If you do only one, do this one.** Ten minutes, with something you must send this week that needs a person to act.

1. Write one reader's name, and the question they will have when it arrives.
2. Write two lines that reader could stop after.
3. Send it to yourself, and open the list it lands in.

**With a person.** Show a colleague the list with everything else covered, and ask, "What will [name] do, and by when?" If the list cuts your lines short, shorten them. Then send the page, and watch the first reply. The decision, or the step already taken, means the lines did their job. "Thanks for the update" from someone who had to decide means the ask never reached the top. **Done means** your colleague named the action and the day, and the first reply didn't ask what you needed.

## Words to use

- **To open.** "Please [do this] by [day]: [the reason]." "Nothing needed from you. [What changed], and [what it means for you]."
- **To ask for a decision.** "I need a yes or no on [one thing] by [day]. I recommend [choice]; the reasons are below."
- **In a review.** "Please change before merging: [what I saw, and where]." "Optional: [suggestion]." "I don't know this part. What happens when [case]?" (Only if you don't know.)
- **When nobody answers.** "Did this reach you? If I don't hear by [day], I'll [a step we can undo]."
- **To leave a long thread.** "We've each said this twice in writing. Can we talk today? I'll write down what we decide."

### Phrases you will hear

- "nit": a small, optional point in a review.
- "for visibility": so that you know. Ask, "Is there anything you need from me?"
- "as per my last message": I already told you. The writer may be annoyed, so answer the point.

## When it backfires

**When it shouldn't start on a page.** Criticism of a person, an apology for real harm, news that will hurt: say it first, and write it afterward. *The hard conversation* shows how.

**When the reader has power over you.** "Please decide by Friday" can read as an order going up. Give the day its reason, and leave the choice with them: "The test window closes on Friday. The next one is the 14th, if you'd rather wait."

**When this team opens differently.** A page with no greeting can look cold. Keep the greeting to one line, put your two lines right after it, and ask how people there like to be written to. *Across borders* goes further.

**When everything is marked urgent.** If each subject says "decision needed", readers stop believing it. Write "nothing needed" as readily as "please".

**In a second language.** *Must*, *should* and *could* can arrive stronger or weaker than you meant. "Before merging", "optional" and a date are harder to misread. Decide the two lines in whichever language is faster, then write them in short sentences.

# Across borders

Five people were discussing Diego's request, and the only word he understood was his own name.

It was the second Tuesday in September. In twenty days the dock scheduler made by Tolva, a company in Montevideo, would go live at the first of Veldhaven's warehouses. Diego, the engineer Tolva had placed with Veldhaven in Rotterdam, needed one favor from its systems team. Every Sunday night the test copy of their warehouse system wiped itself clean. He had spent two days loading a week of real arrivals into it, ahead of a full-day trial on Friday the 18th.

"Can you skip this Sunday's reset?" he asked.

The team's lead looked at the engineer beside her. He said something short, someone answered, and for a minute and a half the room spoke Dutch. After six months in the city, Diego had enough Dutch to buy lunch. Somebody laughed.

The lead turned back to him. "We'll see what we can do."

"Thank you," Diego said. That afternoon he wrote to Mateo, Tolva's co-founder and chief technology officer: "No reset this Sunday."

On Monday morning the test copy was empty. Loading the week again would take until Wednesday. Diego typed a second message to Mateo, "They say yes here and then do nothing," and opened his notes to quote the yes.

There wasn't one.

## A no in other words

He walked to the lead's desk with her sentence instead of his conclusion. "On Tuesday you said, 'We'll see what we can do.' What should I have heard?"

"That you shouldn't plan on it," she said. "If I can, I give you a day. Finance tests on the same copy. I asked them on Wednesday and they said no. I thought you knew."

"And the laugh?"

"Last time we skipped it, the disk was full by Wednesday and nobody could test. We were arguing about whether that would still happen. It goes faster in Dutch."

Then she had a question for him. On Thursday she had sent Tolva her changes to site one's messages, and nobody had answered. "Four days. What's wrong with them?"

Nothing was wrong with them. At Tolva, when nobody answers a list like that, it means go ahead. She had been waiting for a yes that Tolva thought it had given.

Diego says no with the word "no," so that was the word he had listened for. The lead says yes with a day, and Tolva's silence had no day in it. Each side had been clear in its own way.

> **Research says:** In one laboratory's study, first-language speakers of Mandarin Chinese overrated how well Americans with English as their first language understood their Chinese, even when told the listeners knew none. The listeners, in turn, overrated how well they had grasped what the speakers meant. One pair of languages in one laboratory can't measure your meetings, but it is a reason to check on both sides.

The sentence that cost him two days needed no translation. It was already in English, six common words. A tool could have translated every word of the Dutch and still not told him what the lead had promised.

When you work across a border, find out how *this* team says yes, says no, disagrees and goes quiet. Watch what their words turn into, ask about one sentence, and agree in writing what you will both mean. You can start this week, and soon a yes from five time zones away is a yes you can plan on.

> **Line to keep:** Their yes is your guess unless you know how they say no.

## What differs, and what to ask

Two good teams can differ on every row.

| What differs | Watch | Ask |
|---|---|---|
| How a no sounds | What "we'll see" turned into last time | "When I ask for something you can't do, how will you tell me?" |
| Who may disagree with whom | Who speaks after the senior person has spoken | "If I think a number is wrong, should I say so here, or to you first?" |
| What silence means | The last question nobody answered: what happened next? | "If I hear nothing by Thursday, what should I assume?" |
| What interrupting means | Whether the person cut off carries on or stops for good | "Should I cut in, or write it in the chat?" |
| What goes in writing | Which decisions come back as a message, and who sends it | "Do you want this in writing before we talk, or after?" |

Don't fill in the answers from a guidebook, or from a chart that scores countries. The engineer beside the lead grew up in the same city as she did. In that minute and a half he had said a flat no to Diego's request, twice. Their country can't tell you which of the two will answer you.

"They say yes here and then do nothing" is a label with a whole company inside it. Use the observable version from *The exact word*: what would a recording show? One sentence on a Tuesday, and a reset on a Sunday. Diego had an older moment, too. In June the same lead had agreed to update two sites' label printers, and she had ended with "You'll have the day by Friday." Her yes had come with a day. He had had half the answer since June.

Two moments are enough to ask with. Quote the words and ask what you should have heard. Keep the question on the work: "What is it like in your culture?" asks one person to speak for millions.

If you work for the client from another country, offshore or nearshore, you won't overhear how Tuesday's sentence turned out. Ask the first row's question in your first week, before an answer matters.

### Practice: one sentence you misheard

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.** Choose one answer from a client or another team that turned out to mean something else. Write down their words and what happened next, with no adjective and no country. This week, ask one person from that team, alone: "When you said [their words], what should I have heard?" Then offer one from your side: "When we [say or don't say something], it means [what]. Is that how you read it?" Write one line that you will both follow, and send it.

Watch the reply. If they explain the moment, the question was safe to answer. "It's fine" may mean the place or the person was wrong, so try in writing, or ask someone with less to lose. **Done means** they have confirmed or corrected your line in writing, and a person who joined this morning could tell whether it was kept.

## Half a page, from both sides

On Wednesday both teams gave Diego half an hour on a call. The lead wrote her team's habits, Mateo wrote Tolva's, and they agreed this:

- A yes has a name and a day. "We'll see" means not yet, so don't plan on it.
- No reply is not a yes, from either side. After one working day, ask again; after two, phone.
- Either team may use its own language when that's faster. Say so first. Whoever switched gives the result in English, and the other side reads it back.
- Anyone may cut in to correct a number.
- Same-day questions come between two and five in Rotterdam, nine and noon in Montevideo. Anything sent outside those hours waits for the next ones. If it can't wait, phone.
- Any line that fails twice gets rewritten.

Many software teams keep a working agreement; this is one with two companies on it. It binds both sides: Tolva had to give up its silent yes, and its engineers now announce it when they switch to Spanish. And anyone could see whether a line was kept, so nobody has to argue about what "responsive" means.

Before anyone left, each side gave the other's lines a read-back. Mateo went first: "So 'we'll see' is a no." "It's a not yet," said the lead. "When it turns into a no, I'll tell you. Last week I didn't." Without that correction, Tolva would have dropped requests she was still working on.

A question Mateo sends at five in the afternoon reaches Rotterdam at ten at night, and without a rule, somebody has to wonder whether it's urgent. Put both clocks on every time you write. And watch the gap itself: late in October, Rotterdam's clocks change and Montevideo's don't, so five hours becomes four.

By the end of the month Mateo was asking Diego what a sentence from Rotterdam meant, and the lead was asking him about sentences from Montevideo. He gave both of them what the other side had told him, and when. That is the habit of the translator, the thinker type he is growing toward: carrying meaning across a boundary intact.

## Straight, or their way?

You will hear two pieces of advice. One is to be direct everywhere, because careful wrapping gets lost in a second language. It has a strong case: when a truck is heading for the wrong door, "Door seven is closed" has to come at once, from whoever sees it. The other is to follow the local way, and raise things through the people the hierarchy expects. Diego's Tuesday is the case for that one.

Try the listener sketch from *Who is listening* on the lead. She knew that finance shared the copy. She had to decide in front of her own engineers, with Diego waiting. And she stood to lose either way. A yes was a promise finance could break; a no, in public, landed on the project of Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven. "We'll see" was the one answer that cost her nothing that day.

So find out the local way by asking and watching, agree how you will work, be as direct as they allow, and put the substance in writing. The message doesn't bend; the route does. "If Sunday's reset runs, I lose two days" is the same sentence in a full room, in a message or at her desk on Monday. At her desk, she could have said, "Ask finance."

### Practice: the yes that never came

**Situation.** You build software for a client five hours ahead of you. On Thursday's call their architect said of your plan to put orders on a queue, "Interesting. Let's keep it in mind." Work is due to start on Monday.

**First draft (what a careful engineer writes that evening).** "Thanks for the call! As discussed, we'll go ahead with the queue unless we hear otherwise by end of day tomorrow. Happy to jump on a quick call if there are any concerns."

**What's wrong.** "As discussed" claims an agreement, and "unless we hear otherwise" turns silence into a yes the architect never gave. "End of day tomorrow" falls at two different hours on two desks. "Any concerns" leaves the architect to write the whole objection.

**Better.** "On Thursday's call you said of the queue, 'Interesting. Let's keep it in mind.' I'm not sure whether to plan on it. May we start on Monday?

"With the queue, orders wait when your system is slow, instead of failing. I checked that with your March traffic. I haven't checked it at a year-end peak. It takes two weeks, and during the first we can still go back.

"One number is enough: 1 to start Monday, 2 for not yet and what's missing, 3 for no. If I have no answer by Friday, 16:00 your time (11:00 mine), we won't start. I'll phone you on Monday at 15:00 yours."

**Why it works.** It quotes words instead of a reading, sizes the claim, puts both clocks on the deadline and starts nothing on a silence. A no is private and costs one keystroke.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Find an answer you are treating as a yes, though it came with no name and no day. Write their words, your one question, what you have and haven't checked, three answers they can give as a number, and what you will do without one. **Done means** a colleague who wasn't there can sort the reply into yes, not yet or no.

## Words to use

- **When the room changes language.** "Take the time you need. Could I have the result in English when you're there?"
- **When your own side does.** "We need two minutes in Spanish to get this right. Then I'll tell you what we said."
- **When you can't tell what the answer was.** "Should I plan on that, or not yet?"
- **To make a no easy to give.** "If it's a no, please tell me by Friday. I can plan around a no."
- **When nobody answers.** "I haven't heard from you, so this is still open. From [day], waiting costs us [what]."
- **Before you disagree with someone senior.** "I have a different number. Would you like it now, or after the call?"

### Phrases you will hear

- "Let's table this." (In some countries, discuss it now; in others, put it off. Ask: "Now, or later?")
- "We'll take it from here." (They have it. Ask: "Who, and by when?")
- "That could work." (It can be a yes or a maybe. Ask: "Is that a yes for Monday?")

## When it backfires

**When the question sounds like a complaint.** "What does 'we'll see' mean here?" can feel like an accusation, above all in front of others. Ask alone, about your own mistake, with your own team's habit to offer in return.

**When they hold the power.** A client may have no wish to agree habits with a supplier. Then follow theirs, and state yours as information: "A yes from us always has a day in it." Confirm what you understood in writing, so that a correction costs them one line.

**When someone quotes the page to win.** "Line two says no reply isn't a yes" wins the point and costs goodwill. Use the page to settle what a sentence meant. And it describes these people this autumn, so reopen it when someone new joins.

**When the habit isn't the problem.** Someone who keeps breaking a line they agreed, or a room that uses its language to leave you out, is a different case. So is an accent treated as a joke. Those belong to *Difficult people*.

**In a second language.** Ask for the sentence in the chat before you interpret it, because what sounds cold aloud may be plain in writing. If you lose the thread, name the last part you have: "I followed until finance. What came after that?"

---

# With a machine in the room

*In a meeting: ask the question it leaves out*

"Site one trial, Friday 18 September. Fourteen items, fourteen green. What we count: doors the supervisors change. For this call: are we ready?"

An assistant Tolva approved for client work drafted those lines for Thursday's call, from the tickets and the plan. All Friday, Tolva's scheduler would plan the doors at Veldhaven's first warehouse, beside the old paper plan, and the supervisors could overrule it. Go-live was the 28th. Tyler, Tolva's delivery lead, checked each green against its ticket, and all fourteen were right.

But everyone could say yes to "are we ready?" and still decide nothing. The page said what to count. It did not say how many would stop the go-live. Tyler wrote a new question: "How many changed doors would be too many, and who says so?" The page had a line for everyone on the call except one: site one's morning supervisor, who would be changing the doors.

On the call, Tyler opened with his new question.

"As few as possible," said site one's manager.

"And you?" Tyler asked the supervisor.

"I'll change four whatever it does. A forklift is out, or my crew is at the other end."

Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, looked up. "And a truck that can't unload at the door it was given?"

"That one should stop you."

"Then we count those. Six or fewer, we go. Seven, we stay on paper. I'll say which by eight tomorrow evening."

Tyler said it back: "Claire decides by eight. Trucks that can't unload: up to six, we go. Seven, paper."

"And if nobody can reach me," Claire said, "site one's manager decides, on the same number."

That evening the assistant turned Tyler's notes into a summary: "The team confirmed readiness and agreed clear criteria for the trial." The number and the name were gone. He put them back, word for word. On Friday the supervisors changed eleven doors, and five counted. At ten to eight Claire wrote: "Live on the 28th."

## What can't be prepared

A decision is somebody's word, given to the people who will act on it. Let an assistant prepare everything around it: the status, the agenda, the hard questions, the note. Check its facts, and enjoy the time it saves.

> **Line to keep:** Handed a perfect page, a room can still decide nothing.

Three jobs stay with you in every room:

- **Choose the question.** Write one that someone could answer no to, and beside it the name of whoever settles it.
- **Read what nobody asked.** Find the person with no line on the page and ask what they will do. An assistant can list possible gaps; the forklift was in the supervisor's head.
- **Say the decision back,** owner first, while the owner can still correct you. Then make the note say the same.

## Practice: a question that can get a no

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.**

**Situation.** Tomorrow you lead a call about moving a client's backups to new storage. The old copies go on the 1st.

**First draft (what an assistant writes).** "Today we'll review the backup migration, confirm that all workstreams are on schedule and surface any remaining risks. Any concerns?"

**What's wrong.** It asks everyone, so nobody is asked, and silence will pass for a yes. The colleague who restores files isn't in it.

**Better.**

"One decision today: do the old copies go on the 1st? You do the restores. Have you restored anything from the new storage?"

"Not yet."

"What would you need to see first?"

"One full restore. I can try it by the 24th."

"So it's yours: one full restore by the 24th, or the old copies stay. Did I get that right?"

**Why it works.** The question can get a no and goes to whoever has the missing fact. The decision has an owner and a day.

**Your turn (10 minutes, then a real meeting this week).** Have an assistant turn your notes into one page. Replace its question with yours, and ask the person named beside it first. At the end, say the decision back, aloud or in writing. A reply of "we" or "soon" has no owner yet. **Done means** the owner confirmed or corrected your sentence, and someone who wasn't there can tell who decides what, and by when.

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## When it backfires

**Your question leaves others out.** Claire's number told her about a day. On site one's first night live the scheduler stalled for forty minutes, and Thursday's call hadn't asked about a night. Ask each decision the second-question test's *Where does it stop?*

**The room belongs to someone senior.** Send your question ahead: "Could we also settle [this]? I think it's yours to answer."

**Nothing needs deciding.** A question forced into a briefing sounds like an audit.

**In a second language.** The moment may pass while you find the words. Ask late: "Before we finish, can I go back to one thing?"

## Record again

Sixty seconds: what you are working on, and why it matters. Write the point you meant, then check four things: sentences before the point, hedges with no basis, one example, an ask or next step at the end. For *said back*, someone from one of your rooms hears it once and writes the point in one sentence.

Counting fillers is optional; pauses, restarts and searching for a word never count. **Written form.** The same prompt, three minutes of writing.

Then compare the endings of all your takes: this part practiced asking for a decision.

*Safe practice: record only yourself, or others only with their consent and within your employer's rules.*
