# Part 5. Friction

---

# The hard conversation

What is the first sentence of the conversation you are putting off?

By Thursday morning Tyler had seven. "Got five minutes?" "Nothing serious." "How's everything?" "You know I respect your work." "Some people are worried." "I'm not blaming anyone." "We should all be more careful." He had typed them into a note, one under another, and none of them contained the word *merge*.

Tyler leads delivery at Tolva, the Montevideo company whose scheduler sends trucks to their doors at Veldhaven, a food wholesaler in Rotterdam. Two nights earlier, on 6 October, a change written by a coding agent had put the wrong labels on site one's doors for four hours. Its tests had passed, and an engineer Tyler trusted had merged it unread. One of Veldhaven's dock supervisors caught it.

At Wednesday's stand-up he had tried one on everybody: "Let's all be a bit more careful what we merge this week." By noon three engineers had asked whether he meant them. The one he meant wasn't among them.

## What a hint does

Tyler's gentle sentence worried three people who had merged nothing. For the fourth it named no day, no merge and no request, so she had nothing to answer and could only guess how bad it was.

When you hear trouble coming, you want one thing answered first: what happens to me?

Our target: the subject in your first sentence and, if you can promise it, what isn't at stake in your second. Bring facts the other person can check, say what you may have wrong, and ask. You can write all of it down tonight. Then both of you can look at one thing that happened.

> **Line to keep:** A fact they can answer does less harm than a hint they can't.

## The first minute

The shape is the second-question test from *Start here*, adjusted for this room: its limit is what you may have wrong, and its ask is a question. Tyler answered each question on paper.

- **What is the point?** Tuesday's merge went in unread.
- **What does it rest on?** The merge record: twenty past four, no reader's name.
- **Where does it stop?** I don't know what happened before twenty past four.
- **What do you want from me?** Her account, before mine; then a way to get the next one read.
- **Who answers for it?** In August I left "who reads it" with two names and no date.

He opened the record himself. Then he asked Mateo, who runs technology, whether she would stay on site two, since Tyler couldn't promise that alone. He wrote to her: "Could we talk at two, about Tuesday's merge? You're staying on site two, whatever we find. I want to hear what happened before it." An invitation that says only "Can we talk?" starts the conversation without you.

At two, on a video call, he said this:

"This is about Tuesday's merge. You're staying on site two, whatever we find; I've asked Mateo. The record shows you merged at twenty past four, with no reader's name. Some of that is mine: in August I left 'who reads it' without a date. I don't know what happened before twenty past four. What did?"

"I asked you," she said.

"When?"

"In the team chat, at three. 'Tests pass on site two's doors. Who reads this before it goes in?' You wrote one line. 'Great, let's keep site two moving.'"

Tyler found it while she waited. He had answered between two calls, and he had read as far as "pass".

"So you asked who reads it," he said. "I answered something else, and you took that as a yes."

"Yes. And I read the tests and never opened the change. I saw forty passes and stopped." Then: "Until your message this morning, I was sure I was off Veldhaven."

"Then Tuesday's answer is mine too. The unopened change is yours. What would make the next one different?"

"One name on it, before anyone merges. And when I ask a question, an answer to that question."

By four they had it in writing. With no reader's name, an agent's change waits, and she phones instead of typing. Tyler takes "who reads it" back to Mateo and Lucía, Tolva's two founders, on Monday, for one name and a date. In August, Tyler would have moved to the next item. Leaving with a decision that lasts is the habit of the problem-solver, the thinker type he is growing toward.

His limit did the most work. Had he opened with "You merged it unread," his own message would have come out as her defense. Because he said where his knowledge stopped, it came out as the next fact.

## Say what a record would show

Feedback runs on the observable version from *The exact word*: what a recording would show or a number would state. Aim it at the work, where something can change.

| Instead of | Say | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "You were careless." | "The change has no reader's name on it." | Either of you can look. |
| "You never speak in reviews." | "In the last two reviews, I didn't hear your view of the design." | "Never" starts an argument about never. |
| "The client isn't happy with you." | "Their architect asked me twice whether you'd read the spec. What should I tell him?" | It says who and what, and leaves room for an answer. |
| "Great work on the release." | "You wrote the rollback first, so we lost ten minutes instead of a night." | Now the praise can be repeated on purpose. |

It fills the first of four slots: `[what a record would show] [what it cost] [what I may have wrong] [what I'd like next time]`. Filled in: "The change went in with no reader's name. Site one ran on wrong labels for four hours. I may not know who you asked. Next time, phone me and wait." Describing the behavior, its effect and a next step is old advice in feedback training. The third slot is the one to protect when you're short of time.

Put the bad part before the kind part. Only the answer to "what happens to me?" may come earlier. If that answer is the bad part, say it before its reasons: "The senior role is a no for this round. I'll tell you why, and what would change it."

> **Research says:** In one study of people with mixed news to give, taking the receiver's perspective moved them toward the order receivers preferred, with the bad part first. So picture what they're waiting to hear before you choose your order. It is one paper without a direct repeat, and its subject was news, so the step to feedback is ours.

*The update* gives that order's cost: the relief left people less motivated to change, and feedback is for change. So we'd end on it.

## When the feedback is for you

It may reach you as a label, and labels sting. Ask for the day behind it. A client's lead has just told an engineer, "It's impossible to get an answer from you."

"Which day should I look at?" the engineer asks.

"Monday. I asked which field holds the pallet count, and you sent me a link."

"So you needed one field name and I sent you a manual. I'll answer in the thread first and link after. What I'm not sure of: was it only Monday?"

That is a read-back: what I understood, what I will do, what I am unsure of. The engineer never agreed to "impossible". If one fact is wrong, correct that fact and leave the rest standing. If you need time, ask for it with a date, and keep the date.

## An apology they can check

An apology makes a claim: I know what I did to you, and it will be different. Expect the second question: why would I believe that? Answer it first, with a change they can see without taking your word.

### Practice: the apology

**Situation.** On Wednesday, Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, took the night to her chief executive. That afternoon Lucía writes to her.

**First draft (what a careful founder writes).**
"Claire, I'm so sorry for the trouble last night. The change had passed every test, and as soon as your supervisor called, our engineers responded at once. We take this very seriously, and I promise it will never happen again. I know the team is doing everything it can, and I hope we can still count on November."

**What's wrong.** The defense comes before the damage, and "the trouble" could be anyone's. "Never" has nothing under it. The last sentence asks Claire for something while she is still paying for the night.

**Better.**
"Claire, last night our software showed the wrong doors at site one for four hours, and your supervisor had to find it for us. You then had to explain our failure to your chief executive. I'm sorry.

An agent wrote the change, its tests passed, and nobody here read it. Saying who reads such changes was Mateo's job and mine. It was on our list in August, and we didn't do it.

I don't know yet how many trucks went to a wrong door. You'll have the count by Friday noon.

Since this morning, nothing an agent wrote goes to your live sites. Every Friday you'll get a list of what did go live, with the name of the person who read it. I'm not asking you for anything today."

**Why it works.** It opens with what happened to Claire, and "I'm sorry" comes after something to be sorry for. It names whose job it was, and the engineer isn't in it. The promise is smaller than "never", and it can be seen on Friday.

**The second question.** Claire answered in one line: "Why would I believe the list?" Lucía wrote back, "You shouldn't yet. Pick any line and ask to speak to the person named beside it." On Friday the count came before noon. From the list, Claire picked the second line, Thursday night's repair to site one's labels. The name was the engineer from Tyler's call. She explained the change in two sentences, because this time she had opened it. Claire didn't say it was all right. She kept the list.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Write the apology you owe: what you did, what it cost them, what you don't know yet, what has already changed and where they can see it. Cross out every "if", every "but" and every request. **Done means** a colleague who reads it can say what you did, what it cost, and how the other person would check the change.

## Practice: the conversation you're putting off

**If you do only one, do this one.** **With a person.** Fifteen minutes to prepare, then the real conversation, this week.

1. Answer the test's questions as Tyler did. Open the record behind each fact.
2. Find out what isn't at stake and who can promise it. If nobody can, leave it out.
3. Send the subject with the invitation.
4. When you meet, say your first two sentences, your facts, your part, your limit and your question. Then stop.
5. Say back the first thing they tell you that you didn't know. Watch what they do with it: correct it, add to it, or ask about your part.
6. Write down together who does what, by when.

**Done means** you both have that line in writing, and you can name one thing you believed beforehand that they confirmed or corrected.

**Spar with an AI.**

```text
Play a capable colleague I respect. I'll open a conversation about one piece of your work that went wrong. If my first two sentences don't tell you the subject and what isn't at stake, reply only, "Is this about my job?" Otherwise answer as someone with a good reason I haven't heard, including one fact that is partly my fault. Once, reply only "...". Afterward, list every word of mine that a recording couldn't show, and every place where I defended myself before saying your point back.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

- **To invite.** "Could we talk at [time], about [subject]? [What isn't at stake.]"
- **To open.** "This is about [subject]. [What isn't at stake.]"
- **To leave room.** "The record shows [what]. I don't know what came before."
- **Your part.** "My part was [what]. By [day] I'll have changed it."
- **When it's aimed at you.** "Which day should I look at?" "You're right about [part]. I need until [day] for the rest."
- **To end on the change.** "What would make the next one different?"
- **To pause.** "I want to get this right. Could we stop, and finish at [time]?"
- **When they apologize to you.** "Thank you. What I need to see is [what]."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Can I have a quick word?" (A private talk, often about a problem. Ask what it's about.)
- "No hard feelings." (I'm not angry with you.)

## When it backfires

**When you hold the power.** "What happened?" from the person who sets salaries can sound like a trap. Say your own part first, and let them answer tomorrow.

**When they do.** Ask before you give feedback upward: "I noticed something about our Monday calls. Would it help to hear it?" Keep it private and about the work, with the subject in writing first. A no is an answer.

**When it's already decided.** If a role is ending, don't ask for an account that can change nothing. Say the decision, stop, and stay for the questions.

**When an apology can cost you.** Facts in writing can be quoted in a claim. If money, an injury or a contract may follow, find out first who at your company may write it. Rules differ by country, and this isn't legal advice.

**When it isn't a wording problem.** Harassment, discrimination, threats, danger, anything unlawful: there is no first sentence for you to prepare. Keep dated notes, use a formal channel and get help. *Difficult people* ends there.

**When directness costs more than you think.** In some teams a criticism said aloud, even in private, can't be taken back. Ask how this person likes to hear a problem, and let the route change while the facts stay.

**In a second language.** Softeners shrink the subject: "a small issue" may be heard as small. Write your first two sentences word for word. And because "sorry" in English also means "I didn't hear you", make yours a full sentence: "I'm sorry we didn't read it."

# Saying no and pushing back

Before ten on a Monday in October, Bianca, Tolva's product manager, had three requests to answer.

Site three's manager: "Site two's drivers get their door by text from 9 November. Please add site three for the 23rd. It's the same thing."

Claire: "After last Tuesday night, I need the door override on my supervisors' phones before site two goes live on the 9th."

Lucía: "Nothing new at site one before the peak, so your rule for containers waits until January. Can you tell the team and site one's manager today?"

The first two came from Veldhaven, Tolva's client, where Claire runs operations. Lucía is Bianca's own chief executive. On "last Tuesday night", 6 October, a change written by an agent had mislabeled doors at Veldhaven's first warehouse for four hours.

One reply would fit all three. "Thanks, it's on the list." The list was real. It had a hundred and forty lines, and nothing on it had ever been refused.

What would a manager do with those words, seven weeks before the peak?

## Nothing refused, nothing promised

People plan on whatever you haven't refused, so a vague answer costs them a plan. A clean no gives them time: the first sentence says it won't happen, and the rest helps them act on it. It answers the questions of the second-question test from *Start here*, in order:

- **What is the point?** No, to what, by when.
- **What does it rest on?** One reason they can check.
- **Where does it stop?** What you are not refusing, and when asking again makes sense.
- **What do you want from me?** What to do now, without it.
- **Who answers for it?** The name of whoever decided.

> **Line to keep:** Say the no first, and leave them something they can use.

Bianca wrote to site three's manager:

"No, site three won't have driver texts on the 23rd. They have never run on a real morning; site two's first is the 9th. The no covers this peak only. With site two's numbers, I can give you a yes or a no for spring by 15 January. Please plan December without them. I decided this, so bring me the questions."

The answer came within the hour: "Not what I hoped. But I can still find a second person for the gate."

That second person is what a clean no is for. Bianca offered no regret and no compliment, and her message is still gracious. Grace at work is mostly this: an early answer, the true reason, and something they can still use. It came the morning she was asked, while there was time to act, and it said when to ask again. Soften what the no costs them, never the no. And give one reason. Three can sound like a search for one they'll accept.

## Eleven minutes later

Bianca built her answer to Claire the same way:

"No, not before the 9th. Phones need their own login, and your security review allows ten working days a round. August's needed two. If it started tomorrow, a second round would end on the 9th itself. After the peak, I'd say yes. Shall I book the review for January? This is my decision."

Eleven minutes later Claire replied, with Lucía and Veldhaven's chief executive copied: "I asked how my supervisors get through the next bad night. I was sent a policy I already know."

Bianca read her message again and found nothing to correct. What failed was around it. She had refused the phones without asking what they were for. And she had done it in writing, to someone who had spent a week answering upward for a night Tolva caused. A senior person may have to forward your no, and nothing in this one was any use to Claire.

It was also Claire's second no to phones. In August Lucía had promised them on a Monday and taken them back on the Wednesday.

Bianca sent Lucía one line before she did anything else: "The no is right, and I sent it badly. I'm phoning her."

"Good. If she asks me, she'll hear the same no."

Bianca phoned. "Phones are still a no for the 9th. I should have called before I wrote that. What should a supervisor be able to do on the next bad night?"

"Find it in ten minutes, instead of four hours."

"Then phones wouldn't have helped. They'd have shown the same wrong labels. What if a supervisor compares the screen with the signs, every door, at the start of each shift?"

"Send me that and the no, in one message. That one I can pass on."

She passed it on before noon. That night Diego, the engineer Tolva had placed at Veldhaven, walked the first check with the supervisors. The no never moved.

With a senior client, or with anyone in a bad week, the answers stay and the route changes. Ask what the yes was for. Tell your own boss. Say the no aloud, with what they can have. Write it last, in one message they can forward. Asking which problem needs solving is the habit of the framer, the thinker type Bianca is growing toward. That morning it came one message late.

## What you can trade

When someone moves your date or grows your scope, offer a choice. Say what can't all happen, show two versions that can, and name the part that stays in both. Trading scope against time is as old as projects. The part to protect is the check that catches a mistake before customers do.

### Practice: all of it by the 1st

**Situation.** You run a two-person software company. A new ordering page is agreed for the 15th. Domestic orders are built and tested; export orders wait for the customer's product codes; the load test takes two days. On Wednesday the customer's head of sales writes: "We've announced the new page for the 1st. I'm sure you can make it work!"

**First draft (what a careful founder writes).**
"Thanks for letting me know. That's tight, to be honest. We still have export orders, and we're waiting on the product codes, and the load test is two days, so it's a lot. But we'll do our best to get there."

**What's wrong.** The defense comes before the answer, and the answer never comes. "Do our best" will be read as the 1st. The product codes, the one thing they can act on, hide in the middle.

**Better.**
"All of it on the 1st, no. Domestic orders on the 1st, yes, if Monday's load test passes. Export orders need your product codes; if they're here by Friday, the 15th holds for everything. The load test stays in both versions. Which should the announcement say: domestic on the 1st, or everything on the 15th? I need your choice by noon tomorrow."

Their reply: "I need all of it. Can't you skip the load test?"

"No. Without it, your customers would be the test. What I can add from the 1st is export orders by email, which we'd enter by hand. Who decides about the announcement? I'd like to show them both versions."

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Take a date or a scope that someone has changed on you. Write what can't all happen, two versions that can, the part that stays in both, and the choice with its day. Then write your answer to the second push. **Done means** someone outside your work reads it once and can tell you what won't happen and what there is to choose.

## Decided, or still open?

The container rule gives containers packed without pallets a longer slot at the door. Two people unload them by hand in about two hours, against the forty minutes booked, and the next truck waits. Bianca wanted the rule live for the peak. Lucía's message said January.

She asked before she argued: "Is this decided, or still open?"

"Open until four," Lucía wrote.

Then she used sort first, from *Thinking on your feet*. A disagreement is about what is true (agree the test before anyone argues the answer) or what to do (agree the goal). Or it is about who gets something limited (agree a fair rule and name who decides). Bianca phoned to find out which this was.

"An agent wrote that rule's tests," Lucía said. "An agent wrote last Tuesday's."

"If a person reads every test by Thursday and finds nothing, would you ship it?"

"No."

So no test would settle it. Bianca left the tests alone and argued the goal, with a sized claim: "Then this is about December. Diego counted three of those containers a week in September, and each one costs the next truck about an hour. Nobody has counted a December. I'd ship it. I'd change my mind if the planners could book two hours for them by hand."

"Maybe they can. I believe your number," Lucía said. "I still want Claire to say, any day until January, that nothing changed at site one, and be right. It waits."

"Then it waits. I'll tell them."

Lucía answers to Claire for site one, so the decision was hers. What Bianca owed her was one honest view, at its size, while it could still count.

If you are the senior one, less of this may reach you than you need. "Open until four" got Lucía the best argument against her plan before the plan was fixed. Say what is open, and until when.

## "Did you agree with this?"

Many companies ask people to disagree first and commit afterward. It is good advice, and it stops before the hard part: facing the people who will live with the decision. Bianca wrote the no she had argued against twice, for two readers.

To site one's manager, who has a December to run:

"The container rule won't reach site one before the peak. After last week we are changing nothing there until January, so what your supervisors know stays true. I know the cost: about three trucks a week that wait an hour. Could your planners book two hours when the packing list says no pallets? If they can't, tell me, and I'll take that to Lucía, who decided this. You'll have a date from me by 1 December."

To the team, who have work to put down:

"The container rule stays on the test copy. Nothing changes at site one until January, so Claire can say that and be right. The rule itself isn't in question. By Thursday, please leave a note that says what is tested and what isn't, so whoever picks it up in January can start there. Questions to me."

The engineer who had built it asked one: "Did you agree with this?"

"I argued for shipping it, and Lucía heard me before she decided. Her reason is a good one, and it's our plan now. If the planners can't do it by hand, that's a new fact, and I'll take it to her."

"Yes" would have been false. "Lucía decided", with nothing after it, would have handed the team Bianca's objection to carry. Backing a decision means you stop arguing in the rooms that can't change it, and bring new facts to the one that can.

## Practice: one no this week

**If you do only one, do this one.** **With a person.** Find the oldest request you know you won't do. Put the test's answers on paper. If the person is senior or in a bad week, ask what it was for, and say the no aloud before you write it. Then listen to the first thing that comes back:

- "Why not?" Your reason wasn't one they could check.
- "So what do I do?" You left them nothing to use.
- "But you'll try?" They never heard the no. Say your first sentence again, more slowly.

**Done means** they have told you what they will do without it.

**Spar with an AI.**

```text
Play a vice president at my largest client. I will refuse a request: [the request].
Ask me once why. Then say you will call my boss. Then ask what you
are supposed to tell your own boss. Accept the no only if I keep it
and give you something you can use. Afterward, in three sentences,
say whether you heard yes, no or maybe, what you can plan on now,
and where I was unclear.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

- **To find what it's for.** "If you had it on [day], what would you do with it?"
- **The no.** "No, not by [day]. [The one reason.]" "Ask me again on [day], when I'll have [what]."
- **The trade.** "[This] or [that] by then. [The check] stays in both."
- **When you can't refuse.** "I can start today. Which of these two waits?"
- **To someone senior.** "Is this decided, or still open?" "Could I tell you why I see it differently, before you decide?"
- **To back it.** "We're doing [this], because [the reason]. Questions to me."
- **The graceful exit.** "Thank you for asking me first. I'd like to know what you decide."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Can you squeeze it in?" (Do this too, and move nothing. Ask what should move.)
- "That ship has sailed." (It's decided. Ask what can still change.)
- "Let's agree to disagree." (They want to stop. Ask who decides, and when.)

## When it backfires

**When they hold the power.** You may not be free to refuse. Turn the no into an order of work, and write it down: "I'm starting the report. The migration moves to the 20th. Tell me today if you want it the other way."

**When you shouldn't back it.** Carry a choice you would have made differently. Don't carry one that puts your name to something false or unsafe, or that hides a risk from the people who would pay for it. Tell the person deciding, keep dated notes, and use the formal route; *Difficult people* says where wording stops helping.

**When a first-sentence no is rude.** In some rooms it costs the other person their standing. Keep the no and change the route: alone, beforehand, or through someone they trust.

**When everything gets a no.** A two-minute favor doesn't need the whole test, and people find a way around whoever refuses everything. If you can't remember your last yes, ask what your list is for.

**In a second language.** On a call, *can't* is easily heard as *can*. Start with the word no, or say *cannot*, then write the sentence in the chat.

# Difficult people

Behavior you can see is all you can work with.

So this guide goes by what people do. They interrupt, correct you in public, dismiss your work, make a dig, write yes and mean no, go silent, present your work as theirs, or keep moving the date. Go to yours. For harassment, threats or danger, go to the last section.

By a Friday in mid-October, Veldhaven's word for Naomi was *unreliable*. She is the consultant in Seattle who forecasts when trucks will reach the food wholesaler's three warehouses. She can't stop being "unreliable", so the word leaves you nothing to try.

The same week, on a recording: her trial forecast for site three missed most of Tuesday afternoon's trucks. That evening Claire, who runs operations there, wrote to ask what had happened. By Friday morning Naomi hadn't replied. Those facts give you plenty to try. Did the message arrive? Is she waiting for something? Claire sent a smaller question and had an answer within minutes (*They go silent*).

Say what happened in words they would accept. Start from the kindest cause that fits the facts. Then choose your response by how much power you hold and how much you need them. If the right response fails, stop rewording it and change the route: another person, another channel.

> **Line to keep:** A label changes nothing because nobody can stop being one.

Work this way and you can get something done with almost anyone whose behavior can change. You'll also know sooner when it can't.

In six of the eight entries the difficult person is one of this book's leads: Lucía, Mateo, Diego, Bianca, Tyler and Naomi, once each. So read every entry twice, the second time for yourself.

## Before you answer

1. **Write what happened.** Who said or did what, and when, in words a recording would back. Cut every word for what they are or what they meant: *rude*, *careless*, *lazy*, *on purpose*. This is the observable version from *The exact word*: could two people who disagree about the label agree that this happened?
2. **Write your part, then theirs.** Yours first: the late draft, the vague request, the decision they heard about last. Then two innocent explanations you haven't ruled out. Some fit every entry: a norm from another team or country, a second language, a neurotype unlike yours, pressure you can't see.
3. **Sort first.** If you disagree about what is true, agree the test. If it's about what to do, agree the goal. If it's about something limited (the floor, the credit, the hours), agree a fair rule and name who decides.

Describing the act and looking for your own part are old advice. The order is my choice: yours first, while you can still see it. If you are angry, write all three now and answer later. You may hear that anger never works. Sometimes it moves a date, and then the subject is you. *Steady under pressure* shows how to hold a reply overnight.

## Confront it, or acknowledge first?

You will hear two pieces of advice about disrespect. One says confront it at once: what passes in silence can look accepted, and everyone watching is learning what is allowed. The other says acknowledge the person first: someone who feels accused may defend their standing before they hear a single fact.

Each is right about a different moment, so choose by power and by whether you need the relationship. The first time, assume an innocent cause and check. The second time, describe what happened and say what you need. A pattern, or harm to other people, goes to a formal route: someone with the authority to act. The more power they hold, the more private and written every step becomes.

| Where you stand | First time | Second time | A pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| They hold the power, and you need them | Alone, one question about the work | In writing: what happened, what you need | Dated notes to your manager, or to your sponsor on their side |
| They hold the power, and you could leave | Ask once, or let it pass | One written line, and a plan that works without them | Leave cleanly, with the work handed over |
| Peers who will keep working together | Alone, aloud, the same day | What happened, what you need, a rule for both | The person you both answer to |
| You hold the power | Ask what you did first | Alone: what happened, and what changes now | You start the formal route, and say so |

In each entry, **Upward too** is the default: written to be said to a client, a boss or an investor as well as to a peer. **Peers only** can cost you with anyone who has power over you.

## In front of others

### They interrupt

A client's director cuts in at your second sentence, on every call.

Your second sentence may be history, and the director may want the answer your first one should have held (*Give it a shape*). Or the line lags, or the thought will be gone if it waits, or talking over each other is how that team shows interest.

- **Upward too.** Put the answer first, so that a cut costs you only the reasons. Then: "That's the answer. May I add the one risk before we leave it?"
- **If you need them.** Alone, later: "When we change subject early, the risk gets lost. Should I put it first, or send it the day before?"
- **Peers only.** Once, at the same volume: "I'd like to finish this sentence."
- **When it's you.** Write your thought down, and begin with theirs.
- **When it repeats.** Ask whoever runs the call to keep a speaking order. And when someone else is cut off, speak up for them: "Could we hear the rest of that?"

### They correct you in public

Mid-October, a meeting on site two. Claire asked an engineer from Veldhaven's systems team how many door changes had failed in the night's test. "Two," he said. "It was nine," said Diego, the engineer placed at Veldhaven by Tolva, its dock-scheduling vendor. "I have the log open." Diego was right; two was the night before. The engineer didn't speak again that afternoon, and his next warning reached Diego two days late, as a ticket. "He used to walk over," the systems lead said.

Diego had cover. The two teams' page of working rules, agreed in *Across borders*, let anyone cut in to correct a number and said nothing about doing it in front of Claire. Another corrector may fear that someone will act on the wrong figure, or come from a team where a quick correction is a courtesy.

- **Upward too.** "Thank you. I'll check that and send you both the right figure by four."
- **If you need them.** Alone. The engineer's version, when Diego asked what he should have done: "Send it to me while I'm talking. I'll correct it myself."
- **Peers only.** "Nine, then. Let me finish what it means."
- **When it's you.** Cut in only if someone is about to act on the wrong figure. Then give the floor straight back: "The log says nine. Please go on."
- **When it repeats.** Agree a line. The two teams added one to their page: with somebody's boss in the room, the number goes to the speaker first.

### They dismiss your work

"No. That won't work. Next one." Mateo, Tolva's co-founder and chief technology officer, needed less than a minute. Six days earlier, on the night of 6 October, a migration that a coding agent wrote and nobody read had mislabeled site one's doors for four hours. The engineer on contract had brought a design to undo a change like that.

Mateo had seen a real fault and said only the conclusion, in his second language, after a week of short nights. Your part may be that the review was the first anyone saw of the design.

- **Upward too.** Treat the verdict as a claim and ask, alone or in writing, what it rests on. Hers, that afternoon: "You said the undo won't work. I'll fix it or drop it by Thursday. Which step fails?" His: "Step four. It wipes out every door the supervisors moved by hand. The other five are good, and I should have said so."
- **If you need them.** Before the next review: "What do you look at first in a design like this?"
- **Peers only.** In the room: "Which step? I'd rather hear it now."
- **When it's you.** Give the reason with the verdict, or the day you will have it.
- **When it repeats.** Ask for one rule: every rejection names what fails, in the notes. If reasons still don't come, ask who else can review.

### They make a dig

Tyler, Tolva's delivery lead, ran October's retrospective. "In August I wrote 'Mateo and Lucía' beside who reads the agents' work," he said. "I should have written 'whoever's awake.'" People laughed. Mateo didn't.

A joke can be a complaint that never had its own place on an agenda. Tyler had let that line go in August without asking for a day, because asking meant an argument. Mateo's part was plain: he and Lucía, his co-founder, had never set one. Elsewhere, teasing may be how a team shows affection, or a joke may have changed in translation.

- **Upward too.** Answer the true part and move the rest: "That's right, we never set a day. If there's more, I'd like it after this." Mateo said it, and Tyler came. "There is more. I should have asked you in August." Twenty minutes later they had a rule: a line in the notes gets one name, or it isn't a decision. If none of the joke is true, carry on, and ask afterward.
- **If you need them.** Alone, the same day: "Is there something about August we should put on the agenda?"
- **Peers only.** The same question aloud, with time to answer.
- **When it's you.** Say the complaint as one plain sentence, where it can be answered.
- **When it repeats.** Give both dates and say what you need: "Tell me directly, or put it on the agenda." After that, go to *When the right words fail*.

## Between meetings

### They write yes and mean no

In the week after the failed migration of 6 October, Tyler, Tolva's delivery lead, moved the engineer building site two's driver texts to other work for two days. Bianca, the product manager, replied: "Of course. The drivers have waited this long."

Writing carries no voice, and in a second language, as English is for Bianca, a flat sentence may be only flat. Tyler's part: she heard after it was decided.

- **Upward too.** Offer both readings and let them choose. Tyler wrote: "I can read this as 'two days is fine' or as 'you should have asked me first.' Which is it?" Bianca: "The second. Two days is fine. Finding out afterward isn't."
- **If you need them.** Talk, then send the read-back: what you understood, what you will do, what you are unsure of.
- **Peers only.** "That reads like a no. Is it?"
- **When it's you.** Write the no, and what you would accept.
- **When it repeats.** Ask before you decide: "What would you choose?" Then take the words as written, and say so: "I'm reading 'of course' as a yes, and I'll start at noon."

### They go silent

In mid-October Naomi's forecast missed an afternoon at site three. Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, asked why, heard nothing for three days, and wrote again: "I don't need the cause today. Is 23 October still good for your yes or no on site three? One line is enough." Naomi wrote back: "The 23rd holds. I don't know yet why Tuesday missed. On Monday I'll tell you what I've ruled out." She had spent three nights in the gate log, row by row, and hadn't wanted to write before she knew.

Silence can mean a message that never arrived, an answer that needs someone's approval, or a team where no reply means yes (*Across borders*). Your part may be the question. "What happened?" asked for a finished investigation.

- **Upward too.** Ask for something smaller that can be answered truthfully today: a date, a yes or no, the name of whoever knows.
- **If you need them.** Change the channel once. Phone, and ask how they are before you ask where it is.
- **Peers only.** "I've asked twice. Should I take it as a no?"
- **When it's you.** Send the smallest true line you have.
- **When it repeats.** Agree in writing what silence means and what you will do without them. Then do it.

### They present your work as theirs

Early in October, Veldhaven's finance lead asked Naomi, who sells Veldhaven its arrival forecast, why they were paying for it twice. A page from Tolva listed "our arrival forecast." Lucía, Tolva's chief executive, had written four pages and let an assistant cut them to two. The words "from Naomi" went with the rest, and Lucía signed what was left.

Shortening can lose names. "Our" can mean the project's, and in some teams work goes out under whoever presents it. Check your part: is your name on the work itself, where the next person to shorten it would see it?

- **Upward too.** Offer a cause they can accept and ask for one line. Naomi wrote: "Your page says 'our arrival forecast.' I think my name went in the shortening. Could you send finance one line today to put it back?" Lucía's, within the hour, copied to Naomi: "The forecast is Naomi's, and our scheduler reads it. The page was mine, and so is the mistake."
- **If you need them.** Before the next one: "Who presents this, and how will my part be named?"
- **Peers only.** In the room: "I ran those numbers, so send the questions to me."
- **When it's you.** Before you sign a shorter version, check whose names are gone.
- **When it repeats.** Put your name in the first line and send the work yourself to the person who decides. Where credit decides your pay or your contract, take dated examples to whoever sets it.

### They keep moving the date

Renata, Tolva's first investor, wanted the plan for sites two and three by Friday 30 October. Then by Wednesday. At nine on Tuesday evening she wrote: "Tonight?" Lucía had typed "Sure" before she stopped. She had already said it twice, at no visible cost, so why would the date hold?

Renata had been moved too. Her partners had brought their meeting forward.

- **Upward too.** Say what the new date buys, and ask what it is for. Lucía sent: "Tonight you can have the two dates and what each depends on. The cash plan is checked on Friday. Which one is tonight for?" Renata: "The dates. They meet in the morning."
- **If you need them.** Ask for the date behind the date: "What are you preparing for, and when is it?" Renata sent her partners' calendar.
- **Peers only.** "That's the third date. Choose one and I'll keep it."
- **When it's you.** Send the reason with the new date.
- **When it repeats.** Keep the dates in one written line: "The 30th, then the 28th, then tonight." Ask who may move it, and how much notice you both accept. *Saying no and pushing back* covers the date you must refuse.

## When the right words fail

A data analyst shows a sales team the numbers every Monday. One Monday the head of sales says, "Story time." She checks, alone: "Is something wrong in the numbers?" "No, no. It's a joke." The next Monday, again. This time she describes it: "On the 5th and the 12th you introduced the numbers as 'story time,' and nobody asked a question after it. Please introduce them as the numbers." He agrees. Two weeks later, with a customer on the call: "And now, story time."

She did every step well. A response works only if the other person keeps their side of it, and he didn't. Asking him a third time would only repeat the second, so she changes the route and writes to her manager:

"On 5, 12 and 26 October the numbers were introduced as 'story time,' the last with a customer present. On the 14th I asked him to stop, and he agreed. I'd like you to take this to his manager, and to tell me by Friday what will happen."

It took two weeks. The jokes stopped. The two of them are polite, and no more than that. The formal route was simply the next step, and her notes were ready for it.

> **From practice:** Write the note the same day, in the words that were said. A note like that can be checked by someone who wasn't there, and it protects the other person from your memory as much as it protects you.

### Practice: the decision that comes undone

**Situation.** Twice, a peer has said yes in a design review and then asked the manager you share to reopen the choice. You write to him.

**First draft (what a careful engineer writes).**
"I wanted to raise something that's been on my mind for a while. In March you were fine with the queue, and then I heard from our manager that there were concerns, so we reopened it. I let that go. Now the same thing has happened with the cache. I may be reading too much into it, and I know you're busy, but I felt a bit undermined. It would be great if we could be more transparent going forward."

**What's wrong.** It is history in the order it happened, with the request at the end. "Undermined" is a label he can deny, and "more transparent" is nothing he could be seen to do. The hedges protect the writer and leave the one real doubt unsaid: half of this is secondhand.

**Better.**
"On Tuesday you said yes to the cache. On Thursday our manager asked me to reopen it and said the concern was yours. The queue went the same way in March. I only have the second half from her, so I may have it wrong. What did you need on Tuesday that the review didn't give you?"

He writes back: "Time. You two had decided before I'd finished reading."

"So you need the design before the meeting, and I'll send it the day before. What I'm unsure of: will you say it in the review if you're still against it?"

**Why it works.** Two dated events, what they rest on, what may be wrong, and a question that assumes he had a reason. He had one, and the writer was part of it. The read-back turns his reason into two things either of them could check.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Take something that has happened twice. Change the names. Write the latest event with its day, then the earlier one, what you haven't seen yourself, and a question about what they needed. Keep your request until they answer. **Done means** a colleague finds no word in it for what the person is, and can tell what you saw from what you heard.

### Practice: two explanations

**If you do only one, do this one.** **With a person.** Choose someone you have called difficult this month, in a case that doesn't belong under *What is not a wording problem*. Write one line a recording would back, then your part, then two innocent explanations. This week, ask that person one question about the work that could tell the two apart, alone: "Did you get the plan before the call?" Watch for a reason that wasn't on your list. **Done means** someone who likes them reads your line and agrees it happened, and you can say which explanation the answer ruled out.

## Words to use

- **To open.** "Can I check something about Tuesday with you?" "I have only my half of Tuesday. What's yours?"
- **To ask.** "Next time, could you [one act] before [one moment]?"
- **To close.** "So from [day], I'll [act] and you'll [act]. What would you change?"
- **To change the route.** "I don't think the two of us can settle this. I'm asking [name] to help, and I wanted you to hear it from me." (Only when it is safe to tell them.)

### Phrases you will hear

- "No offense, but..." (a criticism follows; listen for the fact in it)
- "I'm just saying." (that was a complaint, and I'd rather not defend it)
- "With all due respect..." (I disagree strongly)

## When it backfires

**They hold the power.** Naming a boss's behavior, however well, can cost you, and anything written can be forwarded. Ask a question about the work, keep your notes, and find out who could act before you need them.

**They deny it, or push harder.** Don't argue the account a second time. "We remember it differently. From next week, I'm asking for [one act]." Then write your note. If pushing harder becomes a threat or a penalty for speaking, go to *What is not a wording problem*.

**A private word isn't private everywhere.** In some teams an email describing someone's behavior is an accusation, and in others so is a closed door. Ask someone who knows the team which is lighter.

**An assistant as the judge.** Paste in the thread, ask "Is she undermining me?", and it has only your side to answer from. Ask it to strike every word a recording wouldn't back.

**Too much of it.** A note on every joke makes you hard to work with. If three people separately describe the same act of yours, take it as yours.

**In a second language.** You don't need a delicate phrase. Write short sentences first: the day, what they did, what you haven't seen, your question. If you can't tell whether a line was a dig, ask if there's something they'd like changed; you may be right to wonder, and the question is safe either way.

## What is not a wording problem

Some behavior has no entry here, on purpose. Harassment, discrimination, threats, retaliation for speaking up, a risk to someone's safety, anything unlawful: none of these is a wording problem. If one is happening to you, it isn't your fault, and it isn't your job to phrase your way out. You don't owe the person a private word first. This book gives you no script for it, because you shouldn't have to handle it alone.

What can help is a record and other people. Write dated notes: what was said or done, where, who was there. Keep them where you will still be able to reach them, within the rules on confidential material. Use formal channels: your employer's complaint procedure, human resources, a manager you trust. If you work as a contractor or alone, ask whether the client's procedure covers you. Look for outside help too: a lawyer, a public body that takes complaints, a support line. If anyone is in danger now, call the emergency services first.

If you see it happen to someone else, write down what you saw and ask them what help they want. Some roles carry a duty to report; find out whether yours does. If your company is too small for any procedure, write one page before it is needed: whom to tell, and a second name in case the first is the problem.

Rules and time limits differ by country and by employer, some are short, and this is not legal advice. Ask someone qualified where you are, and ask early.

# Arguing well

On the night of 6 October, a change written by a coding agent mislabeled doors at Veldhaven's first warehouse for four hours. Three more such changes are waiting. Mateo runs technology at Tolva, whose scheduler picks the doors; he wants an engineer to read each one first. Otávio, Veldhaven's head of information security, wants ten working days. Eight days later they are on a video call.

Mateo: "Somebody reads it before it runs. I read it on the seventh, and I saw the fault in ten minutes."

Otávio: "On the seventh you knew there was a fault to find."

Mateo: "Any of my engineers would have seen it."

Otávio: "None of them did."

Mateo: "None of them read it. That's the rule I'm proposing. And your ten days wouldn't have caught it. Your team checks access, and that change used only the access you gave it."

Otávio: "Then we'll check more. Every change a machine wrote comes to my team, for ten working days, before it goes near a door."

Mateo: "One after another, that's six weeks for the three we owe site two. Site two goes live on 9 November."

Otávio: "So now we are discussing your date."

The change had passed its tests. Otávio answers for whatever an outside company does inside Veldhaven. In August he had said "Clear" in a review and objected by email the next morning. This time he objected out loud, which was better for everyone and harder on Mateo. Each had been right at least twice, and after twenty minutes they were no closer to a rule.

## Which argument is this?

Count the questions in those lines. Would a reader have caught the fault? That one is about what is true. Should the rule protect the doors, whatever happens to the date? That one is about what to do. Whose hours get spent, and who can stop a change? That one is about something limited. Three questions were open, and both of them kept answering one with a reason that belonged to another.

**Sort first**, the tool from *Thinking on your feet*, works on disagreements too. A disagreement is about **what is true** (agree the test before anyone argues the answer) or **what to do** (agree the goal). Or it is about **who gets something limited** (agree a fair rule and name who decides).

Anyone can prepare a case. In an argument, the second question comes from someone with a case of their own. Yet two people who disagree about the answer can still agree on what would settle it. Find that first. Then you can press each other's reasons as hard as the work deserves, and give up a point without giving up your case. You can both leave with something you will keep.

> **Line to keep:** Agreeing on what would settle it is the part of an argument both of you can win.

If you can't tell what would settle it, ask, "What would you need to see?" and sort the answer. If it's already going badly, find the line below that sounds like yours and start there.

| What you hear | What is missing | Start with |
|---|---|---|
| The same sentence, a third time | A sign that it was heard | Their side, until they say yes |
| Two people sure, and nobody has looked | A test | The test before the answer |
| "So now we're discussing your date" | What each side stands to lose | The cost of being wrong |
| Agreed facts, opposite plans | A goal | The goal, then the plan |
| Two claims on the same hours or money | A rule | The rule, then the decider |
| A point you can't answer | Its size | Give the point, keep the rest |
| "That's not what you said on Wednesday" | What changed, and why | Change your mind in public |
| Nothing new for ten minutes | An ending | When nobody moves |

Take the fact first whenever somebody could check it this week. A plan argued on an unchecked fact gets argued twice.

## Their side, until they say yes

When a sentence comes back a third time, stop answering it. Say it back. Twenty minutes in, Mateo did:

"Let me say your side, and you correct it. The ten days aren't the point. After a bad night you're the one who gets asked. You need to say who looked at the change, and why you believed they'd find anything. Is that it?"

"Nearly," Otávio said. "Who looked, yes. I also need somebody who can say no before it runs, with time to say it."

"Who looked, why you'd trust them to find it, and somebody with the power and the time to say no."

"Yes."

Work for that yes before you object to anything. This is the **read-back** from *Listening people can feel*, used with someone you disagree with. Saying the other side first is very old advice; the skill is in how well you say it. Use their words, and if you can make their case better than they did, make it. Mateo's first try left out the power to say no, the part Otávio cared about most, and for twenty minutes he had argued against something else.

## The test before the answer

"Any of my engineers would have seen it." "None of them did." Both were sure, and neither had looked.

Choose the statement worth looking at. Take away each thing you said, one at a time, and ask whether your conclusion still stands. Mateo could lose the ten minutes and the date and keep his rule. Without "any of my engineers would have seen it", he had nothing.

Then agree what you will look at, and what each result would mean, before anyone sees a result. Decide it afterward and each side can read the result its own way. Mateo and Otávio wrote this down:

"Tyler picks six changes that agents have written since July. On copies of three, one of Otávio's reviewers hides a fault that would send a truck to the wrong door. An engineer at Tolva who has seen none of the six reads them all, and marks each one she would refuse to sign. If she stops all three, reading is enough. If she misses one, it isn't."

Tyler runs delivery at Tolva. Testers have long hidden faults to test their own checks. The last two sentences do the work here, agreed while nobody knew whom they would hurt.

### The cost of being wrong

They nearly didn't write it. Otávio's line about the date was fair: Mateo had a reason to want one answer, and it is hard to look honestly for an answer you can't afford. Otávio had a reason too, and hadn't said it. So say what you stand to lose, and ask for theirs, before you design anything.

"It's my date as well, yes," Mateo said. "If reading isn't enough, site two may slip, and your board has just kept that date on our word. What does it cost you if I'm right?"

"I have told Claire ten days," Otávio said. Claire runs operations at Veldhaven. "If reading is enough, I have to take that back."

"Then whichever way it goes, she hears it from both of us, on the same call."

Being wrong would now cost each of them one short sentence, said beside somebody who had risked the same. If you want an honest test, first make losing it something a decent person can live with.

## The goal, then the plan

Some arguments survive every fact. You agree on what happened and want opposite things done. Leave the plans alone and write the goal as something both of you could watch happen, the **observable version** of a purpose.

Mateo had argued for speed and Otávio for control, two labels nobody can check. The goal they could both sign was this: "No change sends a truck to a wrong door without a named person having checked it for exactly that. Site two is live before the December peak." Against that goal, both plans came up short. Ten days of access review did nothing for the first sentence. Reading did little for it while nobody was free to say no.

If you can't write one goal you both accept, that's the disagreement. Say it in one line and take it to whoever owns the goal.

## The rule, then the decider

When there isn't enough of something for both of you, no argument makes more of it. Otávio has two reviewers. In the weeks before the peak, every supplier who touches Veldhaven's systems wants them.

Agree how the choice gets made before you argue any one case. Make the rule about the work ("whatever can move a truck goes first"), because a rule about people ("Tolva waits") starts the argument again every week. Then name the person who decides the case your rule didn't foresee.

"And when my reviewer says no?" Otávio asked.

"Then it's no, with the reason in writing, until Claire has heard both of us. She decides the same day."

"She will like that less than we do," Otávio said. Claire agreed to it anyway.

## Give the reason, or keep them listening?

You may have been told to show your reasoning. At its best, a reason is something the other person can check, and without one you are asking to be trusted. You may also have been told that reasons make people defend harder. That has a best case too. A "because" that arrives after someone has taken a position in front of others can hand them something to fight.

My rule: give a reason when it invites checking, and hold back the "because" whose only job is to prove someone wrong. Look at Mateo's third line. "That change used only the access you gave it" was true, and it was said to win. The same fact can invite: "I believe that change stayed inside the access we agreed in August. Could your team confirm it from the log?"

Give one reason, your strongest, and stop; *The pitch* has the nearest finding. An argument adds its own cost: offer three reasons, and the other person can answer the weakest and leave you defending a sentence you never needed.

## Give the point, keep the rest

A good point against you stops somewhere. There are two ways to miss the place: give nothing, or give everything to make the discomfort end. Ask of their point what you would ask of your own, the third question of *the second-question test*: *Where does it stop?* Then concede exactly that far.

Otávio showed how, once he had looked at the log. "Ten days would not have caught it. Ten days is for access, and the access was right. So I take it back for changes that stay inside the access you have. A change that asks for more still gets all ten."

He gave the whole point and kept the ten days that still did something. The practice below fills in the pattern:

`You're right that [the exact point]. So [what I change]. It doesn't reach [what I keep], because [the reason].`

Concede only what you now believe. A point given as a move, to get one back, is a small lie.

### Practice: one point, at its size

**Situation.** A design review. You propose that the mobile app retries failed payments by itself. The client's architect says, "If the first attempt timed out, a retry can charge the customer twice."

**First draft (what a capable engineer says).**
"Well, the provider is supposed to catch duplicates, so in practice that would be pretty rare. But sure, if it's a concern, we can take retries out."

**What's wrong.** "Supposed to" and "pretty rare" rest on nothing anyone has looked at. Then the whole design goes, including the part her point never touched.

**Better.**
"You're right: after a timeout we don't know whether the first attempt went through. So we won't retry timeouts. It doesn't reach refused connections, because nothing got as far as the provider. Those were seven in ten of last month's failures, by our log. I'd keep retries for those."

"So the design was wrong."

"For timeouts, yes. I hadn't separated the two. For refused connections I still think it's right, and one refused connection that charged someone would change my mind."

**Why it works.** Her point is said and granted in full, and the line where it stops has a reason she can check. The second answer grants it again and names what would end the rest.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Write down the best point anyone has made against a piece of your work. Fill in the pattern, say it aloud, and answer "So you were wrong?" in two sentences. **Done means** a colleague who hears both can tell you what you gave up, what you kept, and what would make you give up the rest.

## Change your mind in public

On Friday the engineer read all six. She stopped two of the three with hidden faults and passed the third. Its own tests had passed too: the agent had written them, and none looked at the doors the fault moved. Before anyone told her the score, she closed the changes, wrote her own tests from each brief, and ran them. They caught the third fault at once, and she hadn't known there was one left to find.

On Monday Claire joined the call, and Mateo went first:

"On Wednesday I said any of my engineers would catch it by reading. She caught two of three, so I was wrong about reading on its own. What stopped the third was a test she wrote from the brief. So I'm proposing both. A named engineer reads and signs every change an agent writes, and checks it against tests a person wrote. One reader and three faults is a small trial. If you've told anyone that reading is enough because I said so, tell me who, and I'll correct it."

Say what you claimed and when, what moved you, and what you think now, at its size. Then go after the old version, because people may still be acting on it. That step is easy to skip, and it is why people can believe your next claim: they watched you take the last one back.

"And I told you ten days for everything," Otávio said to Claire. "Ten are for new access. For the rest, their signature reaches us one working day ahead, and we can stop it. I'd put my name to that." Both could now say what each control catches and where it stops. They ran the rule as a trial until site two's go-live, and the three changes were in by the end of the month.

## When nobody moves

They didn't settle everything. Otávio wanted no agent-written change to run after ten at night. Mateo wanted the quiet hours, when the fewest trucks wait. Neither could name a test that would fit before November, and after two rounds nothing new was being said.

Stop there, and stop in writing. "We disagree about one thing: whether these changes may run at night. Until it's decided, they run by day. Claire decides on 30 October." With a name and a day, an unfinished argument costs you a line on a page. Without them, it can come back in every meeting under a new subject.

> **From practice:** Before a review starts, write its question on the shared page in words both sides accept. When someone makes a fine point about something else, anyone can point at the sentence without sounding rude.

## On the page

In a thread nobody hears a yes, so it is easy to keep adding reasons. Once the same point has gone back and forth twice, write one message with their side, your concession and the test in it, or pick up the phone.

Ask an assistant for a case on your side, then for the other side. If it writes both, its agreement settles nothing, but it may show you an objection you haven't met. Which fact would change your mind, and what you will say when it turns up, are yours to answer for.

### Practice: the trial that costs too much

**Situation.** You run a small software company. Your head of sales wants the free trial cut from thirty days to fourteen. The thread is nine messages long, and it's your turn.

**First draft (what a careful founder writes).**
"I do hear you, but thirty days is standard for tools like ours. Everyone I talk to says a month is the minimum, the last three customers signed in week four, and a short trial makes us look desperate. Changing the emails would also take a week. I just don't think it's right for our kind of customer."

**What's wrong.** Five reasons at one volume, and the weakest is the easiest to answer. Nothing says where the head of sales is right, or what would end the thread.

**Better.**
"Your side, as I understand it: people decide in the first week or not at all, so days fifteen to thirty cost us support time and teach us nothing. Correct me if that's not it.

You're right about support. I checked the tickets: eleven hours a week go to trials past day fourteen, and I'd left that out.

Where I still disagree is one fact. I think the larger companies decide late. I've read six of last quarter's forty trials, so that's all it rests on.

Could we count all forty on Thursday, by size and by the day they decided? If three or fewer of the twelve larger ones decided after day fourteen, I'll cut it to fourteen. How many would change your mind?"

**Why it works.** Their side comes first, one point is granted with its number, and five reasons become one fact to count. The writer says what result would change their mind, and asks for the same.

**Your turn (15 minutes).** Take a real thread. Write: their side, the point you give, the one thing still in dispute, what would settle it, and what you'll do if it goes against you. **Done means** a stranger who reads only your message can say what would settle it, and the reply starts with a yes or a correction.

## Practice: what would change your mind

**If you do only one, do this one.**

**With a person.** Choose a disagreement that's still open this week, with someone you can talk to.

1. On a card, write your claim in one sentence. Under it, write the one thing that would make you give it up. If you can't, you are not ready to argue yet.
2. Write your guess at theirs.
3. Say their side until they say yes. Then ask, "What would you need to see?", and tell them yours.
4. Together, write one sentence that begins "This is settled when".

Watch what they name. If it can be checked, you have a test. If it's something they want, sort again. If neither of you can name anything, stop and ask who decides. Looking for the fact that would move you both is a known exercise; the sorting keeps it useful when no fact would.

**Done means** the sentence is in writing, you have both said yes to it, and someone who wasn't there could tell whether it has happened. If you would rather think before you answer, do all of it in messages.

**Spar with an AI.** Rehearse the argument you most want to win.

```text
You disagree with me about [the question]. Your position is [their side, in two sentences].
Argue it honestly. Do not agree with me to be polite.
Do not answer my objections until I have said your side well enough that you would sign it. If I get it wrong, correct me once.
Change your mind only about what I have actually shown, and say exactly which part.
After six exchanges, stop. Tell me my weakest reason, the point of yours I avoided, and whether I gave up more or less than you had earned.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

- **Their side.** "Let me say your side, and you correct it."
- **To sort it.** "Are we disagreeing about what happened, or about what to do next?" "What would settle this for you?"
- **Before a test.** "Before we look: which result would change your mind, and which would change mine?"
- **Your stake.** "You should know what I stand to lose here: [it]."
- **A changed mind.** "On [day] I said [claim]. Since then [what happened]. I now think [new claim]."
- **An ending.** "We disagree about one thing: [it]. Until [name] decides on [day], we'll [what happens meanwhile]."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Let's agree to disagree" (let's stop here): ask who decides, and what happens until then.
- "I'm just playing devil's advocate" (I'm arguing a side that may not be mine): ask, "Is it a worry of yours?"

## When it backfires

**They can end it.** Someone with more power doesn't have to argue with you. Give your claim, its one reason and what would change your mind, once, in private or in writing. Ask, "What would you need to see?" If the answer is nothing, it is decided, and that is worth knowing. Never propose a test of your boss's claim in front of the people who report to them.

**You're the one who can end it.** When you hold the power, people may say yes to your version of their side because it's yours. Ask for the correction: "Which part would you say differently?" And name your stake first, because it is hard for them to ask.

**It isn't an argument.** How a person is being treated, or whether they are safe, is nothing to test or trade. *Difficult people* says where to take it.

**The test costs more than the mistake.** Two engineers disagree about a variable's name. Whoever owns the file decides.

**Their side, said to beat it.** Restate them in a weaker form and you've turned a courtesy into a trap. Treat a read-back that gets no yes as your fault until you've tried twice.

**A question that sounds like an accusation.** In some teams "What would change your mind?" means "You're being stubborn." Ask it of both of you: "What would we need to see?" Where disagreeing in front of others costs someone their standing, have the argument before the meeting.

**In a second language.** Saying their side takes words you may not have ready. Ask for time, write it, and read it out: "I've written your side in two sentences. Tell me what's wrong." Written down, nobody can mistake a word you searched for as a point you gave up.
