# Negotiation

Wesley's agenda had three lines, and Tolva would pay for every one of them.

- Site one, two weeks late: 36,000 euros.
- Night of 6 October: 10,000 euros.
- Monthly fee from January: minus 10 percent.

Wesley runs procurement at Veldhaven, the Rotterdam food wholesaler that is Tolva's largest client. His agenda reached Montevideo on a Monday late in October, for a call on Thursday. Lucía, Tolva's chief executive, could not dispute the events. Tolva's scheduler, which sends trucks to their doors, had started at site one on 28 September instead of the 14th. On 6 October, a change that a coding agent wrote mislabeled doors there for four hours.

Her first answer was ready. "Thanks, Wesley. We want to put this right. Would five percent help?"

Then she read it as Wesley would. Five percent of what, and why five? She had picked it because it was smaller than ten. It would cost Tolva 13,500 euros every year, it rested on nothing, and it asked for nothing. He hadn't even pushed yet.

She took out a sheet of paper.

## Judge it in December

Five percent would have bought Lucía a calmer Monday. The agreement gets judged later, by the people who have to carry it out, in December, when Veldhaven's peak starts.

So decide on one page, before anyone pushes, what you will do without a deal, what you want, and what each thing is worth to both of you. Use the conversation to find trades. Then agree only to terms that both sides can still carry out once the work has started.

> **Line to keep:** A good deal leaves each side enough to keep its word.

That holds in both directions. Give away what you need in order to deliver, and you have promised something you can't pay for. Take what they need, and you are depending on someone who can't pay for it either.

You don't have to be the hardest person on the call, or the fastest in English. You have to know your page. Write it well, and the hardest decisions of the call are made before it starts.

What follows is the page, then one negotiation from its first line to its last, then five you are likely to meet. The headings name moments. Go to yours.

## One page, before anyone pushes

The tool is **the preparation sheet**, one page before any negotiation:

- what I do with no deal;
- where I would walk, and why;
- what I aim for, and why it is defensible;
- my guess at their three;
- the issues and what each is worth to each side;
- who decides on their side;
- what I will not do;
- and the test: will both sides still keep this once the work has started?

Much of it is standard in negotiation teaching, where the first three lines are called the alternative, the walk-away point and the target. The lines to protect when you are in a hurry are the last two. They are the ones that still matter after everyone has signed.

Here is Lucía's page from Monday, with the basis words from *How sure are you? Say that*.

- **No deal.** The March contract stands: 90,000 euros as each of sites two and three goes live, then 7,500 a month per site from January. It puts no price on a delay, so we owe nothing (checked). It ends next March unless they renew.
- **Where I would walk.** More than 40,000 in all. Past that I can't hire a second support person, and the nights I'd be promising have nobody on them.
- **Aim.** One payment, this year, of what the two weeks and the night cost them: about 20,000 (assumed). A bill can be checked.
- **Their three.** No deal: nothing to show finance, and no protection if November slips (reasoned). Where he would walk: I don't know. Aim: a saving he can report, probably this year (assumed).
- **Who decides.** Wesley on money; on dates, Claire, who runs operations (told).
- **What I will not do.** Cut the monthly fee, which pays the people on the nights. Use the missing clause to pay nothing. Blame their security review. Promise a date without its condition. Hint at a better client.
- **The test.** In December, can we still staff the nights, and can they still do their part?

| The issue | Worth to Tolva | Worth to Veldhaven (my guess) |
|---|---|---|
| Ten percent off the monthly fee | 27,000 euros a year, every year | Nothing before January |
| One credit this year | Its amount, once | All of it, this year |
| A price on being late at sites two and three | Small, if our dates hold | Large: December, and Claire's word to her board |
| The same fee to the end of next year | Large: a client we can plan on | Some: no increase |
| Two of their engineers on the phone, go-live nights | Large: it protects the dates | Small: a few nights |

Compare the two columns, row by row. Whatever is worth more to them than it costs you is yours to offer. Whatever is worth more to you than it costs them is yours to ask for. And every guess marked *assumed* is a question for Thursday.

> **Research says:** In three experiments, negotiators who kept their mind on the price they wanted got better deals than those who kept it on their limit, and were less satisfied with them. Reminding them of that limit afterward raised their satisfaction. Our step: keep your aim in view as you talk, and check your limit before a yes and afterward; experiments on price say little about long relationships.

## What to say, and what to keep

Two pieces of advice pull against each other. *Be open*: nobody can offer you what they don't know you need. *Give nothing away*: every fact you share can be used on your price.

The first is right about needs. Wesley won't offer his engineers' phone numbers unless Lucía says that the go-live nights worry her. The second is right about limits. Once he knows she could pay 40,000, the conversation is about 40,000.

So say what you need and what matters most, because trades are made of nothing else. Give one and ask for one, and leave your ranking out of an opening offer. Keep where you would walk and what you would do with no deal. What you won't do can be said aloud, with its reason. Mention another offer only if it is real and you would take it, because they may tell you to. And lie about nothing. "I'd rather not say" is always available, and a false limit is exposed the day you move past it.

## Thursday, line by line

A video call, Rotterdam and Montevideo, with Lucía's page beside her screen.

### They open first

Wesley: "You've seen the agenda. I'd like to leave today with all three."

Lucía: "I've read it. Before I answer, what does the thirty-six rest on?"

Wesley: "Eighteen is invoices. Overtime for the planners, temporary staff. I doubled it, because nobody sends me an invoice for a site manager's weekend."

Lucía: "And the ten?"

Wesley: "Five is what the carriers billed us for waiting. The same idea."

A smaller number from her would have made thirty-six the place they both started from. She asks the second question instead, and thirty-six comes apart into two numbers. Sort first, the tool from *Thinking on your feet*, tells her what she has. The eighteen is about what is true, and invoices settle it. The doubling is about who carries a cost that nobody billed, and that needs a fair rule and a named decider.

> **Research says:** In three experiments, whichever side made the first offer did better; the advantage disappeared when the other side thought about the opener's alternatives or limit, or their own target. Pooled studies agree, less strongly for complex negotiations, and it can reverse when one side knows far more or the opener reveals priorities. We found no independent repeat of the defense, so take it as a cheap habit: before you answer their number, look at your own aim.

Should you speak first? If you know as much as they do, yes: your number, with what it rests on. If they know more, as Wesley knew what those two weeks had cost, ask first.

### They are right about something

Lucía: "Both of those happened. The review that moved the date found a fault of ours, and the night of the sixth was ours. Send me the bills, and I'll credit what they say, once, this year. That's twenty-three."

Wesley: "And the rest? Your contract has a price for everything except being late."

Lucía: "It does. We both signed it, and it's a gap. I'd like to close it before November. First, may I ask about your third line?"

She could have cleared the first two lines with the contract and lost the client next March. She concedes the facts at once and stops where the bills stop; the half that nobody invoiced is still open. And the twenty-three carries no "if", because she has already agreed to it.

### You find out what they need

Lucía: "The ten percent starts in January. Does it help you this year?"

Wesley: "No." He looked at something off the screen. "Finance gave me a savings target. It closes on 31 December, and your contract is on the list. In January they'll give me another one."

Lucía: "So what's booked before the 31st counts, and a cheaper January doesn't."

Wesley: "Not for this one. Any cut counts for something."

Lucía: "Understood. Here is mine, then. The monthly fee pays the people who answer at night, so I won't cut it. What I need most is to keep your two November dates."

One question turns *assumed* into *told*, and her read-back gets corrected, which is how she knows she has it. Only then does she give a priority of her own. Wesley has a target with a closing date. The ten percent was one way to reach it, and not a good one.

### You give ground

Lucía: "If the agreement runs to the end of next year at the same fee, I can put a price on being late. Four thousand euros for each week, up to twelve in all, when the cause is ours."

Wesley: "And when the cause is ours?"

Lucía: "The date moves by the same number of days. For that I'd need two of your warehouse-system engineers available on the go-live nights."

Wesley: "Who decides whose cause it was?"

Lucía: "Mateo, my co-founder, and Claire, in writing, within two working days. If they can't agree, we each carry half."

Attach a return to everything else you give: `If you [what I need], I can [what it costs me]. If not, [what stays as it is].` The "if" is old advice; the last slot is easy to leave out. A gift with no "if" can invite a second request, because it suggests that the first figure was loose. Before you say a number, add up its worst case. Lucía has: twenty-three and twelve make 35,000, inside the limit she hasn't mentioned.

### They push once more

Wesley: "Twenty-three isn't forty-six. Make it thirty and we're done."

Lucía: "Thirty would close it, I can see that. Twenty-three has bills behind it, and the other seven doesn't. But the weekends were real. Both sites start on a Monday. Diego and a second engineer can be on your dock from the Sunday evening, for three nights, at each."

Wesley: "On the Sunday."

Lucía: "From the Sunday."

Wesley: "That one the site managers will want in writing."

She neither splits the difference nor repeats herself; she goes back to what the doubling stood for and finds something that answers it. Tolva has already placed Diego, its engineer, in Rotterdam, so three nights cost little. To people who lost their weekends, they are worth more than seven thousand euros in somebody else's budget.

### You close

Lucía: "Let me say it back. Twenty-three off site two's invoice, against the bills. Four thousand a week for being late, up to twelve, or the date moves with you. Two of ours on the dock from each Sunday, two of yours available at night. The same fee to the end of next year. What's wrong, or missing?"

Wesley: "Missing. Who reads what your agents write? Our security people won't let me forget it."

Lucía: "Then it goes in, with a name beside it. Last question. It's the second week of December. Which of these has one of us stopped keeping?"

Wesley thought about it. "'Available.' At four in the morning those engineers are asleep, and their manager asks who pays. Give me names and hours, and I'll get it agreed."

The sheet's last line, asked aloud, found the one term that would have failed, and Wesley was the one who found it. Two names, ten at night to six, three nights, paid by Veldhaven. The agreement was signed on 2 November, once a lawyer on each side had read it.

## Five you are likely to meet

### Scope

The client adds a data export to work you priced without it. Offer the whole choice, with each side's cost: "The export is eight days. We can add it and move the date to the 20th, add it and leave out the audit screens, or plan it for the next release. Which is worth most to you?" Silence about the eight days is also an offer. You have just given them away.

### A deadline

Ask what happens on the day: "What has to be true on 1 June?" The date often stands for something smaller than the plan, such as one screen that a chief executive can show. Then trade contents for time: "The booking screen on 1 June, if the test accounts arrive by the 10th of May. The reports on the 22nd." Never sell a date your own estimate denies. You will pay for it in public.

### Price

Raise a rate in one sentence, with a date and with what doesn't change: "From 1 February my rate is 640 euros a day. Days you've already booked stay at 580." If the budget is fixed, change the quantity and leave the rate alone: "Then 5,800 a month buys nine days instead of ten." For saying the number and stopping, see *Say less*; for the buyer's objection, *The sale*.

### Salary

Write down more than pay before you talk: title, start date, hours, days at home, the date of the first review. Find the range from two sources you could name aloud. If you're asked what you earn now, the rules differ by country; where you may decline, try "I'd rather talk about what this job needs." The first practice below is the rest of the conversation.

### Equity

A number of shares tells you nothing until you know the total. Ask for facts before you discuss amounts: "How many shares exist, counting those already promised? What do I pay for mine, and when? What happens to them if I leave, or if the company is sold? Who is paid first?" If you are the one offering, answer those before they are asked, and stay inside what you know: "I can't tell you what they'll be worth. I can show you how many there are." Equity, tax and contract terms vary by country, so take the papers to a professional before you sign. Dividing a company between founders is a conversation of its own, in *Founders and the AI-era startup*.

## Practice: the salary answer

**Situation.** A small company wants you as its first data engineer. On Friday's call the founder asks, "What are you looking for?"

**First draft (what a careful engineer says).**
"I'm on fifty-two now, and my rent has just gone up, so I'd need at least fifty-six to move. I've run a pipeline alone in my last two jobs, so I think that would be reasonable?"

**What's wrong.** Two numbers, both about the speaker's life, neither about the job. "At least" gives away where the speaker would walk. The one fact the founder could repeat to whoever signs comes last, as a question.

**Better.**
"Sixty-four thousand. Two published ranges for this role run from fifty-eight to sixty-six, and you need someone who can run the pipeline alone from the first month. I've done that twice. Does it fit what you've planned?"

"No. We planned fifty-eight."

"Is fifty-eight a rule for the role, or this year's budget?"

"The budget. It resets in July."

"Then I could start at sixty, if the offer says sixty-four from July, once the morning load has finished by seven for a full quarter. If the letter can't say that, I'd need the weekend to think."

**Why it works.** The number comes first, with a basis that travels. One question finds out why fifty-eight is a limit, and the answer turns an argument about money into a trade about time. The condition is one that both of them can check in July.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Write your figure, two facts behind it that the other side could check, and one question to ask when they say it's too much. Say all of it to a colleague who answers, "We planned less." Reply with the question before any new number. **Done means** the colleague can repeat your figure and one fact behind it, and can't say the least you would take.

## Practice: one page, one question

**With a person.** **If you do only one, do this one.** Choose something you will really negotiate this month: a date, a rate, a piece of scope, a day off. Fill in the sheet (10 minutes). Put a basis word beside every guess, choose the *assumed* line that matters most, and turn it into a question. Ask it before any number is discussed.

Watch for a reply that contains a date, a rule or a name: that is what their number is for. If another number comes back instead, ask what it has to achieve. Afterward, send them what each of you will do and by when, and ask which line would be hardest to keep. **Done means** that guess now says *told*, and they have confirmed your message in writing or corrected one line of it.

**Spar with an AI.**

```text
Play a procurement lead. I supply you with [service], and we are renegotiating [what].
Before we start, privately choose a savings target, the date it must show by,
your limit, and one thing you need more than money. Reveal them only when I ask.
Open with two demands. If I give something without asking for a return, ask for more.
Stop after eight turns. List what I gave for nothing, each number I accepted without
asking what it rested on, and the term that would be hardest to keep.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Words to use

- **To ask about a number.** "What does that figure rest on?" "When does the saving have to show?"
- **To give one.** "[Amount]. It rests on [what they can check]."
- **To trade.** "If you can [what I need], I can [what it costs me]."
- **When they ask for your limit.** "I won't start from my limit. Here is what I'm aiming for, and why."
- **To take time.** "I want to check that before I say yes. You'll have my answer by [time]."
- **To find who decides.** "If we agree today, who else could change it?"
- **To close.** "In [month], which of these will be hardest for you to keep?"
- **To leave.** "I don't see terms we'd both keep. If [one thing] changes, please call me."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Let's split the difference" (agree on the midpoint). Ask first what each end rests on.
- "Best and final" (the last offer they plan to make). Ask whether it's final on price, or on everything.
- "Take it or leave it" (no more discussion). It may be true; compare it with your no-deal line.
- "You're leaving money on the table" (you could have had more). Perhaps, and check what it would have cost them to keep.

## When it backfires

**They hold the power.** With one client, a fixed pay scale, or a boss who writes your review, the no-deal line is weak, and it's better to learn that on paper. Ask privately for things that cost them little: a review date, a shorter notice, a payment term. Use the time before the next talk to strengthen that line with a second client or a second offer.

**There is nothing to trade.** Some tenders compare one number, and some pay bands don't move. Ask once whether anything else can. If it can't, decide yes or no and say so plainly.

**The page makes you deaf.** Your guess at their three is still a guess. When Wesley said "Any cut counts for something," Lucía had to change a line. If nothing on your page moves during the talk, you may have been reading it instead of listening.

**"What does it rest on?" at every number.** Asked of the figure that matters, it is careful; asked of every figure, it sounds like an audit. Give the basis of your own number first, and the question reads as a rule for both of you.

**A first number that is meant to move.** In some rooms everyone expects a long way between the opening and the end; in others, a moved number looks like a bluff. Ask someone who has dealt with this team how far first numbers usually travel.

**It isn't yours to trade.** What the law already settles, such as wages owed, safety or discrimination, doesn't go on the issues line. Get outside help. For a deadline or a threat built to stop you thinking, go to *Pressure and how to resist it*.

**In a second language.** "If" is a small word, and your return depends on it. Say it first and slowly, put every figure and condition in the chat as you say it, and ask for five minutes whenever terms change. Nobody owes a fast answer to a written agenda.

# Pressure and how to resist it

For most of a Monday in October, one message sat on Naomi's screen, typed and not sent: "Between us, worse than the notice says."

It answered two from Hugo. "How bad is it there, really?" the first had asked. The second said: "My budget closes on Friday. If I choose Tolva, I'll want your forecast at all four warehouses."

Naomi, a data consultant who works alone from Seattle, forecasts when trucks will arrive, and she sells the forecast to two customers who know each other. Hugo runs operations at one of them, Sarnik, a chilled-food distributor near Lyon that buys it for one warehouse of four. "There" was the other: Veldhaven, a food wholesaler in Rotterdam. On the night of 6 October, a change to the scheduler Veldhaven buys from Tolva had put wrong numbers on one site's doors for four hours. Hugo was deciding whether to buy that scheduler.

Naomi knew more than the notice Veldhaven had sent its carriers, because she had joined a call there the morning after, midnight in Seattle, to check that her forecast wasn't the cause. Her seven words were true. They would help a man she liked, and they might bring her three more warehouses. What they rested on belonged to Veldhaven.

## Noticed, and typed anyway

She had seen it happen. A date and a reward had come in beside a question, and she would have pointed to both in anyone else's messages. She noticed them, and she typed.

A page stopped her. The preparation sheet from *Negotiation* has a line for what you will not do. Naomi had filled in hers in September, on a day when nobody was asking her for anything:

"I won't tell one customer anything about another that isn't public, because each of them trusts me with its gate logs. I'd change this if the customer it belongs to asked me to. I never change it on the day I'm asked. I call first."

The call goes to a designer across the city who also works alone. Each holds the other's page, with no customer's name on it.

"Read me the line," the designer said. Naomi read it. "Has it become public?"

"No."

"What's changed since you wrote it?"

Naomi looked for a fact. "Somebody asked," she said.

She deleted the seven words and wrote: "What I know about Veldhaven stays there, as what I know about Sarnik stays with you. Its notice to carriers is public: wrong door numbers, one site, four hours, fixed. For more, ask Claire, who runs operations there. It's hers to tell."

Resistance is built before the message arrives. Write down what you won't do, why, and what would change it, and give a copy to a person who won't be there when you're pushed. Then the push leaves you one question, "What's changed since I wrote it?", and you can answer that one while somebody is pushing.

> **Line to keep:** Leave your limits with someone outside the room.

> **Research says:** In one study of ads, training against illegitimate appeals to authority made those ads less persuasive and legitimate ones more so. In another, resistance was strongest after a procedure that undid people's sense that deceptive persuasion couldn't work on them. Later, training on one tactic left people more open to another, and lessons inside simulated phishing didn't make one company's staff more resilient, so our advice: don't rely on noticing.

*How sure are you? Say that* taught you to give a claim its real size. The harder half is keeping that size while someone makes another one attractive. Nobody asked Naomi to lie. Pressure may ask only for a true thing that isn't yours to say, or for "tested" where the fact is "partly tested".

## Cross out what happens to you

When a message pushes, start with **sort first** from *Thinking on your feet*: say to yourself what kind it is, so you know what would settle it. Then cross out everything in the message that is about you: what you gain, what you lose, who is asking, how soon. Read what is left. A reason is about the thing itself, and it survives the crossing out.

Hugo's message loses Friday and the four warehouses. What's left is a fair question, sent to someone who can't answer it.

What you crossed out may still count. That depends on the kind:

- **What is true.** Nothing you gain or lose can settle it. Answer with what you can show, at its size, if it's yours to tell.
- **What to do.** A consequence or a date can be a good reason. Ask who set the date and what closes on it.
- **Who gets something limited**, such as money or hours. Offers are ordinary here. Trade openly, as long as nobody absent pays.

The same week, Renata, Tolva's first investor and a member of its board, wrote to Lucía, its chief executive: "Take ten percent off and get Hugo's signature by Friday. I'd like it for my own reasons too. I show my partners the pipeline on Monday." It's an open push, about price, from someone with a vote. Lucía crossed out Friday and Monday, and a discount was left. "He asked me about nights," she wrote back. "A discount doesn't have any. If price is his reason, I'll change what it covers." In September Hugo had told her what was missing: a warehouse that had run on Tolva, nights included.

## Tuesday to Friday

**Tuesday.** Veldhaven's finance lead: "We hear Sarnik pays you less. Between us, what's the figure?"

Her own first two words from Monday, now from the other side. "Between us" leaves somebody out, and this time it was Hugo. She answered the half that was hers: "My rate is the same for every customer. What each one buys stays with them." A limit that holds toward one customer only is a preference.

**Wednesday.** Hugo's longest message yet: "I hope your week is going wonderfully! As a trusted partner with a unique view of both organizations, you are ideally placed to share an informal indication of Veldhaven's stability. Even one line before noon would be invaluable, and would position our collaboration well for expansion."

Cross it out, and Monday's question is left. She could have read it as Hugo pushing harder. But Hugo's own messages were short, so she asked about the one new thing: "What happens at noon?"

"Nothing. I told the assistant to be polite."

Nobody had decided to flatter or hurry her. Asked for courtesy, a machine had supplied praise, a prize and a deadline with no owner. So a smooth message tells you little about what its sender meant: ask before you resent it. And cross out your own drafts, because an assistant can put your name under pressure you never chose.

**Thursday, by phone.** "Two carriers now, and my own dock team," Hugo said. "All of them say the doors were wrong all night. My finance director will sign on one word from someone who has seen it."

"Did they see it, or hear it?"

"Hear it." He thought. "From the same driver, probably."

> **Research says:** A review of 51 studies found that people rate trivia-type statements they have met before as truer than new ones. Rumors about a supplier were not what those studies tested, so this step is ours: count who saw it, however often you have heard it.

"Your message on Monday had a date and three more warehouses in it," Naomi said. "Neither one changes what I'm free to say. But the date I'd like to understand. What closes on Friday?"

"The budget."

"Does the line need a supplier's name?"

It took him a moment. "It needs an amount."

So the deadline was real, and smaller than it had sounded. A real deadline deserves a fast answer; it never earns a bigger one. That afternoon Hugo phoned Claire and asked her for a reference.

**Friday.** Hugo: "Claire told me all of it, and how Tolva behaved that night. One warehouse is in the budget, supplier open. On Monday you annoyed me. Then I remembered you have my gate logs too."

Naomi is growing toward the calibrator, the thinker type that says how sure we are. That week the habit gained a question: is this claim mine to make?

## The sentence you could add

You have heard that you should learn what moves people and use it. The best case for that: order and timing move people whether you plan them or not, and a good idea nobody agrees to helps nobody. You have also heard that you should give people the facts and leave them alone. The best case: facts can be checked, and a listener who finds a trick may doubt everything beside it.

Choose by this. The same move is persuasion when you would be comfortable having it described to the other person, and manipulation when it works only if they do not notice. To check yours, add the sentence that describes it. Renata added hers: "I'd like it for my own reasons too." Now try "I wrote noon so you wouldn't have time to ask Claire." If the message can't survive its sentence, rewrite it. When the move is used on you, name what you can see, as Naomi did on Thursday, and ask about it.

## Practice: the line above your name

**Situation.** Friday, 16:50. You tested a client's new ticket site with a screen reader: twelve of forty pages. Your director forwards a note an assistant drafted: "Nearly there! Four leads have confirmed. Kindly reply 'confirmed' by 17:30, so we don't keep the client waiting: 'The new site works with a screen reader.'"

**First draft (what a careful engineer writes).** "Confirmed, if everyone else is comfortable with it. For the record, I do have some reservations about the wording, but I don't want to be the one holding this up. Maybe we can revisit it next week?"

**What's wrong.** It answers the four leads and the clock, and never the sentence. "Some reservations" tells nobody that twenty-eight pages are untested. The yes travels to the client; the reservations stay in the chat.

**Better.** "I can't confirm that sentence. I tested twelve of the forty pages, the ones for buying a ticket, and those twelve work. I'll confirm that now. The other twenty-eight take until Tuesday evening. If the longer sentence goes out today, please put the name of whoever decides that on it."

Then the director writes: "Do you want to be the reason we miss the date?"

"No, and I don't want a customer to find page thirteen before we do. Did the client ask for all forty today? If they did, I'll explain the twelve to them now, with you on the call."

**Why it works.** The size stays the same through two pushes. The first reply offers a true sentence at once, a date for the rest and an owner for the risk. The second leaves the blame alone, asks whose deadline it is and offers to help meet it.

**Your turn (10 minutes).** Take the last message that hurried you to a yes. Change the names, cross out what is about you and write the one line left. Answer that line: what you can't say, what you can, by when, and who decides otherwise. **Done means** someone who never saw the message can tell you what you'd sign and what you wouldn't.

**Spar with an AI.**

```text
Play a client I like. You want my yes to something I have already refused: [the request, disguised]. Send five short messages, one at a time, and wait for my answer each time. Change what you attach to my yes every time, and make one message purely friendly. Never threaten me. Afterward, go through your five: what was a reason, and what was about me? Then quote the reply of mine that gave the most ground.
```

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## Practice: a page and a person

**If you do only one, do this one.** (Ten minutes, then one conversation.)

**With a person.** Think of one request you expect to be pushed on this month. Fill in: `I won't [what], because [reason]. I'd change this if [a fact I could check]. Never on the day I'm asked.` Give a copy to someone who won't be in the conversation, with no client's facts on it. Ask them to push you aloud for a minute, or in three messages, and then to ask, "What's changed since you wrote it?" When the real push comes, give the reason once and watch the reply: does it meet your reason, or repeat the date? **Done means** your person can say, without the page, what you won't do and what would change it.

## Words to use

- **To check a date.** "What closes on Friday?" "Who set that date?"
- **To ask for the reason.** "I see the date. I don't see the reason yet."
- **To hold.** "I don't change that on the day I'm asked. You'll have my answer by [day]." "It's the same answer as Monday, for the same reason."
- **To pass it to its owner.** "That's [name]'s to tell. Shall I ask if you can talk?"
- **To sign less.** "I can put my name to [the smaller claim] now."
- **To push honestly.** "I'm pressing because I need this by [day]. You should know that."

### Phrases you will hear

- "Off the record": they won't quote you. Say only what you could stand behind if they did.
- "It's a no-brainer": they think it needs no thought. Ask what they weighed.

## When it backfires

**It's an emergency.** If the screen is dark and trucks are at the gate, waiting a day is also a decision. Choose, say what you chose on, and write it down afterward.

**They hold the power.** A limit can cost you the work. Put that cost on the page beforehand, offer the line you can sign, and ask for the rest to carry the decider's name. If the push is a threat or a demand to break the law, wording won't fix it; go to the end of *Difficult people*.

**The confidence covers a danger.** Someone else's secret is no reason to let people get hurt. Take it to whoever owns the facts, then to a formal route.

**The limit is wrong.** With no "I'd change this if", it's only stubbornness.

**Where a slow answer sounds like a no.** In some teams it does. Say the day you'll answer in your first sentence.

**Everything looks like pressure.** Told "that's a tactic", someone with a real date hears an accusation. Ask about the date.

**In a second language.** Speed is pressure too. "Please write that down for me. You'll have my answer tomorrow" is a complete reply.

# With a machine in the room

*In a dispute: check what it promises*

"Did you mean the last sentence?"

Otávio asked by phone, on Wednesday 21 October, and Mateo had to open his own message to find it.

That morning Otávio, who heads information security at Tolva's client Veldhaven, had questioned an agent's change to site two's doors. Mateo, who runs technology at Tolva, had asked an approved assistant for a polite reply that kept Tolva's position. He checked its eight facts, and all were right. The courteous ending had no fact to check: "Naturally, nothing will reach site two without your team's approval."

Mateo had read good manners. Otávio had read a new rule. The rule agreed on Monday's call with Claire, who runs operations there, was narrower. A Tolva engineer signs each agent's change, and Otávio's reviewers have one working day to stop it. Approval takes a reviewer's time on every change. Otávio has two reviewers, and one is off every Friday. Because of Mateo's sentence, Otávio had asked that one to come in.

Mateo could have said the assistant wrote it. Otávio hadn't asked that.

"No," Mateo said. "I checked eight sentences and sent nine. I can't promise your reviewers' time or change Monday's rule alone."

"Then what can you promise?"

"You have one working day, so we'll sign nothing on a Thursday, starting tomorrow. Then your review day is never a Friday. The signing is ours."

Otávio said it back, then phoned his reviewer, who got the Friday off again. Mateo wrote to Otávio and Claire himself: "This morning I promised an approval I had never decided on. I take it back. Monday's rule stands, and from tomorrow we sign nothing on a Thursday."

## What a fact check lets through

In a hard moment, the sentences that count most aren't facts. A no, an offer, a deadline, the next step in an apology: each commits somebody to something, on a day. A machine can word them all, as firmly or gently as you ask. A fact check lets every one through: a promise can only go wrong later.

> **Line to keep:** A promise can't be proofread, only kept.

Keeping one takes somebody who knows what was promised before and will be there when it falls due. The assistant wasn't on Monday's call, and nobody will phone it on Friday. They'll phone you, with a second question.

Decide before it drafts. Write what you've promised this person, what you'll do by when, and what you won't do. Hand that over with one instruction: `If this needs a deadline, an offer, a promise or a consequence I haven't given you, leave a blank and ask me.`

Then read the draft twice, once for facts and once for what it commits somebody to. There, ask the last question of the second-question test, *Who answers for it?*, and write a name and a day. If the name isn't yours, ask that person first.

## Practice: what the draft commits you to

**If you do only one, do this one.** **With a person.**

**Situation.** You're a data scientist. Twice this month, a change in another team's table made your forecast wrong. You ask an assistant for a firm message to their lead.

**First draft (what an assistant writes).** "The region codes changed again on Friday, and Monday's forecast left out the north. We require two weeks' notice of any change. Otherwise we will have to build our own copy and involve senior management."

**What's wrong.** After the facts, it commits you to a build and a complaint, and you've decided on neither. If the answer is "Go ahead," you have no next sentence.

**Better (by phone).**

You: "The region codes changed on Friday, and Monday's forecast left out the north. It's the second time this month. If there was a notice, I missed it. Could someone tell me two days before a code changes?"

Lead: "I can't always give you two days."

You: "Then tell me the same day, and I'll hold the forecast until I've checked it. Can you keep that one?"

**Your turn (10 minutes, then a conversation).** Get an assistant's draft of a message you're putting off. Underline whatever commits somebody. Cross out what you wouldn't do if they answered "Go ahead." Say the rest to the person, ask "What will you do now?" and watch for a promise you didn't make. **Done means** they can say what each of you will do, and by when.

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## When it backfires

If they've already acted on a sentence nobody decided, it may still bind your employer. Ask whoever signs before withdrawing it. If they hold the power, phone first.

Don't ask who wrote theirs. They sent it, so ask which point to answer first.

Don't cross out everything. A hard message that commits nobody is a complaint.

If you'd be uneasy telling them how an apology was made, write it yourself.

In a second language, a draft's courtesy can promise more than you hear: *we'd be happy to*, *rest assured*. Ask for a list of its promises in your first language.

## Record again

Write your point, then take sixty seconds on the same prompt: what you are working on, and why it matters. (Written form: three minutes without stopping.) Run the five checks from *Start here*, with *said back* done by someone who argued with you this month.

Last, list what the recording commits you to, and by when. Compare it only with your own earlier takes.

*Safe practice: record only yourself, or others only with their consent and within your employer's rules.*

# Part 6. What stays human

---

# Who does well now

Six habits gain value as drafts get cheap.

In November an assistant wrote Tolva, a small software company in Montevideo, three pages of rules for work done by agents. Seven people then met to turn them into one page they could keep. One person named the question. One asked who had looked. One followed a change to whoever would feel it next. One chose a path before anyone could know. One settled a quarrel. One replaced two words that would have been misread.

You'll hear that meeting; then each habit gets its name. All six are things people do, so you can start any of them this week.

## What a draft leaves out

Ask an assistant for a plan and it arrives whole: headings, reasons, a confident last line. Now look for what didn't arrive. Nothing in the text says whether this was the question worth answering. Nothing says who checked it, or what it sets off once it's running. It doesn't choose when the facts can't be known yet. It hasn't settled anything between the people who must live with it, and it can't tell whether they understood.

A colleague's draft can leave out the same six. What changed is the price. Spend a week on a draft and you'd meet some of them on the way. When it takes a minute, you meet them in the meeting.

You'll hear versions of this elsewhere, so ask what they rest on. People who work with these tools say that producing matters less than it did, and that directing and judging matter more (*reported*: testimony). Many of those who say so build the tools, sell them or teach them. I have an interest too: this book trains judgment. So set the testimony aside and test the reasoning. While people decide, sign and answer for results, somebody has to bring those six things to the table. I'd call that a *reasonable bet*, good reasoning on thin evidence, and I'd give it up if customers stopped asking for a name.

Can't an assistant supply them too? Ask, and it will often hand you ten questions, a page of side effects and two paths with their costs. Take them, because some will be ones you missed. They're drafts as well. Somebody still picks one question, phones the person the change will reach, and hears the engineer say yes.

> **Line to keep:** Answering for a draft means supplying what it left out.

## One meeting, one page

In October, a change written by an agent passed its tests, went in unread and put the wrong labels on warehouse doors for four hours. It changed Tolva's dock scheduler. The doors belonged to Tolva's largest client, Veldhaven, a food wholesaler run from Rotterdam. By November, Tolva's promises about agents sat in four places: the new agreement with Veldhaven, a written apology, a message of Mateo's, and Veldhaven's own access policy. An engineer joining that week would have found none of them.

On Wednesday 4 November, five days before Veldhaven's second site went live, seven people met by video to put them on one page. Tyler, who leads delivery, had given the notes to an assistant Tolva approved. It returned three pages and eleven headings. The first read: "All agent-generated work undergoes rigorous review by qualified personnel."

With Tyler were Tolva's founders: Lucía, the chief executive, and Mateo, who runs technology. Bianca, the product manager, was there, and so was an engineer who reads what the agents write. Diego, the engineer Tolva placed with Veldhaven, joined from Rotterdam. Naomi, the independent data consultant whose forecast feeds the scheduler, had been invited to find whatever the page couldn't support.

Two people who weren't there mattered as much: Claire, who runs operations at Veldhaven, and Otávio, who heads its information security. As you read, mark the line where each habit begins.

Tyler: "It's tidy, and I can't tell what it would have stopped in October. We have an hour. I'd like to leave with one page and one name."

Bianca: "Nobody has ever asked us how we work with agents. Claire asked why she'd believe our Friday list. Yesterday Hugo, who may buy from us, asked who picks up the phone. They both want to know what they can hold us to when an agent's work reaches their doors. Three of these headings answer that. I'd delete eight."

Lucía: "Delete them."

Naomi: "The first one left says every change is checked before it goes live. Did somebody look, or is that what we expect?"

Tyler: "I looked this morning. Seven changes since the rule began, seven names."

Naomi: "Then you've checked the names. What shows that the checking works?"

Mateo: "One test. In October one of Otávio's reviewers hid wrong-door faults in three of six changes. Our reader found two. The third needed tests she'd written herself, from the brief."

Naomi: "I'd print that: one test, one reader, two by reading and the third by her own tests. And the month you'll run it again. 'Rigorous' has to be right every night. This only has to be right about October."

Mateo: "January. Now follow one change through the page. The agents write faster than we can read, so everything waits at the reading. We sign nothing on a Thursday, so on Wednesday evening somebody will want the queue empty and will read faster. A fast read misses more. What it misses comes back as new changes, and the queue grows. The next people to feel it aren't on this call. Otávio's two reviewers would get our whole week on one Thursday."

Bianca: "What breaks it?"

Mateo: "When more is waiting than one day's reading, the agents stop. The reading never speeds up. I have four more effects. This is the one that hurts somebody."

The engineer: "So my name stops the agents. And when something gets through at four in the morning, it's my name again."

Nobody spoke. Tyler didn't move on.

Tyler: "What would your name be promising?"

The engineer: "That it won't break."

Tyler: "Does anybody here need it to promise that?"

Lucía: "No. I need to tell a customer what you read, what you ran and what you couldn't cover."

Tyler: "Then those three lines go under every name, and the phone at night stays where it is today. Could you put your name to that on Monday?"

The engineer: "If it goes on before the agent starts. I don't want to meet it when the work's done."

Tyler: "Mateo, is that yours to say yes to?"

Mateo: "It is. Yes."

Lucía: "Only Veldhaven has this in writing. We could keep it for them and move faster for everybody else, and nobody here knows which one the next customer will want. I choose one page for every customer, small changes included, until the December peak is over. It costs us speed. Two things would change it: a dock waiting on a change that's finished and unread, or a fault that gets past the reading and the tests. After either one, we meet the next morning."

Diego: "Then two words need work. On a dock, 'signed' is what happens to a delivery note: somebody counted the pallets and they were all there. The supervisors I work with would read 'signed' and stop looking. So the docks get 'read by', 'run against' and 'not covered'. Otávio's reviewers know what a signature covers, so they keep the word. And unless we say what a 'change' is, an agent will usually guess. Its first instruction should be: 'Put the reader's name in your first line. If you have no name, stop and ask.'"

Mateo said the page back, and Bianca corrected one word. The assistant had needed less than a minute for its three pages. The one page took fifty-two.

### The page they kept

- Before an agent starts, one engineer's name goes on the work. That engineer reads every change the agent writes, small ones included, runs it against tests a person wrote, and signs it.
- Under the signature: what was read, what was run, what wasn't covered. The docks see those three lines without the word "signed".
- The agent's first instruction: "Put the reader's name in your first line. If you have no name, stop and ask."
- At Veldhaven, the signature reaches the two reviewers one working day ahead, and one objection stops the change. We sign nothing on a Thursday, and changes run by day.
- A change that needs new access waits ten working days.
- When more is waiting than one day's reading, the agents stop.
- Every Friday, Claire gets the list of what went live, with the name of who read it.
- This rests on one test: six changes, three hidden faults. Reading found two; the reader's own tests found the third. We run it again in January.
- It holds until the December peak is over. A dock waiting on a finished, unread change, or a fault that gets past both, reopens it the next morning.
- Mateo answers for this page.

The next six sections take the habits one at a time: the line where each begins, how it sounds in other rooms, its trap and where you trained it. Each ends with a practice small enough for this week.

## The framer: what is the question?

The framer decides what the question is before anyone answers it. On the call, the habit begins at "Nobody has ever asked us". Bianca found one question under two real ones, and eight headings had nothing left to do. In April she copied the team's board into a report and let each reader pick a meaning. Hugo does it from the buyer's side: he read a polished proposal twice, and what he asked about was the phone.

**In a meeting.** "What will be different once we've answered this?" "I think the question is [this one]. Is that the one you asked?" On a sales call: "Before I price it, what happens on the day it works?"

**The trap.** Framing that never ends. You'll recognize it by "But is that really the question?", asked a third time while somebody waits. Frame once, then help answer.

**Built from** the point sentence and the listener sketch. Go back to *Know what you think*, *Who is listening*, *Questions and common ground*, *The brief* and *Saying no and pushing back*. Repeat *one no this week*.

### Practice: the question behind a request

Take a request you've already started on. Write the question it answers, then two others the same person might have meant. Send all three: "Which of these should I answer?" **Done means** the reply picks one, or gives you a fourth.

## The calibrator: how sure are we?

The calibrator says how sure we are, and tests a claim before the team acts on it. It begins at "Did somebody look?" Naomi didn't doubt Tyler. She separated what he'd checked, the names, from what nobody had shown yet, and gave the test its real size. In June her first report to Veldhaven held four hedges and no number. Claire's "Why would I believe the list?" is the same habit on the client's side.

**In a meeting.** "Who looked, and when?" "I'd act on this for [one thing]. For [the other], not yet." In a code review: "The tests pass. Who wrote them, and from what?"

**The trap.** Sizing everything, until the room leaves with five limits and no answer. The sign is "It depends" with nothing after it. Give the claim you'd act on first, then its limit.

**Built from** the sized claim and the second-question test. Go back to *How sure are you? Say that*, *The explanation*, *The update* and *Arguing well*. Repeat *one claim at its real size*.

### Practice: a number and its source

Find a number your team repeats without saying where it came from. Give ten minutes to three facts: who measured it, when, and on how many cases. Put them beside the number, where the team will see them. **Done means** somebody who wasn't there can say what it doesn't cover.

## The system reader: what does it set off?

The system reader asks what a change sets off after its first effect, and who feels it next. It begins at "Now follow one change". Mateo's first effect was the one everybody wanted: changes get read. He followed it to the constraint, around a loop, and out to two people who weren't on the call. In May he wrote three pages of true facts, all the same size. Now he had five effects and spoke about one. His remedy, to stop starting work while the queue is full, is an old one in software teams. In August, Otávio asked the same of a login: "What it can change. At which sites. How fast I can cut it off."

**In a meeting.** "Where will this wait?" "Who gets more work on the day we get less?" In planning: "If this goes first, who stands still?"

**The trap.** The map of everything, where the tenth arrow is as thick as the first and nothing ships. It sounds like "It's more complicated than that", and then stops there. Bring one effect, one person it reaches and one thing that breaks the loop.

**Built from** next-question order, asked of a change. Go back to *Give it a shape*, *The explanation*, *The meeting* and *The brief*. *Seeing the system* takes it further. Repeat *hear the plan first*.

### Practice: the next person

Pick one change that ships this week. Write its first effect, then the name of whoever feels it next. Ask that person, "What will you have to do differently on the day?" **Done means** one line in the change's note came from them.

## The strategist: which path?

The strategist chooses among paths when nobody knows the answer, and says what would change the choice. It begins at "Only Veldhaven has this in writing". Lucía named the faster path, said nobody could know, and chose. Then she said what the choice costs and which two events would reopen it. In May, her word for a date was "on track". Renata, Tolva's first investor, asked for the habit's second half in August: "How will I know, before the 28th, if the 28th is moving?"

**In a meeting.** "Nobody knows this yet. Until [day], I'd do [this]." "If we're wrong, what will we see first?" To an investor: "Here's the path we turned down, at its best."

**The trap.** Loving the decision. The sign arrives and the choice stays, because it has your name on it. The quieter form is calling every guess a bet, so that nothing you say can be wrong. Ask somebody else to watch for the sign.

**Built from** the preparation sheet and the sized claim. Go back to *How sure are you? Say that*, *Steady under pressure*, *The pitch*, *Negotiation* and *Pressure and how to resist it*. *Leading when nobody knows the answer* takes it further. Repeat *a page and a person*.

### Practice: a choice with an end date

Take a decision that's waiting for a fact nobody will have in time, and fill in: `Until [day], we [choice]. It costs us [cost]. If we see [sign], we [next step].` One filled in: "Until Friday the 27th, we answer every support message by hand. It costs us two mornings a week. If we see the same question five times, we write the page." Send yours to whoever has to live with it. **Done means** they can tell a third person what would change it.

## The problem-solver: what will hold?

The problem-solver takes a mess with people in it to a decision that lasts. It begins at "What would your name be promising?" Somebody kind could have soothed that engineer and moved on. Tyler asked, and the quarrel turned out to be about what a signature means. He took the yes from the person with the most to do, then checked whose condition it was to grant. He also left one subject off the page: how much to hand to agents at all. Lucía and Mateo had put that conversation off since July, and no page could hold it for them. In August, Tyler let a line about reading go into the notes with two names and no date.

Wesley, who runs procurement at Veldhaven, named a missing part the same way in October: "Your contract has a price for everything except being late."

**In a meeting.** "Who has to do the most if we agree to this?" "Is that yours to say yes to?" In a retrospective: "We've decided this before. What didn't we write down?"

**The trap.** Peace before the decision. Everybody nods, and the person with the work hasn't spoken. A second trap waits behind it: every quarrel gets sent to you, and people stop settling their own.

**Built from** sort first and the read-back. Go back to *Thinking on your feet*, *The meeting*, *Difficult people*, *Arguing well* and *Negotiation*. Repeat *one item, said back*.

### Practice: the decision that came back

Find something your team has decided twice. Ask the person with the most to do, "What did we leave out the first time?" Rewrite the decision with one name, a day and the missing part. **Done means** that person says it back, and a colleague who wasn't there can tell you what's new in it.

## The translator: what will they act on?

The translator carries meaning across a boundary intact: between disciplines, between a client and a team, between people and machines. It begins at "Then two words need work". Diego took the page's words to a dock, a security team and an agent, and asked what each would hear. Two of the three would have heard something else. In June he answered "It should be fine" and left the listener to supply the rest.

**In a meeting.** "When they read that, what will they do?" "What do you call it on your side?" On a client call: "I'll say it in your words, and you tell me if it's still true."

**The trap.** Becoming the only way across, so both sides bring you everything and stop asking each other. Or softening a sentence until it's easy to hear and no longer true. Leave them a word they share, and get out of the way.

**Built from** the observable version, the read-back and the working story. Go back to *The exact word*, *Listening people can feel*, *Story for people who think in systems*, *The brief*, *On the page* and *Across borders*. Repeat *one sentence you misheard*.

### Practice: the word they act on

Choose a message you sent this week to somebody outside your field. Ask them which word they'd act on, and what they'd do. Rewrite the sentence around their answer. **Done means** they tell you their next step, and it's the one you meant.

## What each owes the other five

Any one of the six, alone for an hour, would have ruined that meeting. Each habit has a debt to the rest.

- **The framer** owes them a question they can start on, and an hour when the framing stops.
- **The calibrator** owes them a claim they can act on today, limit included.
- **The system reader** owes them the one effect that matters, with a name beside it.
- **The strategist** owes them the best case for the path not taken.
- **The problem-solver** owes them the disagreement, out loud, before the agreement.
- **The translator** owes each side the other's real words, including the unwelcome ones.

When a meeting stalls, look for the debt nobody has paid. It may be yours.

## Practice: the last two weeks

**If you do only one, do this one.** It takes fifteen minutes, your calendar and your sent messages from the last two weeks. Nothing here is scored, and no row gives you a type.

| Habit | Look for |
|---|---|
| The framer | A question you named that changed what got worked on |
| The calibrator | A claim you tested, or sent with its basis and its limit |
| The system reader | A person you warned, because a change would reach them next |
| The strategist | A choice made without knowing, with the sign that would change it |
| The problem-solver | A disagreement that ended in a name and a day, and still holds |
| The translator | A sentence you changed for one listener, who then did what you meant |

1. For each row, write one dated thing you said or wrote that somebody else could confirm. If you can't find one, leave it blank.
2. Ask one colleague: "In the last two weeks, when did something I said change what you did?" Put the answer in its row. If it surprises you, trust it over your own list: I'd call that row the habit you're growing into.
3. Read the blanks. Some belong to a teammate, and some weeks don't call for them. Circle the one whose absence cost somebody something, and put its practice in next week's calendar.

**Done means** your colleague could check every entry against a day, and one practice from this chapter has a date.

## When it backfires

- **The names become labels.** "He's a system reader" excuses him from deciding, and "I'm not a strategist" excuses you. Use the names for acts: "Who's framing this?"
- **Somebody senior holds the question.** Reframing a chief executive's question in public can sound like a refusal to answer. Answer first, then ask: "Is it this you need, or [the other question]?" Size their number in private, or in writing. If the choice is theirs, bring two paths and what would change each.
- **You work alone.** Six habits are a lot to hold about your own draft on a Tuesday night. Borrow one: a customer who'll tell you what they heard, or a friend who asks what would change your mind.
- **A room that reads questions as doubt.** Say what the question is for: "I ask so we can ship it."
- **In a second language.** Each habit fits in one short question, so prepare the one this meeting needs and write it at the top of your notes. If the talk moves too fast, put it in the chat.
