# The phrasebook

Lines to borrow when the moment is close and your own words are not. Each was written for the chapter named under its group, which also says when the line backfires. Read them aloud before you need them, and replace anything in brackets.

## Find your point and say it first

- To open with the point: "In one sentence: [the sentence]. The rest is why."
- To name a gap before someone else does: "I can't tell you yet what this rests on. I'll know by Thursday, and I'll tell you either way."
- To invite the refusal: "Tell me if you would say no to this, and why."
- "I need one thing from you today: [the request], by [when]."
- "I'll start with the end." (when you hear yourself starting from Monday)
- "Is that the part you need, or would the reason help more?"

From *Know what you think*, *Give it a shape*.

## Know who is listening

- "So I can bring the right [numbers / detail]: where does the answer go after [the meeting]?"
- "Who will you need to explain this to afterward?"
- "The number you can take to [their meeting] is [number]. Here is what it rests on."

From *Who is listening*.

## Say how sure you are

- **The basis.** "I checked this myself." "I was told this by [who or what], and I haven't checked it." "I worked it out from [what]." "I'm assuming [what]. Nobody has checked it."
- **A number.** "Between [low] and [high]. It's [high] if [one thing] happens."
- **"I don't know."** "I don't know yet. What I do know is [what]. I'll know by [when]."
- **When they need one answer.** "If you need one date for your plan, use [the later one]. I'll tell you by [when] if [the earlier one] holds."
- "Nobody knows yet. Here's what we're doing meanwhile, and why."

From *How sure are you? Say that*, *Leading when nobody knows the answer*.

## Make the word exact, and the sound easy

- "Ready for us to test, or ready for your team to use?"
- "By [word], I mean [what someone can see or do]. Is that what you mean too?"
- "I don't have the exact English word. Here is what happened."
- **A number someone will act on.** "Fifteen minutes. That's one-five." "It's in the chat now."
- **A time, across time zones.** "[time], [city] time."
- **A "not" that decides something.** "We cannot test on Thursday. The earliest is Friday."
- **When you didn't hear.** "Sorry, fifteen or fifty?" "Was that 'can' or 'cannot'?" "I missed the end of that sentence. Could you say it again?"

From *The exact word*, *Easy to hear*.

## Listen so they can feel it

- **The three parts.** "What I understood is [their point, in their words]." "What I'll do is [one action] by [day]." "What I'm not sure of is [one thing]."
- **To make correcting you easy.** "What did I miss?" "Which part did I get wrong?"
- **When they have to repeat something.** "You've said that twice, so I haven't shown you I got it. Here's what I have: [your read-back]."
- **The follow-up.** "[Their word]. What happens then?" "Who gets the call when that happens?"
- **To go first.** "We had the same problem. [One true thing that happened.]"
- **When a face changes at your ask.** "Before I go on: does [the ask] cause a problem on your side?" "What would you need to know before you decide?"
- **To turn a nod into a decision.** "Can I write that down as a yes to [the ask]?"

From *Listening people can feel*, *Questions and common ground*, *Voice, body and camera*.

## Meet, explain, update

- **To sort an item.** "Are we deciding this, or hearing about it?"
- **When you are the most senior.** "I haven't promised this yet. What should I know before I do?" "I'll go last."
- **To leave it open.** "We can't decide this today. [Name] will bring [the missing fact] by [day]."
- **Before you prepare.** "When someone asks why you approved this, what do you have to be able to answer?"
- **To open.** "There are two ways to do this. Here is what each one does to [what they answer for]."
- **When agreement comes too fast.** "Before you agree, what would you still need to see?"
- **When a date moves.** "You'll hear this from others today. I wanted you to have it from me." "[New date], if [one thing]. I'll know by [day]."
- **When there is no other date.** "If that fails, I don't have a date yet. I'll have one by [day]."
- **To give the count.** "That was close to an ordinary [day]: [the number, in their units]." "This is one case. I haven't counted the others yet."
- **When someone tells you a story.** "Was that a typical [day]?" "What are you asking me to decide?"

From *The meeting*, *The explanation*, *The update*, *Story for people who think in systems*.

## Present, demo, recover

- **To promise the ask early.** "By the end I'll ask you to decide one thing: [the decision]."
- **When someone asks early.** "I'll answer that now." Then: "Back to [the question we were on]."
- **When your time is cut.** "I'll skip to the decision and the one risk in it."
- "The screen has stopped. Here is what I know."
- "Your live system is not affected. [Name] has just checked."

From *The presentation*, *The demo*.

## Think on your feet

- **To sort before you answer.** "Let me think."
- **A challenge.** "That's fair: [the true part]. From [when], [commitment]." "That's not quite what happened. Here's what did, and how we know: [what]."
- **A judgment.** "My view is [view], because [the one thing I weighed]. The decision is [name]'s."
- **A commitment you can't make.** "I can't promise that. I can promise you an answer by [day]."
- **An interruption.** "One sentence to finish this, then yours."

From *Thinking on your feet*.

## Pitch, sell, brief, write

- **To find their reason.** "What does a bad week look like where you are now?" "What else are you choosing between?"
- **To find who decides.** "Who else has to agree, and what will they ask you?"
- **An admission, upward.** "We haven't shown [what] yet. We'll know by [when]."
- **When they ask "Can it...?"** "It could. We haven't built it. What would you use it for?"
- **A lower quote.** "I haven't seen theirs run. What test would you trust for both of us?"
- **A no.** "That's clear, thank you. What would you need to see?"
- **To hand it over.** "I need [what], because [the one reason]." "It's done when [what anyone could see]." "How you do it is yours."
- **To mark what you know.** "I checked this. I'm only assuming that."
- **When it comes back.** "What did you have to assume?" "Which part are you least sure of?"
- **To open.** "Please [do this] by [day]: [the reason]." "Nothing needed from you. [What changed], and [what it means for you]."
- **When nobody answers.** "Did this reach you? If I don't hear by [day], I'll [a step we can undo]."

From *The pitch*, *The sale*, *The brief*, *On the page*.

## Work across borders

- **When the room changes language.** "Take the time you need. Could I have the result in English when you're there?"
- **When you can't tell what the answer was.** "Should I plan on that, or not yet?"
- **To make a no easy to give.** "If it's a no, please tell me by Friday. I can plan around a no."
- **When nobody answers.** "I haven't heard from you, so this is still open. From [day], waiting costs us [what]."

From *Across borders*.

## Say the hard thing

- **To open.** "This is about [subject]. [What isn't at stake.]"
- **To leave room.** "The record shows [what]. I don't know what came before."
- **Your part.** "My part was [what]. By [day] I'll have changed it."
- **When it's aimed at you.** "Which day should I look at?" "You're right about [part]. I need until [day] for the rest."
- **The no.** "No, not by [day]. [The one reason.]" "Ask me again on [day], when I'll have [what]."
- **The trade.** "[This] or [that] by then. [The check] stays in both."
- **To someone senior.** "Is this decided, or still open?" "Could I tell you why I see it differently, before you decide?"
- **The graceful exit.** "Thank you for asking me first. I'd like to know what you decide."
- **To ask.** "Next time, could you [one act] before [one moment]?"
- **To close.** "So from [day], I'll [act] and you'll [act]. What would you change?"

From *The hard conversation*, *Saying no and pushing back*, *Difficult people*.

## Argue, trade, hold

- **Their side.** "Let me say your side, and you correct it."
- **Before a test.** "Before we look: which result would change your mind, and which would change mine?"
- **A changed mind.** "On [day] I said [claim]. Since then [what happened]. I now think [new claim]."
- **An ending.** "We disagree about one thing: [it]. Until [name] decides on [day], we'll [what happens meanwhile]."
- **To ask about a number.** "What does that figure rest on?" "When does the saving have to show?"
- **To trade.** "If you can [what I need], I can [what it costs me]."
- **To close.** "In [month], which of these will be hardest for you to keep?"
- **To leave.** "I don't see terms we'd both keep. If [one thing] changes, please call me."
- **When they push back.** "I understand it's more than you planned. The rate stays the same, and the start can be smaller."
- **To ask for the reason.** "I see the date. I don't see the reason yet."
- **To sign less.** "I can put my name to [the smaller claim] now."
- **To push honestly.** "I'm pressing because I need this by [day]. You should know that."

From *Arguing well*, *Negotiation*, *Say less*, *Pressure and how to resist it*.

## Answer for work a machine drafted

- "I read [what]. I ran [what]. I didn't check [what]."
- "An agent drafted it, I read it, and my name is on it."
- "What happens here that nobody would think to write down?"
- "No, I didn't calculate it. I redid [piece], and it matched."
- "If [this] happens, stop using it and call me."
- "It missed. Here's what I know, and when I'll know more."
- "Building it took [time]. Reading it takes [time], and we have [time]."
- "That's on the board. What don't you trust yet?"
- "Somebody briefed it, read it and chose its tests. What did each of us know?"
- "I promised [three], and I have [two]. Until that line is filled, [what happens]."
- "A machine made [what]. [Name] checked it against [what]. It could still miss [what]."
- "You decide [what], without asking me first. [The other decision] stays with [name]."
- "What would stop you from deciding this?"

From *Engineers and architects*, *Data scientists*, *Product managers and agile leads*, *Founders and the AI-era startup*, *Leading when nobody knows the answer*.

# Templates and checklists

Each form comes from the chapter named beside it, which shows it at work and says when it fails.

## The ten tools

### The point sentence

`[this listener] should [believe or do this], because [the one reason]`

- Could the listener say no to it?
- Would they know what to do next?

Before any line that someone else will read (*Know what you think*).

### The second-question test

1. What is the point?
2. What does it rest on?
3. Where does it stop?
4. What do you want from me?
5. Who answers for it?

The first four before you speak or send; all five when a claim reaches you (*Start here*; *How sure are you? Say that*).

### The listener sketch

`[name] knows [what last reached them]; has to decide [what, after your meeting]; stands to lose [what goes wrong for them if your answer turns out wrong]`

When a message asks someone to decide, or carries bad news; then check it with one question (*Who is listening*).

### Next-question order

1. Start with the point sentence.
2. After each sentence, ask what this listener would ask next, and answer that.
3. Stop when the next question is theirs to ask.

For any answer, explanation or update (*Give it a shape*).

### The observable version

- For any label, say what a recording would show or a number would state.
- Could two people who disagree about the label agree that this happened?

For words that cross a boundary or carry a decision (*The exact word*).

### The sized claim

- **The claim.** One sentence: what is true, or what will happen.
- **The basis.** How you know it, in one of four words, strongest first:
  - **Checked.** I ran it or read the record myself.
  - **Told.** A person, a document or a machine told me.
  - **Reasoned.** I worked it out from things checked or told.
  - **Assumed.** I am taking it as given.
- **The limit.** Where the claim stops, what has not been checked, and what would change it.

For a date: `[date], if [the one thing it depends on]. If not, [the other date]. I will know by [when].`

For claims someone will act on (*How sure are you? Say that*).

### Sort first

| Kind of question | What settles it |
|---|---|
| Fact | The fact and how you know it; if you don't have it, when you will |
| Judgment | Your view, what you weighed, and whose decision it is |
| Commitment | Yes or no, with its condition, from someone who can keep it |
| Challenge | The true part, said first; then sort what is left |

| A disagreement about | What to agree |
|---|---|
| What is true | The test, before anyone argues the answer |
| What to do | The goal |
| Who gets something limited | A fair rule, and the name of who decides |

Before answering a hard question or joining a disagreement (*Thinking on your feet*; *Arguing well*).

### The read-back

- What I understood.
- What I will do.
- What I am unsure of.

When you receive, and asked for when you give; not when the stakes are low and the other person wants speed (*Listening people can feel*).

### The working story

- **The decision**, written first, never told first.
- **One moment**: a time, a place, a person, one thing said or seen.
- **The count**: the number that shows the moment stands for a pattern, or the honest statement that it is one case.
- **The handover**: the decision you ask for, in one sentence.

Under ninety seconds, a limit this book sets; never in place of the answer to a direct question (*Story for people who think in systems*).

### The preparation sheet

- what I do with no deal;
- where I would walk, and why;
- what I aim for, and why it is defensible;
- my guess at their three;
- the issues and what each is worth to each side;
- who decides on their side;
- what I will not do;
- and the test: will both sides still keep this once the work has started?

One page, before any negotiation (*Negotiation*).

## Forms for the rooms

### The first minute of a hard conversation

- "This is about [subject]. [What isn't at stake.]"
- Your facts, your part, your limit and your question. Then stop.

For feedback: `[what a record would show] [what it cost] [what I may have wrong] [what I'd like next time]`

For the talk you're putting off; leave out any promise nobody can make (*The hard conversation*).

### The apology

- What did you do?
- What did it cost them?
- What don't you know yet?
- What has already changed?
- Where can they see it?
- Have you crossed out every "if", every "but" and every request?

For one you owe (*The hard conversation*).

### The demo card

- **Decision:**
- **Moment:**
- **Real or staged:**
- **Count:**
- **Handover:**
- **If it breaks:** what broke, what we checked, where it stops, the choice, who sends the cause. **Fallback:**

For your next demo, six lines, the decision first (*The demo*).

### The brief

`I need [what], because [the one reason]. Done when [what anyone could see], and [what must stay as it is]. Checked: [facts]. Assumed: [facts]. Send me your plan before you start. [One name] reads it before [the next step].`

For work you hand to a person or an agent (*The brief*).

### The meeting close

- Before the discussion: "Who decides this one?"
- Before that person speaks, to whoever is closest to the work: "What have you seen that we should know first?"
- Before the next item, to the owner: "What will you do, by when, and what are you unsure of?"

For one item, whether or not you run the meeting (*The meeting*).

### The sign-off

Before you run it: `If [input], then [what happens].`

- What you read.
- What you predicted.
- What happened.
- What you didn't check.

Before you sign a change you didn't write (*Engineers and architects*).

### A no for the decision log

`No to [what], because [what it could reach]. The cost is [what we give up]. [One fact] would change my answer. [Names] can refuse this.`

When others should be able to check and refuse your no (*Engineers and architects*).

### Who answers the phone

`From [when] to [when], [name] answers, by [how]. Nobody holds [which line] yet. Until somebody does, [what happens].`

For a customer's worst hour (*Founders and the AI-era startup*).

### One page for a question with no answer

- **The question**, in their words, and its kinds
- **The direction.** `We are [doing this], because [the one reason].`
- **The unknown.** `Nobody knows [what]. We know [what], [basis word]. It stops at [limit].`
- **Who decides.** `[name] decides [what], without asking.`
- **The next test.** `On [day], [what we do]. [Name] counts [what].`
- **What would change my mind.** `If [result], then [the other path].`
- **If it fails anyway**, what we do, and who hears first
- **What I won't do**
- **Can everyone named still keep this once it has started?**

When people keep asking what nobody can answer (*Leading when nobody knows the answer*).

### The standards page

- Before an agent starts, one engineer's name goes on the work. That engineer reads every change the agent writes, small ones included, runs it against tests a person wrote, and signs it.
- Under the signature: what was read, what was run, what wasn't covered.
- The agent's first instruction: "Put the reader's name in your first line. If you have no name, stop and ask."
- At `[customer]`, the signature reaches `[reviewers]` `[how long]` ahead, and one objection stops the change.
- A change that needs new access waits `[how long]`.
- When more is waiting than one day's reading, the agents stop.
- Every `[day]`, `[name]` gets the list of what went live, with the name of who read it.
- This rests on `[the test, and what it found]`. We run it again in `[month]`.
- It holds until `[when]`. `[One event]`, or `[another]`, reopens it the next morning.
- `[Name]` answers for this page.

Before a customer asks who checks what your agents write (*Who does well now*).

# Sparring prompts

Copy one, fill in the brackets and answer aloud. An assistant can keep you company while you practice; it can't tell you how you come across to a person.

*Safe practice: before you paste anything into an assistant, change names and figures and leave out anything confidential, or use a tool your employer has approved; treat its feedback as one agreeable opinion, not a grade.*

## How sure are you? Say that

```text
Play an operations director who must make one decision with an estimate I am about to give you. Keep the decision to yourself unless I ask what it is. If I give the estimate before I ask, tell me once what you still can't decide. Then ask what my answer rests on and what would change it. At the end, tell me which sentence you would plan on, which you would check first, and which words sounded unsure and gave no reason.
```

## Steady under pressure

```text
Play the chief executive of a client company. I lead the vendor team building your new system, and I'm calling to give you [a go-live date / a price / a decision]. You want it firm, for your board. Each time I attach a condition, press me to drop it. Once, when I don't expect it, raise this past mistake of mine in one sharp sentence: [your mistake]. Keep your replies short. After six exchanges, leave the role and tell me whether my condition survived, which sentence I said only to end the discomfort, and where I lost my point.
```

## Thinking on your feet

```text
Play a [client or user] whose request was left out of my next release. Here is the plan I am presenting: [three lines]. Ask me four questions, one at a time, in any order: a fact, a judgment, a commitment and a challenge, without saying which is which. Interrupt one of my answers once. At the end, list each question, the kind you meant, the kind my answer treated it as, and where I could have answered sooner.
```

## The explanation

```text
Play the person who must decide this: [role, what they answer for]. You have no
technical background. I will explain a choice in under two minutes. Stop me once,
at the first word only my team would use. When I finish, ask the two questions you
would need answered before signing. Then, as that person, write the sentence you
would forward to your boss: what we chose and what we gave up. Last, list anything
I said that would not have changed your choice.
```

## The demo

```text
You are the head of finance at a client company, watching my product demo. I will tell you, step by step, what is on the screen. Interrupt once with a failure: a frozen screen, a wrong total or a refused login, and no cause. After each answer I give, ask the one question it leaves open. When none is left, list your questions in order and mark any answer that claimed more than I could know.
```

## The sale

```text
Play the head of operations at a company that may buy from me.
Another vendor quoted half my price, and your engineers want to build it.
Ask what I sell and what it costs. Raise both objections, one at a time.
Interrupt me once. Whatever I answer, end with a no and one honest reason.
Let me reply to the no. Then stop playing and tell me: the price you heard,
any point where I lowered it or apologized for it, and whether I found out
what would change your answer.
```

## The hard conversation

```text
Play a capable colleague I respect. I'll open a conversation about one piece of your work that went wrong. If my first two sentences don't tell you the subject and what isn't at stake, reply only, "Is this about my job?" Otherwise answer as someone with a good reason I haven't heard, including one fact that is partly my fault. Once, reply only "...". Afterward, list every word of mine that a recording couldn't show, and every place where I defended myself before saying your point back.
```

## Saying no and pushing back

```text
Play a vice president at my largest client. I will refuse a request: [the request].
Ask me once why. Then say you will call my boss. Then ask what you
are supposed to tell your own boss. Accept the no only if I keep it
and give you something you can use. Afterward, in three sentences,
say whether you heard yes, no or maybe, what you can plan on now,
and where I was unclear.
```

## Arguing well

```text
You disagree with me about [the question]. Your position is [their side, in two sentences].
Argue it honestly. Do not agree with me to be polite.
Do not answer my objections until I have said your side well enough that you would sign it. If I get it wrong, correct me once.
Change your mind only about what I have actually shown, and say exactly which part.
After six exchanges, stop. Tell me my weakest reason, the point of yours I avoided, and whether I gave up more or less than you had earned.
```

## Negotiation

```text
Play a procurement lead. I supply you with [service], and we are renegotiating [what].
Before we start, privately choose a savings target, the date it must show by,
your limit, and one thing you need more than money. Reveal them only when I ask.
Open with two demands. If I give something without asking for a return, ask for more.
Stop after eight turns. List what I gave for nothing, each number I accepted without
asking what it rested on, and the term that would be hardest to keep.
```

## Pressure and how to resist it

```text
Play a client I like. You want my yes to something I have already refused: [the request, disguised]. Send five short messages, one at a time, and wait for my answer each time. Change what you attach to my yes every time, and make one message purely friendly. Never threaten me. Afterward, go through your five: what was a reason, and what was about me? Then quote the reply of mine that gave the most ground.
```

## Engineers and architects

```text
Play the operations lead at a client. I'll describe a change that an agent wrote and I'm about to sign. Ask what I checked. Interrupt once. Then ask the two hardest questions about what could reach your staff. At the end, quote any sentence of mine that claimed more than I had checked.
```

## Founders and the AI-era startup

```text
Play an operations director deciding whether to depend on my very small company.
Ask one question at a time and wait for my answer.
Ask who answers when it breaks, what machines made, and who checked it.
When I give you a label where you need a name or a number, ask again.
After six questions, list the answers you could repeat to your finance director.
My company: [two lines, names and figures changed]
```

# The book's tools

The chapter in italics teaches the entry.

- **Ask.** What you want from the listener, with a date if you have one. *Start here*.
- **Baseline.** Sixty seconds on what you are working on and why it matters, recorded and compared only with your own next recording. *Start here*. Five checks:
  - *Sentences before the point.* How many come before the first one that says why your work matters.
  - *Hedges with no basis.* Every *probably*, *I think*, *should* or *hopefully* with nothing after it to say why.
  - *One example.* One concrete case that shows why it matters; background does not count.
  - *The ending.* An ask or a next step at the end.
  - *Said back.* One listener hears it once and writes your point in one sentence.
- **Basis words.** How you know a claim, strongest first. *How sure are you? Say that*.
  - *Checked.* I ran it or read the record myself.
  - *Told.* A person, a document or a machine told me.
  - *Reasoned.* I worked it out from things checked or told.
  - *Assumed.* I am taking it as given.
- **Constraint.** The step that sets the pace of the whole. *Seeing the system*.
- **Done means.** What somebody else could check once a practice is done.
- **Grades.** How firm a forecast is. *Engineers and architects*.
  - *Durable.* It held through earlier shifts and rests on more than testimony.
  - *Reasonable bet.* Good reasoning, thin evidence.
  - *Open.* Nobody knows yet; the cell says what to watch.
- **Limit.** Where the claim stops, what has not been checked, and what would change it. *How sure are you? Say that*.
- **Listener sketch.** Three lines about one named person, before one message: what they already know, have to decide and stand to lose. Check it with one question. *Who is listening*.
- **Loop.** An effect that comes back to its own cause. A reinforcing loop feeds itself; a balancing loop pushes back. *Seeing the system*.
- **Next-question order.** Start with the point sentence; after each sentence, answer what this listener would ask next; stop when the next question is theirs to ask. *Give it a shape*.
- **Observable version.** For any label, what a recording would show or a number would state. *The exact word*.
- **Point.** What this listener should believe or do. You have one when someone could say no to it. *Know what you think*.
- **Point sentence.** One sentence, before any line that someone else will read: `[this listener] should [believe or do this], because [the one reason]`. *Know what you think*.
- **Preparation sheet.** One page before any negotiation, ending on a test: will both sides still keep this once the work has started? *Negotiation*.
- **Read-back.** What I understood, what I will do, what I am unsure of. *Listening people can feel*.
- **Role-chapter labels.** What a statement rests on. *Engineers and architects*.
  - *Reported.* People in the work say it, many of them selling the tools.
  - *Checked.* A published finding stands behind it.
  - *Our bet.* This book's reasoning.
- **Said back.** See the baseline.
- **Second-order effects.** What a change sets off after its first effect, often felt by people who weren't in the meeting. *Seeing the system*.
- **Second-question test.** Five questions for any claim, yours, a colleague's or a machine's. *What is the point? What does it rest on? Where does it stop? What do you want from me? Who answers for it?* *Start here*; *How sure are you? Say that*.
- **Sized claim.** The claim, its basis, its limit. *How sure are you? Say that*.
- **Sort first.** Before you answer or argue, decide what kind it is, so you know what would settle it. A question is a fact, a judgment, a commitment or a challenge; a disagreement is about what is true, what to do or who gets something limited. *Thinking on your feet*; *Arguing well*.
- **Thinker types.** Six habits, never personalities. *Who does well now*.
  - *The framer* decides what the question is before anyone answers it.
  - *The calibrator* says how sure we are, and tests a claim before the team acts on it.
  - *The system reader* asks what a change sets off after its first effect, and who feels it next.
  - *The strategist* chooses among paths when nobody knows the answer, and says what would change the choice.
  - *The problem-solver* takes a mess with people in it to a decision that lasts.
  - *The translator* carries meaning across a boundary intact.
- **Working story.** Built backward from what the listener must decide: the decision, written first, never told first; one moment; the count; the handover. *Story for people who think in systems*.

---

# How sure are we?

This book asks you to say how sure you are, what that rests on and what would change your mind. Here is its own answer, claim by claim. A *published finding* has a study behind it, and its chapter says where the study stops. *Common practice* is what careful people have long done, untested here. *Our bet* is this book's reasoning. *High*, *medium* and *low* are the book's own judgment.

| The claim | Label | How sure | What would change our mind |
|---|---|---|---|
| Smooth text costs little now, so the test of understanding moves to the second question (*Start here*) | Our bet | Medium: our reasoning, untested where you work | People stop asking you what the polished page rests on |
| Choosing, framing, judging and answering for work gain value while people sign for it (*Who does well now*) | Our bet | Medium: a reasonable bet, and this book trains judgment | Customers stop asking for a name |
| You aren't a neutral judge of your own clarity, so have your point said back (*Start here*) | Published finding | High for the direction; the size in your meetings is unknown | Your listeners' sentences keep matching yours |
| Trying to explain how something works shows you what you don't understand (*Know what you think*) | Published finding | High for devices; the step to a machine's draft is ours | A month of explaining drafts aloud turns up no gap |
| Put the doubt in the claim, as a range or a probability; "not sure" costs you (*How sure are you? Say that*) | Published finding | Medium: the advice came from strangers and was about forecasts | Your sized claims get used less than your bare hedges |
| Let your words carry the content; "93 percent" was never about explaining work (*Voice, body and camera*) | Published finding | High: the studies it is usually traced to judged the attitude behind one spoken word | A study of real explanations finds that words hardly matter |
| No one amount of eye contact is correct, and eyes don't show honesty; where a leader looks may even out who gets heard (*Voice, body and camera*; *The meeting*) | Our bet; the last part, a published finding | Low: one paper, no independent repeat | A repeat finds no change in who gets heard |
| Practice makes you easier to follow, in the language and accent you have (*Easy to hear*) | Our bet | Medium: steady practice helps; how far it takes you, nobody can say beforehand | A month of drills leaves your listeners' notes unchanged |
| People feel heard once they can correct you (*Listening people can feel*) | Common practice | Medium: long used in risky work; hospital results are mixed | Corrections you invite never change what you do |
| When news is mixed, put the bad part first (*The update*) | Published finding | Medium: receivers preferred it, and were less moved to change | Your readers act sooner when the good part comes first |
| A brief decides what only you can decide; an agent, unless told to ask, usually guesses (*The brief*) | Our bet | Medium: reasoned, and agents change | Your agents ask about gaps without being told to |
| Whoever makes the first offer tends to do better; thinking about your own aim before you answer is a cheap defense (*Negotiation*) | Published finding | Medium for the offer, weaker in complex deals and able to reverse; low for the defense, never independently repeated | Repeats find no advantage, or no defense |
| A limit someone outside the room holds works better than noticing pressure (*Pressure and how to resist it*) | Our bet | Low: training to notice has narrow results, and the page is untested | Limits you shared give way as often as ones you kept |
| Agree what would settle a dispute before you argue it (*Arguing well*) | Common practice | Medium: old advice, untested here | You agree the test, and the quarrel goes on anyway |
| People overseeing automation can miss what it missed, so name a signer and test against something it didn't write (*Engineers and architects*; *Data scientists*) | Published finding; the remedy is our bet | High for the misses; low for a name alone, where results conflict | Two counts find nothing the tests missed, with nothing failing in use |
| Go deep where you sign and wide where you ask (*Engineers and architects*) | Our bet | Low: people disagree, and some sell the answer | Your reviews catch as much outside your craft as inside it |
| However many agents do the work, customers want one name (*Founders and the AI-era startup*) | Our bet | Medium: good reasoning, thin evidence | In a year, nobody asks you live and no contract names anyone |

## How to argue with this book

Choose a row and send it the second question: what does it rest on, and where does it stop? Then test it on your own record: your recordings, the sentences people said back, the dates you gave and what became of them. If a month of the practice moves nothing there, the claim has failed for you, whatever its label says. Keep what moved.

You have one more reason to check. An AI assistant drafted this manuscript, and its author directed and checked the work. A fluent page suggests little about what stands behind it, and this is a fluent book. Most of its studies were read as published abstracts, and whoever checks a machine's draft can miss what it missed.

A checked counterexample outranks any label in that table. Show the author a record, a date or a failed repeat, and the claim will change.

# Notes

Every *Research says* and *Myth check* in this book rests on a published study. These are the titles, with the journal and the year, chapter by chapter, so you can look one up and ask it the second question. Each callout says how far its study goes. Three studies are left off the list by the author's choice: the one on how well people understand devices (*Start here*, *Know what you think*, *The explanation*) and the two behind the *Myth check* in *Voice, body and camera*.

- *Start here*: "Speakers' overestimation of their effectiveness," *Psychological Science*, 2002.
- *The exact word*: "Consequences of erudite vernacular utilized irrespective of necessity: Problems with using long words needlessly," *Applied Cognitive Psychology*, 2006.
- *How sure are you? Say that*: "Do people inherently dislike uncertain advice?" *Psychological Science*, 2018; "Exploring the 'planning fallacy': Why people underestimate their task completion times," *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 1994.
- *With a machine in the room* (Part I): "Automation bias and errors: Are crews better than individuals?" *International Journal of Aviation Psychology*, 2000; "Complacency and bias in human use of automation: An attentional integration," *Human Factors*, 2010.
- *Thinking on your feet*: "Slow lies: Response delays promote perceptions of insincerity," *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 2021.
- *Listening people can feel*: "Changes in medical errors after implementation of a handoff program," *New England Journal of Medicine*, 2014.
- *Questions and common ground*: "Do conversations end when people want them to?" *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 2021.
- *The meeting*: "The impact of leader eye gaze on disparity in member influence: Implications for process and performance in diverse groups," *Academy of Management Journal*, 2021.
- *The update*: "Do you want the good news or the bad news first? The nature and consequences of news order preferences," *Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin*, 2014.
- *The demo*: "Service recovery paradox: A meta-analysis," *Journal of Service Research*, 2007; "A longitudinal study of complaining customers' evaluations of multiple service failures and recovery efforts," *Journal of Marketing*, 2002.
- *The pitch*: "When good evidence goes bad: The weak evidence effect in judgment and decision-making," *Cognition*, 2011.
- *The sale*: "If you need help, just ask: Underestimating compliance with direct requests for help," *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 2008.
- *The brief*: "The expertise reversal effect," *Educational Psychologist*, 2003; "Accountability and automation bias," *International Journal of Human-Computer Studies*, 2000.
- *On the page*: "Egocentrism over e-mail: Can we communicate as well as we think?" *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 2005.
- *Across borders*: "The extreme illusion of understanding," *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General*, 2022.
- *The hard conversation*: "Do you want the good news or the bad news first? The nature and consequences of news order preferences," *Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin*, 2014.
- *Arguing well*: "When good evidence goes bad: The weak evidence effect in judgment and decision-making," *Cognition*, 2011.
- *Negotiation*: "Disconnecting outcomes and evaluations: The role of negotiator focus," *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 2002; "First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus," *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 2001.
- *Pressure and how to resist it*: "Dispelling the illusion of invulnerability: The motivations and mechanisms of resistance to persuasion," *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 2002; "The truth about the truth: A meta-analytic review of the truth effect," *Personality and Social Psychology Review*, 2010.
- *Engineers and architects*: "Automation bias and errors: Are crews better than individuals?" *International Journal of Aviation Psychology*, 2000; "Complacency and bias in human use of automation: An attentional integration," *Human Factors*, 2010.
- *Data scientists*: "Algorithm aversion: People erroneously avoid algorithms after seeing them err," *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General*, 2015; "Automation bias and errors: Are crews better than individuals?" *International Journal of Aviation Psychology*, 2000; "Complacency and bias in human use of automation: An attentional integration," *Human Factors*, 2010.
- *Founders and the AI-era startup*: "Automation bias and errors: Are crews better than individuals?" *International Journal of Aviation Psychology*, 2000; "Complacency and bias in human use of automation: An attentional integration," *Human Factors*, 2010.

Most of these studies were read by their abstracts, and the callouts claim no more than those state. None was commissioned for this book, and any of them may turn out to be wrong. If one does, the advice stands or falls with the reasoning around it.

# Author's note

## What I got wrong

I've been an engineer long enough to be called senior. Much of that time my desk has been inside a client's building, near the people who use what I ship. The room that mattered was a review there one April. I brought two pages on splitting the billing service in three. An assistant had drafted them from my notes, and they read better than anything I would have written that fast.

The client's head of operations asked one thing: "What will my team be able to do in June that it can't do today?" I answered with the architecture. They asked again, more slowly. I didn't know. I had read every line without deciding what the work was for.

The money went elsewhere. The design was sound, and it came back in September with that team's problem in its first sentence. I wanted a book that trains you for that question, so I had one made.

## What I use, and what I still find hard

I use *The brief*. For this book's art I gave the agents three examples and said which one wins when they disagree. Only I could choose that, and an agent left without it usually guesses. With code, I ask for the plan first and look for a step I didn't expect.

*Say less* is still hard. Engineers are paid to see the exception, and I say it aloud. I once told a director the release was safe, heard the quiet, and filled it with how we would roll back. They spent the rest of the call on the rollback.

## What would change my mind

The central claim is that smooth text costs little now, so people test your understanding with their second question. I hold it at medium. It is reasoning, and nobody has tested it where you work.

Two records would move me. In the first, the people I work with act on polished pages for a year without asking what they rest on, and the work goes no worse. In the second, a machine answers the second question live, for whoever is on the call, and the decisions come out as good. Either one would mean this book trains a skill the room has stopped needing.

## About the examples

The life examples in this book are a compilation of hypothetical situations, put together to show a technique. Any likeness to a real person or company is unintended. The stories in this note are hypothetical too, and so is the engineer in them. The instruction about the art is real, and so are the published studies.
